TL;DR: WaveLander: a hierarchical RL framework that decouples vertical landing decisions from low-level stabilization for UAVs landing on wave-disturbed platforms; shown robust, generalizable performance in simulation without explicit switching rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Landing UAVs on marine platforms is hard due to stochastic platform motion, time-varying attitude, and uncertain touchdowns; model-based methods need accurate prediction and online optimization, while end-to-end learning has high training costs and limited interpretability.

Method: A hierarchical control architecture where an RL policy maps platform-relative observations to a scalar vertical velocity reference, while a conventional low-level controller handles attitude stability and lateral tracking, effectively reducing the problem to a low-dimensional, timing-aware vertical landing control.

Result: Simulation with randomized wave-induced disturbances demonstrates robust landing performance and generalization to unseen disturbances, indicating the approach can recover marine UAVs without explicit switching logic.

Conclusion: Hierarchical RL can enable robust marine UAV landings by decoupling decision from stabilization, reducing control complexity, enabling smooth landings, and generalizing to unseen disturbances.

Abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) on wave-disturbed marine platforms remains challenging due to stochastic platform motion, time-varying platform attitude, and uncertain touchdown conditions. Existing model-based methods often require accurate motion prediction and online optimization, while end-to-end learning approaches may suffer from high training complexity and limited interpretability. This paper presents WaveLander, a hierarchical control framework via reinforcement learning (RL) that decouples vertical landing decision-making from low-level flight stabilization. The RL policy maps a compact platform-relative observation to a scalar vertical velocity reference, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains attitude stability and lateral tracking. This formulation reduces dynamic platform landing to a low-dimensional, timing-aware control problem and enables smooth landing behavior without explicit switching rules. Simulation results under randomized wave-induced platform motions show that WaveLander achieves robust landing performance and generalizes to unseen disturbance conditions, demonstrating the potential of hierarchical learning-based control for marine UAV recovery.

</details>


### [129] [Adaptive Companionship for Group-Following Robots: Handling Dynamically Changing Group Formations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01287)
*Cong-Thanh Vu,Yen-Chen Liu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An adaptive group-accompaniment method for social robots using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and an MPPI controller improves group companionship performance and safety, with natural social behavior as perceived by users.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Humans in groups lack fixed formations, making natural companionship challenging for robots. Existing methods struggle with dynamic group layouts and semantic understanding of group interactions; leveraging VLMs can provide semantic reasoning to infer companion positions, group dynamics, and social distances.

Method: Detect group members; create perceptual visual representations of the interaction space as input to a Vision-Language Model (VLM); use the VLM's semantic reasoning to determine companion positions and social dynamics; integrate with a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller to ensure stability and safety during accompaniment.

Result: Experimental evaluation across five scenarios shows 15% higher success rate and 25% lower collision rate versus baselines; user study indicates companionship behaviors are perceived as natural and socially appropriate.

Conclusion: The VLM-based adaptive group-accompaniment approach with MPPI enables effective, natural, and safe robot companionship in dynamic group settings, demonstrating the feasibility of semantic reasoning for social navigation in robots.

Abstract: Accompanying a group of humans is an essential aspect of developing human-like social cognition in robots. However, human groups typically do not follow fixed formations, which poses significant challenges for robots in maintaining natural companionship behaviors. In this paper, we propose an adaptive group-accompaniment method for social robots based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), leveraging their semantic reasoning capabilities to infer companion positions, maintain social distances, and understand group dynamics. The members of the group are first detected, and a perceptual module generates visual representations of the interaction group space as input to the VLM, which is then combined with a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) controller to ensure stability and safety. Experimental evaluations across five scenarios show that the proposed method enables robots to accompany the group effectively, demonstrating a 15\% improvement in success rate and a 25\% reduction in collision rate compared to baseline approaches. Additionally, a user study indicates that the generated companionship behaviors are perceived as natural and socially appropriate.

</details>


### [130] [The Three Dimensions of ROS 2 Middleware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01304)
*Sanghoon Lee,Taehun Kim,Angelo Corsaro,Kyung-Joon Park*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A survey of ROS 2 middleware (DDS, Zenoh) framing architectural limits in Space, Time, and State. It analyzes discovery, data exchange, and state management, reveals trade-offs under constrained wireless conditions (space abstraction vs. temporal guarantees; state continuity vs. overhead), and proposes a principled roadmap for robust, scalable middleware.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and quantify the fundamental architectural limits of robot middleware under dynamic wireless environments and to provide a framework for analyzing trade-offs among spatial, temporal, and state dimensions.

Method: Systematic literature review and conceptual framing. The authors define three structural dimensions—Time (temporal predictability for control loops), Space (spatial abstraction from topology for modular deployment), and State (contextual continuity despite dynamic node participation and intermittently connected devices). They analyze middleware architectures (discovery, data exchange, state management) and categorize existing implementations and studies by the trade-offs among these dimensions.

Result: The paper organizes.middleware research around the Space–Time–State trade-offs, highlighting that spatial abstraction can mask network variability and weaken temporal guarantees, while mechanisms for state continuity add computational/network overhead that competes with time-critical communications. It identifies gaps in current modeling/analysis approaches and synthesizes architectural patterns, outlining a roadmap for robust and scalable middleware architectures.

Conclusion: A principled research roadmap is offered, emphasizing architectural patterns and improved modeling/analysis to enable robust, scalable ROS 2 middleware under dynamic, resource-constrained wireless environments.

Abstract: ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2) has emerged as the de facto standard for modern robot software development, with middleware implementations such as the Data Distribution Service (DDS) and Zenoh forming the core infrastructure for distributed robotic communication. Despite their architectural flexibility, these middleware systems exhibit structural limitations, particularly under dynamic and resource-constrained wireless environments. This paper presents a systematic survey of ROS 2 middleware and introduces a conceptual framework to examine its architectural limits through three structural dimensions required by distributed robotic systems, namely Space, Time, and State. We first provide a structured analysis of middleware architecture and operational dynamics, including discovery, data exchange, and state management mechanisms. Building on this foundation, we formalize Time as temporal predictability for control loops, Space as spatial abstraction from physical topology to enable modular deployment, and State as contextual continuity despite dynamic node participation and intermittent connectivity. Through a comprehensive review of existing implementations and prior studies, we organize middleware research according to the structural trade-offs that arise among these dimensions. Under constrained wireless conditions, spatial abstraction can obscure network variability and weaken temporal guarantees, while mechanisms that preserve state continuity introduce computational and network overhead that competes with time-critical communication. These interactions reveal structural trade-offs that characterize the practical limits of contemporary robot middleware. By synthesizing architectural patterns and identifying gaps in current modeling and analysis approaches, this survey outlines a principled research roadmap for robust and scalable robotic middleware architectures.

</details>


### [131] [Neuro-Symbolic Safety Guidance for Vision-Language-Action Models via Constrained Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01378)
*William English,Hao Zheng,Rickard Ewetz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Neuro-symbolic safety guidance for flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enables predictive collision avoidance by correcting intermediate trajectory predictions with a minimum-norm constrained optimization during denoising; yields improved safety and task success on SafeLIBERO, especially for long-horizon tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address safety gaps in flow-matching VLA systems, which currently only prevent collisions from the robot's next action and react too late. The goal is predictive collision avoidance integrated into the trajectory generation process.

Method: Integrate a minimum-norm constraint-based safety correction into the iterative denoising steps of neural flow matching. The safety module enforces symbolic constraints on predicted trajectories, enabling corrections during trajectory generation to prevent collisions before they occur.

Result: On SafeLIBERO, the approach achieves 82.8% collision avoidance and 81.6% task success, outperforming single-step methods by 6.3 percentage points in collision avoidance and 19.8 points in task success, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks where distribution shift is pronounced.

Conclusion: A neuro-symbolic safety guidance mechanism can transform reactive safety into predictive collision avoidance for flow-matching VLA models, improving reliability on longer-horizon tasks and under distribution shift.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated promising generalization capabilities across robotic manipulation tasks, yet their real-world deployment remains limited by the lack of effective safety measures. Specifically, existing safety measures only prevent collisions caused by the robot's next action. In this paper, we propose a neuro-symbolic safety guidance mechanism for flow matching based VLAs that enables predictive collision avoidance. Flow matching based VLAs determine the next actions by predicting a trajectory (a sequence of actions) through an iterative neural flow matching process. Our method formulates safety enforcement as a minimum-norm constrained optimization problem that corrects safety violations during the denoising process of noisy intermediate trajectory predictions. By analyzing predicted trajectories and applying corrections during iterative denoising, our approach anticipates collisions before they become unavoidable. This interleaving of symbolic constraint satisfaction with neural trajectory generation enables predictive collision avoidance rather than reactive intervention. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, our method achieves 82.8% collision avoidance and 81.6% task success, a 6.3% and 19.8% improvement respectively over single-step methods, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks where compounding distribution shift is most pronounced. Video demonstrations of our approach are included on our project page at https://willenglish.tech/SafetyGuidedFlowMatching/.

</details>


### [132] [CommonRoad-Game: A Human-in-the-Loop Simulation Framework for Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01382)
*Yunfei Bi,Youran Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CommonRoad-Game is a lightweight, real-time, human-in-the-loop simulation framework integrated with CommonRoad to enable deterministic multi-agent testing of motion planners and human driving behaviors with logs and reproducible scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of existing simulators (dataset-based, poor real-time human interaction, weak integration with autonomous driving ecosystems, and heavy computation) by enabling fast prototyping and interactive evaluation.

Method: Develop multi-threaded architecture with synchronization between simulation time and wall-clock time; scenario generation module that records logs; integration with CommonRoad; supports multi-agent simulation and interaction between autonomous and human-driven vehicles.

Result: Demonstrates stable temporal synchronization, scalability to multiple agents, and seamless integration with CommonRoad-compatible motion planners; publicly available code at GitHub.

Conclusion: CommonRoad-Game provides a practical, efficient platform for systematic testing of motion planners in human-in-the-loop scenarios, enabling reproducible experiments and analysis of human driving behavior.

Abstract: Motion planning algorithms should be evaluated in human-in-the-loop environments to ensure they produce safe and efficient behaviors during interactions. However, existing simulation platforms often rely on recorded datasets, lack dedicated interfaces for real-time human interaction, or remain weakly integrated with an autonomous driving ecosystem. Moreover, many human-in-the-loop simulators are computationally intensive by design, making them less suitable for rapid prototyping and flexible experimentation in early-stage autonomous driving research. To address these limitations, we present CommonRoad-Game, a lightweight human-in-the-loop simulation framework tightly integrated with the CommonRoad platform, focusing on the systematic testing of motion planners with human participation and the analysis of human driving behaviors in interactive scenarios. We introduce a multi-threaded architecture with a robust synchronization mechanism that aligns simulation time with wall-clock time, enabling deterministic and temporally consistent interaction between autonomous and human-driven vehicles. In addition, the framework provides a scenario generation module that records driving logs, allowing diverse and reproducible test cases to be constructed from human-in-the-loop experiments. Experimental results demonstrate that CommonRoad-Game achieves stable temporal synchronization, supports scalable multi-agent simulation, and seamlessly integrates CommonRoad-compatible motion planners to generate interactive driving scenarios. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunfei-Bi8/CommonRoad-Game.

</details>


### [133] [BIFROST: Bridging Invariant Feature Representation for Observation-space Sim2Real Transfer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01410)
*Yunfu Deng,Josiah P. Hanna*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: BIFROST learns a cross-domain bisimulation-based shared history encoder to map equivalent long-term behavior from paired sim/real sequences into nearby latent states, enabling zero-shot sim2real transfer of policies trained in simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is an underlying shared structure between simulated and real task dynamics; current methods address gaps separately, which may miss cross-domain commonalities. Exploiting this shared structure from raw observations can enable zero-shot transfer.

Method: Train a shared history encoder on paired cross-domain data using a cross-domain bisimulation loss; ensure observation-action sequences that produce similar long-term outcomes are encoded close across domains; train policies in simulation over these latent states and deploy zero-shot to real-world; evaluated on sim2sim visual navigation, sim2real contact-rich manipulation, and visual servoing with both visual and dynamics gaps.

Result: BIFROST achieves effective transfer where domain adaptation and co-training baselines fail, demonstrating zero-shot transfer under both visual and dynamics domain gaps across the studied tasks.

Conclusion: Cross-domain bisimulation-based shared representations can capture task structure common to simulation and reality, enabling zero-shot sim2real transfer; applicable to other domains with paired cross-domain data, though data requirements and representation capacity may constrain performance.

Abstract: Sim2real transfer for robot policy learning suffers due to mismatch between simulation and reality. Existing methods typically address each gap in isolation through separate adaptation modules, which are composed or layered when both gaps coexist. Yet the basis for attempting sim2real in the first place is that there is shared structure between a task in simulation and reality, where equivalent actions from equivalent configurations produce equivalent long term outcomes regardless of domain specific differences in rendering or physics. In this paper, we study whether we can identify and exploit this shared structure from raw observations to train a policy that enables zero shot transfer. We introduce BIFROST, which learns a shared history encoder on paired cross-domain data via cross-domain bisimulation objective: observation-action sequences leading to equivalent long-term behavior are mapped to nearby latent states, regardless of domain. Policies trained on these latent states in simulation transfer zero-shot to reality. We provide empirical evidence on sim2sim visual navigation and sim2real contact rich manipulation task and visual servoing task that BIFROST achieves effective transfer where domain adaptation and co-training baselines fail under both visual and dynamics domain gaps.

</details>


### [134] [SE(2) Navigation Mesh](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01454)
*Shuyang Shi,Kaixian Qu,Changan Chen,Ines Kast,Yuntao Ma,Marco Hutter*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces SE(2) NavMesh, a yaw-aware polygonal representation of traversable space for ground robots, with online updates from streaming point clouds and a novel ASA pathfinding that optimizes position and heading.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional representations either lack explicit traversability structure (point clouds, occupancy maps), are computationally heavy (dense meshes), or assume yaw-invariant NavMeshes unsuitable for constrained, non-circular robots.

Method: Define SE(2) NavMesh as polygons parameterized by pose (x, y, θ); evaluate traversability using footprint masks; build a graph with yaw-specific layers and translational/rotational connections; introduce ASA pathfinding—A*-based search augmented with string-pulling to optimize both position and heading; provide an online, incremental update mechanism from streaming point clouds during ongoing geometry reconstruction.

Result: Simulations show SE(2) NavMesh captures >50% more traversable area than classical NavMeshes; ASA-based planning outperforms sampling-based baselines in constrained settings; real-world experiments demonstrate real-time online generation and successful navigation across diverse environments.

Conclusion: SE(2) NavMesh delivers a richer, orientation-aware navigation representation that enables efficient planning for non-circular robots, with real-time online updates validated in both simulation and physical robot trials.

Abstract: Global navigation for ground robots in complex multi-level environments requires representations that accurately capture traversable regions while enabling efficient path planning. Current approaches present key limitations: Point clouds and volumetric occupancy maps lack explicit surface structure for traversability estimation, whereas direct pathfinding on dense triangle meshes is computationally prohibitive. Navigation meshes mitigate these challenges through polygonal abstraction of the underlying mesh, but assume yaw-invariant traversability, rendering them unsuitable for non-circular robots in constrained spaces. We propose SE(2) Navigation Mesh (SE(2) NavMesh), a polygonal representation of traversable regions that encodes yaw-dependent traversability. Our method evaluates traversability using footprint masks and constructs a graph over yaw-specific layers with explicit translational and rotational connectivity. Grounded in this representation, we develop an A*-String Pulling-A* (ASA) pathfinding strategy that hierarchically optimizes robot position and heading. We also present an online method that incrementally updates the SE(2) NavMesh from streaming point clouds during concurrent geometry reconstruction. In simulation, the SE(2) NavMesh captures over 50% more traversable area than classical NavMeshes, and the SE(2) NavMesh + ASA pipeline consistently outperforms sampling-based baselines in constrained environments. Extensive real-world experiments on a physical robot validate real-time online generation and successful navigation across multiple environments.

</details>


### [135] [A Reconfigurable Rocker-Bogie Robot for High Step Climbing and Turning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01554)
*Kento Koizumi,Tomoaki Ohba,Yuta Saito,Takeya Morito,Kenji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Reconfigurable rocker-bogie rover with actuated bogies and rear omnidirectional wheels enabling 4- and 6-wheel configurations; achieves zero-radius turning faster and with lower torque; climbs a 40 cm step in 6.4 s.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve maneuverability and energy efficiency of rock crawlers by reducing actuators while preserving climb capability; enable zero-radius turning via differential-drive in 4-wheel mode.

Method: Motors at bogie joints actively swing bogies to switch between four-wheel and six-wheel configurations; omnidirectional wheels mounted on rear ends of rockers enable smooth turning under a differential-drive model in four-wheel mode; experimental validation on a prototype measuring turning performance, torque, and step climbing.

Result: Zero-radius turning at speeds more than five times those of a conventional six-non-steerable-wheel rockers-bogie; total average wheel torque reduced to about 17%; successfully climbed a 40 cm step with an average climbing time of 6.4 s.

Conclusion: The proposed reconfigurable mechanism yields superior turningability and climb performance with substantially fewer actuators, validating the viability of switchable 4/6-wheel configurations for high-dynamic mobility in rough terrain; promising for planetary rovers and related field robotics.

Abstract: This study proposes a reconfigurable rocker-bogie mechanism that achieves efficient turning motion with a small number of actuators while maintaining high step-climbing capability. By installing motors at the bogie joints and actively swinging up and down bogies, the system enables switching between four-wheel and six-wheel configurations. Omnidirectional wheels are mounted on the rear ends of the rockers, allowing smooth turning in the four-wheel configuration based on a differential-drive model. Experimental evaluation using a prototype robot demonstrated that the proposed mechanism achieves zero-radius turning at a speed more than five times that of a conventional rocker-bogie mechanism equipped with six non-steerable grip wheels, while requiring only approximately 17% of the total average wheel torque. In addition, the robot successfully climbed a 40 cm step with an average climbing time of 6.4 s, confirming its high turning and step-climbing performance.

</details>


### [136] [Multi-Rate Nonlinear Model Predictive Control for Wall-Supported Bipedal Locomotion of Quadrupedal Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01574)
*Taizoon Chunawala,Jeeseop Kim,Kaveh Akbari Hamed*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Layered MR-NMPC framework for wall-assisted hybrid bipedal locomotion in constrained environments, integrating contact-point planning with SRB dynamics; validated by simulations showing improved stability and 2.9x higher success rate vs heuristic MPC.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-time planning for legged locomotion requires simultaneous optimization over discrete contact sequences and continuous CoM/orientation trajectories under unilateral constraints, underactuation, and dynamic switching.

Method: High-level MR-NMPC plans discrete contact trajectories and continuous CoM/orientation using a single rigid body (SRB) model; low-level nonlinear WBC with virtual constraints enforces full-order dynamics via quadratic programming and tracks MR-NMPC references.

Result: Extensive numerical simulations on Unitree A1 show robust wall-assisted bipedal locomotion on rough terrain with disturbances; MR-NMPC achieves ~2.9× higher success rate than conventional MPC with heuristic foot placement in negotiating irregular terrain at high speeds.

Conclusion: The proposed MR-NMPC layered framework enhances dynamic stability and performance for constrained, fast locomotion with wall-assisted support, outperforming heuristic-foot-placement strategies and suggesting strong potential for real-time, whole-body planning and control in challenging environments.

Abstract: This paper presents a novel layered planning and control framework based on multi-rate nonlinear model predictive control (MR-NMPC) that enables quadrupedal robots to perform hybrid bipedal locomotion with wall-assisted support in constrained environments. Real-time trajectory optimization for this locomotion presents significant challenges, as the controller must simultaneously plan for both the contact points and the continuous trajectories of the robot's center of mass (CoM) and orientation within the robot's nonlinear dynamics while accounting for unilateral contact constraints, underactuation, and the switching nature of the robot's dynamics. At the high level of the control framework, an MR-NMPC is proposed, which dynamically plans both the discrete-time trajectories of the contact points and the continuous-time trajectories of the CoM and orientation, using a single rigid body (SRB) dynamics model. By incorporating contact-point planning within the multi-rate optimal control framework, this approach enhances dynamic stability compared to heuristic foot placement strategies. At the low level of the control framework, a nonlinear whole-body controller (WBC) based on virtual constraints and a quadratic program enforces full-order dynamics and tracks the MR-NMPC references. The proposed approach is validated through extensive numerical simulations demonstrating the robust wall-assisted bipedal locomotion of a Unitree A1 quadrupedal robot on rough terrains and under external disturbances in a constrained environment. Comparative analysis shows that the proposed MR-NMPC achieves a 2.9 times higher success rate compared to conventional MPC with heuristic-based foot placement strategies in negotiating irregular terrain at high speeds.

</details>


### [137] [Path planning for unmanned naval surface vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01631)
*Daniel G. Schwartz*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A dual-stage real-time path-planning framework for unmanned surface vehicles combining a global planner (Grassfire, a Grassfire modification, and a modified Probabilistic Roadmap) with a local planner that routes behind moving obstacles using contextual observations; simulations compare to D* and discuss related dynamic planners.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tackle real-time avoidance of fixed and moving obstacles for unmanned surface vehicles, a challenging problem with real-time constraints.

Method: Global planner: three-path integration (Grassfire, modified Grassfire, modified PRM). Local planner: high-level decision logic based on obstacle direction relative to global path to route behind obstacles; validations via simulations; includes D* baseline for comparison.

Result: Simulation results validate the approach; the local planner enables routing behind moving obstacles; the paper discusses how the method compares with D* and other dynamic planners.

Conclusion: The proposed hybrid global/local planning framework with decision logic offers novel, effective real-time obstacle avoidance for USVs, unifying fixed and moving obstacle handling and highlighting advantages over traditional planners in dynamic scenarios.

Abstract: There nowadays is a myriad of approaches to real-time avoidance of fixed obstacles for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and, to a lesser extent, also the task of avoiding moving obstacles such as boats, ships, swimmers, and other USVs, but both topics still present challenges. This paper offers novel approaches to both of these problems. It uses a combination of a global path planner, which finds a path from a start point to a goal point that avoids fixed obstacles (given that their locations are known in advance), and a local path planner, which can circumnavigate a moving obstacle (as well as any previously unknown fixed obstacles). The global planner is novel in that it employs a combination of three path planners, one known in the literature as Grassfire, one that is a new modification of Grassfire, and one that is a new, and arguably more intuitive, version of the well-known Probabilistic Roadmap. The local planner is novel in that it employs a higher-level decision logic based on its observations regarding the direction of movement of the obstacle relative to the USVs global path. This logic enables the USV to determine the best strategy for avoiding the obstacle by systematically routing the vehicle behind the obstacle rather than running parallel to it until the opportunity to pass appears. Simulations are provided that validate these claims. For comparison with other systems, the simulations include an implementation of the well-known D* algorithm, and the discussion covers additional dynamic path planning systems, which, like D*, do not necessarily route the vehicle behind the moving obstacle.

</details>


### [138] [One Demonstration Is Enough for Real-World Robotic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01651)
*Yuwan Liu,Hongze Yu,Song Liu,Yuhan Wang,Junge Zhang,Yaodong Yang,Yuanpei Chen,Ceyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AutoSERL enables one-shot, fully automated intervention in real-world robot RL, using a single demonstration and three complementary mechanisms to guide exploration, recover from failures, and terminate guidance when autonomous success is achieved.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robot RL on hardware suffers from costly data collection and difficulty in reward specification; existing methods require many demonstrations or continuous human intervention. A one-shot, automated intervention framework could significantly reduce human effort while maintaining safety and performance.

Method: Three mechanisms: (1) sliding window intervention to steer exploration away from local optima and unsafe deviations; (2) safety recovery with predefined trajectory recovery points to detect and correct failure states; (3) intervention termination criterion to disable guidance once autonomous policy can complete the task, preserving exploration advantage.

Result: Evaluated on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms (insertion, hanging, hinge-based tasks). AutoSERL outperforms SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES across all tasks; matches HIL-SERL; achieves 100% success on insertion tasks; shows improved robustness to positional variations; available code and videos on project site.

Conclusion: AutoSERL demonstrates that a single demonstration with fully automated intervention can match or exceed one-shot and multi-demonstration baselines while maintaining exploration during learning and robust performance in real-world, contact-rich manipulation tasks.

Abstract: Learning effective robot control policies on physical hardware is challenging due to costly data collection and the difficulty of reward specification. Prior work has incorporated demonstrations into reinforcement learning (RL), yet existing approaches either require large numbers of demonstrations or depend on continuous human intervention during training. To address these limitations, we present AutoSERL, a framework that leverages a single demonstration to fully automate the intervention process in real-world robot RL. The framework includes three complementary mechanisms to accomplish certain tasks: a sliding window intervention mechanism that continuously guides exploration to prevent local optima and unsafe deviations, a safety recovery mechanism that detects and corrects failure states via predefined trajectory recovery points, and an intervention termination criterion that automatically disables guidance once the policy can independently complete the task, preserving its exploration advantage. We evaluate AutoSERL on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms, spanning insertion, hanging, and hinge-based tasks. AutoSERL consistently outperforms SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES -- a dedicated one-shot imitation learning baseline -- across all tasks while matching HIL-SERL, achieves 100% success rate on insertion tasks, and demonstrates improved robustness to positional variations, all from a single demonstration. Code and videos are available on our project website: https://autoserl.github.io/.

</details>


### [139] [Imagining the Sense of Touch: Touch-Informed Manipulation via Imagined Tactile Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01684)
*Zhiyuan Zhang,Adeesh Desai,Jyun-Chi Hu,Yosuke Saka,Quan Khanh Luu,Jiuzhou Lei,Davood Soleymanzadeh,Bihao Zhang,Minghui Zheng,Yu She*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TacImag predicts tactile observations from vision and proprioception to guide manipulation, enabling touch-informed control using only visual data at test time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome fragility, calibration, and maintenance of tactile hardware by leveraging tactile knowledge without deploying tactile sensors.

Method: Train on paired visuotactile demonstrations to learn a model that imagines tactile observations (e.g., force fields, tactile images) from vision and proprioception; during deployment, use visual observations to drive policies via imagined tactile signals.

Result: In six simulated and four real-world tasks, imagined tactile signals consistently improve manipulation performance without tactile hardware. Real-world gains: ~44.4% for contact-sensitive tasks via imagined force fields and ~23.3% for texture-sensitive tasks via imagined tactile images. Tactile imagination acts as contact-aware supervision rather than simply recovering missing tactile data.

Conclusion: Tactile imagination enables touch-informed manipulation without tactile sensors, with effectiveness dependent on how well the tactile representation aligns with task needs; the approach reduces hardware requirements while providing robust performance improvements.

Abstract: Tactile sensing can substantially improve contact-rich robotic manipulation, yet its practical deployment remains limited by the fragility, calibration requirements, and maintenance burden of tactile hardware. This raises a fundamental question: can robots benefit from tactile knowledge without requiring tactile sensors at deployment? We present TacImag, a tactile imagination framework that predicts tactile observations from vision and proprioception and uses the generated signals to guide manipulation policies. Trained from paired visuotactile demonstrations, TacImag enables touch-informed manipulation using only visual observations at test time. We evaluate TacImag on six simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks. Across simulation and real-world experiments, imagined tactile observations consistently improve manipulation performance without requiring tactile hardware. In real-world experiments, imagined force fields improve contact-sensitive tasks by 44.4% on average, whereas imagined tactile images improve texture-sensitive tasks by 23.3%, revealing that the effectiveness of tactile imagination depends strongly on the relationship between tactile representation and task requirements. Our results further suggest that tactile imagination does not simply recover missing tactile measurements. Instead, it acts as a form of contact-aware supervision that transforms subtle visual interaction cues into representations that are easier for manipulation policies to exploit.

</details>


### [140] [CoRe: Combined Rewards with Vision-Language Model Feedback for Preference-Aligned Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01721)
*Hexian Ni,Tao Lu,Yinghao Cai*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-component reward design: Formal Rewards (FR) designed from task knowledge and Residual Rewards (RR) learned from observations. Introduces CoRe, a framework that combines FR and RR with vision-language model feedback to learn preference-aligned policies without human input. FRM iteratively designs/optimizes FR with VLMs; RRM learns RR from video-level preferences using VLM-generated labels, providing nuanced rewards that complement FR. Demonstrates superior policy learning efficiency/effectiveness on ten simulated robotic manipulation tasks and five real-world tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reward design is central and challenging in RL: handcrafted rewards are hard to specify and can bias policies; learned rewards from preferences can be inefficient and unstable. Inspired by dual learning in cognitive science, the work decomposes rewards into explicit FR and implicit RR to align policies with human intent without direct human labeling.

Method: CoRe framework with two modules: Formal Reward Module (FRM) uses vision-language models to iteratively design/optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback; Residual Reward Module (RRM) learns RR from video-level preferences by generating preference labels via VLMs, capturing nuanced rewards that supplement FR; the combined FR+RR is used to train RL policies.

Result: Extensive experiments indicate CoRe outperforms existing approaches in policy learning effectiveness and efficiency across ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-world tasks; results are supported by project website containing videos.

Conclusion: FRM and RRM work in concert to automatically construct reliable, efficient rewards that are aligned with human intent, reducing reliance on human-designed rewards and preference data, and improving RL performance.

Abstract: Reward design remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Hand-crafted rewards are often difficult to specify and may lead to suboptimal policies, while learned rewards from preferences can suffer from inefficiency and unstable training. Inspired by the dual nature of human learning explored in cognitive science, we decompose rewards into two complementary components: Formal Rewards (FR), explicitly designed based on task knowledge, and Residual Rewards (RR), learned from observations to capture implicit and nuanced preferences. Based on this decomposition, we propose CoRe, a hybrid framework that integrates FR and RR with vision-language models (VLMs) feedback to achieve preference-aligned policies without human involvement. Our contributions are twofold: (1) We propose a Formal Reward Module (FRM) that leverages VLMs to iteratively design and optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback, enabling the continual improvement of policy during training; (2) We introduce a Residual Reward Module (RRM) that learns RR from video-level preference by employing VLMs to generate preference labels and capturing nuanced rewards that complement FR, ensuring alignment with human intent. Through the synergy of FRM and RRM, CoRe enables the automatic construction of reliable rewards that are efficient and preference-aligned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoRe outperforms existing approaches in terms of policy learning effectiveness and efficiency on ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-worlds. Videos can be found on our project website: https://core-2026.github.io/

</details>


### [141] [Lightweight Safe Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End UAV Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01794)
*Shenghui Zhang,YuXuan Gao,Songwei Zhao,Jifeng Hu,Zijing Zhang,Hechang Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A safety-constrained, perception-control framework for UAV navigation using sparse inputs; lightweight encoder; constrained MDP; Lagrangian-safe PPO; curriculum learning; outperforms RL baselines in safety, success rate, and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense perception for UAV navigation is computationally heavy and risky; existing RL lacks explicit safety, may lead to unsafe exploration, instability, especially at high speeds; safe RL methods relying on action projection can destabilize; need efficient, safely constrained navigation with sparse sensing.

Method: A lightweight network encodes sparse observations into collision-risk features using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. The task is formulated as a constrained Markov decision process within a hierarchical control architecture and solved with a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Curriculum learning is employed to stabilize training.

Result: Experiments across varying obstacle densities and flight speeds show higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency than existing RL baselines.

Conclusion: The framework effectively integrates perception and control under explicit safety constraints, enabling safer, more efficient autonomous UAV navigation with lightweight onboard computation; promising for deployment in sparse-sensing, high-speed scenarios.

Abstract: With the rapid development of autonomous aerial systems, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in applications such as inspection, environmental monitoring, and rescue, creating growing demand for reliable autonomous navigation. However, autonomous UAV navigation in dense environments remains challenging under sparse perception and dynamic constraints. Most reinforcement learning (RL) methods lack explicit safety mechanisms, leading to unsafe exploration, unstable training, and risky behaviors, especially during high-speed flight. Even in safe RL approaches, safety is often enforced by projecting policy outputs onto a safe action set, which may introduce instability. Meanwhile, many learning-based methods rely on dense inputs or large networks, increasing computational burden and limiting lightweight onboard deployment. Facing the above challenges, we propose a safety-constrained perception-control integrated framework for UAV navigation. A lightweight network encodes sparse observations into collision-risk-aware features using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. We formulate the task as a constrained Markov decision process within a hierarchical control architecture and solve it using a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Curriculum learning further improves training stability. Experiments with varying obstacle densities and flight speeds demonstrate higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency than existing reinforcement learning baselines.

</details>


### [142] [VLA-Corrector: Lightweight Detect-and-Correct Inference for Adaptive Action Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01804)
*Yi Pan,Miao Pan,Qi Lu,Jiaming Huang,Man Zhang,Siteng Huang,Xin Li,Jie Zhang,Yongliang Shen,Xuhong Zhang,Wenqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VLA-Corrector adds a lightweight online corrective mechanism (LVM + OGG) to action-chunked vision-language-action policies, enabling event-triggered replanning to counteract open-loop drift in contact-rich tasks while keeping backbone unchanged.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce policy-call frequency and maintain temporal coherence in VLA policies without sacrificing closed-loop reactivity, especially in contact-rich, long-horizon manipulation tasks.

Method: Introduce Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) that compares predicted vs actual visual features; detect persistent deviations; on detection, truncate remaining actions and perform corrective replanning via Online Gradient Guidance (OGG); adapt action horizon dynamically; compatible with existing VLA backbones without retraining.

Result: The approach reduces compounding errors by interrupting stale action chunks and invoking online correction, preserving efficiency of chunking while improving robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich interventions.

Conclusion: VLA-Corrector provides a practical, plug-in method to enhance robustness of VLA policies under perturbations by triggering adaptive horizon replanning, potentially with broad applicability across VLA models without retraining.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have recently achieved strong progress in embodied intelligence. To reduce policy-call frequency while preserving temporal coherence, most generative policies adopt an action chunk mechanism, executing multiple future actions in an open-loop manner under a fixed action horizon. However, this "predict-then-blindly-execute" paradigm sacrifices closed-loop reactivity: in contact-rich physical interactions, even small local perturbations can rapidly amplify within the open-loop blind spot, leading to compounding errors and ultimately task failure. To address this limitation, we propose VLA-Corrector, a lightweight corrective inference framework for action-chunked VLA policies. Without modifying the backbone policy weights, VLA-Corrector introduces a lightweight Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) that continuously compares predicted and actual visual feature evolution, enabling online detection of visual dynamics deviations. Once persistent deviation is detected, the system triggers a truncation event, discards the remaining stale actions, and invokes corrective replanning via Online Gradient Guidance (OGG). The detect-and-correct mechanism of VLA-Corrector naturally induces an event-triggered adaptive action horizon: it preserves long-horizon execution when the current chunk remains reliable, and invokes short-horizon corrective replanning when execution begins to drift. In doing so, VLA-Corrector mitigates the trade-off imposed by static horizons between execution robustness and policy-call frequency. It can be integrated into different VLA models without further retraining the VLA backbone, interrupting compounding errors while preserving much of the efficiency benefit of action chunking and substantially improving robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [143] [DL-SLAM: Enabling High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting SLAM in Dynamic Environments based on Dual-Level Probability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01860)
*Ziheng Xu,Qingfeng Li,Xuefeng Liu,Chen Chen,Jianwei Niu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: DL-SLAM introduces a dual-level probabilistic framework that fuses semantic and geometric cues to form pixel- and object-level dynamic probabilities, enabling removal of dynamic elements from the static map and yielding better tracking and semantic mapping in monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limitations of prior dynamic SLAM methods: purely geometric pixel-wise uncertainty maps cause ambiguous object boundaries and transiently static objects are either ignored or inappropriately fused into the static map, leading to artifacts. A dual-level approach aims to leverage semantics to disambiguate dynamics and use a static map to refine probabilities.

Method: Compute pixel-level dynamic probabilities from combined semantic and geometric cues; lift these probabilities to 3D and aggregate per object to obtain object-level dynamic probabilities; prune Gaussian splats dynamically at the object level; use the static map to provide geometrical guidance to refine pixel-level probabilities, forming a feedback loop in a monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM pipeline.

Result: DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches by up to 13% in tracking accuracy and produces high-fidelity semantic maps with artifact-free static maps due to object-level pruning of dynamic Gaussians and the semantic–geometric fusion.

Conclusion: A dual probabilistic framework that integrates semantics with geometry enables robust separation of dynamic and static elements in monocular 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM, reducing artifacts and improving pose estimation and semantic map quality.

Abstract: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled significant progress in dense dynamic Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). Prevailing methods typically discard predefined dynamic objects, ignoring that transiently static objects offer valuable geometric constraints for pose estimation. A recent work attempts to leverage this potential by employing per-pixel uncertainty maps to quantify the magnitude of motion. While this approach enables transiently static objects to enhance pose estimation, it erroneously integrates these objects into the static map, resulting in persistent artifacts. Moreover, its reliance on purely geometric information leads to ambiguous object boundaries in the uncertainty maps. To overcome these limitations, we present DL-SLAM, a monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM system built upon a novel dual-level probabilistic framework. Our method computes dynamic probability maps by combining semantic and geometric information. These pixel-level probabilities are lifted to 3D and aggregated to derive an object-level dynamic probability for each instance. Object-level probability enables the categorical pruning of dynamic Gaussians, resulting in an artifact-free static map. The static map, in turn, provides a geometrically consistent guidance to refine the pixel-wise probabilities, enhancing their reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches, improving tracking accuracy by up to 13\% while generating high-fidelity semantic maps.

</details>


### [144] [SPLC: Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01925)
*Zixuan Chen,Hao Fu,Haiwen Hu,Shiquan Zheng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces SPLC, a social-preference learning framework for offline crowd robot navigation that avoids manual reward design by generating preference data via a social-preference mechanism; validated in simulation and on TurtleBot4, with code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL methods require reward functions to elicit socially compliant crowd navigation, but crafting such rewards is difficult due to complex pedestrian dynamics and reward bias. A data-driven approach to learn social norms is therefore highly desirable.

Method: Propose Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC): a social preference feedback mechanism that automatically generates preference data using principled criteria reflecting pedestrian dynamics and social norms; integrates SPLC with offline RL to learn policies without hand-crafted rewards.

Result: Empirical results show SPLC-augmented offline RL achieves consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines on standard performance metrics; real-world TurtleBot4 experiments validate practicality; code and video demos are available at the provided GitHub repository.

Conclusion: SPLC eliminates the need for detailed reward design by learning from social-preference data, improving social compliance and navigation performance in offline RL for crowd navigation, with demonstrated real-world applicability and reproducibility.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant potential for crowd robot navigation in human-robot coexistence applications. However, the inherent complexity of pedestrian motion renders the design of effective reward functions for promoting socially compliant robot behaviors a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) algorithm to eliminate the need for detailed reward design. Its core innovation lies in the introduction of a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data through principled preference evaluation criteria. By explicitly accounting for the intricacies of pedestrian dynamics, the pipeline mitigates the reward bias and facilitates the systematic quantification of broad social norms, thereby fostering socially compliant behaviors. Extensive experiments integrating SPLC with offline RL methods demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across standard performance metrics. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the TurtleBot4 further validate the effectiveness of SPLC in practical human-robot coexistence settings. Our code and video demos are available at https://github.com/sklus949/SPLC.

</details>


### [145] [PhysMani: Physics-principled 3D World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01938)
*Peng Yun,Shouwang Huang,Hao Li,Jinxi Li,Jianan Wang,Bo Yang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PhysMani: a physics-informed 3D Gaussian world model coupled with a future-aware policy, enabling robust manipulation of fast-moving targets; introduces PhysMani-Bench with 16 tasks and achieves higher success than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current embodied AI struggles with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting for dynamic targets in unstructured 3D environments; a physics-based dynamics model combined with learning-based planning is needed.

Method: Propose PhysMani: a physics-principled 3D Gaussian velocity-field world model learned via online optimization, ensuring divergence-free dynamics; a policy model with learnable token-based cross-attention that incorporates predicted 3D future dynamics; introduce PhysMani-Bench for dynamic manipulation tasks.

Result: Demonstrates superior success rate compared to strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments across 16 tasks.

Conclusion: PhysMani effectively bridges geometry and dynamics for dynamic manipulation; the benchmark validates robustness and real-world transfer.

Abstract: Manipulating fast and dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments remains challenging for embodied AI. Existing visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting. We propose PhysMani, a framework that couples a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy model. The world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast and physically grounded future dynamics prediction. The policy model integrates the predicted 3D scene future dynamics through a learnable token based cross-attention module. We introduce PhysMani-Bench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks, and demonstrate a superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.

</details>


### [146] [A Stereo Visual SLAM System Using Object-Level Motion Estimation and Geometric Filtering Based on Cross Disparity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02005)
*Sujan Kumar Dhali,Bhaskar Dasgupta*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A dynamic stereo SLAM framework (OCD SLAM) that extends ORB-SLAM2 to handle dynamic scenes by combining cross disparity-based dynamic feature detection with object-level motion classification via SMOKE and Kalman tracking, yielding improved trajectory accuracy on KITTI datasets; ablation confirms cross disparity's contribution beyond 3D object detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard SLAM relies on a static-world assumption; in dynamic environments, moving objects and dynamic features degrade pose estimation and mapping. There is a need to robustly identify and exclude dynamic elements to maintain accurate localization and mapping.

Method: Introduce cross disparity, a measure comparing standard stereo disparity with a new cross disparity that leverages temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points. Integrate SMOKE-based 3D object detection with Kalman tracking to classify motion at the object level. Use the static subset of features for pose estimation within an ORB-SLAM2-like framework, enabling joint static/dynamic separation and improved localization.

Result: On KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw sequences, OCD SLAM significantly improves trajectory accuracy versus ORB-SLAM2 and several dynamic-SLAM baselines. Ablation studies show cross disparity effectively detects dynamic features missed by the 3D object detector alone, particularly on KITTI Raw.

Conclusion: Combining cross disparity-based feature-level motion segmentation with object-level tracking yields robust dynamic SLAM, outperforming baselines and enhancing resilience to dynamic scene elements. The cross disparity component provides complementary dynamics detection beyond 3D object detection.

Abstract: This paper presents OCD SLAM, a dynamic stereo visual SLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM2 by jointly addressing dynamic objects and dynamic features in the scene. Usual visual SLAM systems operating in dynamic environments often fail in the presence of moving objects, due to the static-world assumption used in pose estimation and mapping. To address this predicament, we introduce a novel geometric approach based on the discrepancy between disparity and a newly proposed notion called ``cross disparity'', which exploits both temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points. Complementary to this feature-level motion analysis, OCD SLAM integrates a 3D object detection module (SMOKE) with Kalman filter-based object tracking to perform object-level motion classification, enabling robust separation of static and dynamic scene elements for accurate pose estimation. The proposed approach has been evaluated on various sequences from the KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw datasets. Results demonstrate that OCD SLAM achieves significant improvement in trajectory accuracy compared to ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the cross disparity module in the KITTI Raw dataset and show that this method is able to detect dynamic features that are missed by the 3D object detection scheme alone.

</details>


### [147] [Cross-Platform Control for Autonomous Surface Vehicles via Adaptive Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02037)
*Ruiheng Jiang,Thomas Bi,Raffaello D'Andrea,Aswin Ramachandran*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: An adaptive RL policy enables zero-shot cross-platform trajectory tracking for autonomous surface vehicles, using a teacher-student latent dynamics representation and simulated randomized dynamics, achieving strong real-world generalization to two platforms without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address cross-platform heterogeneity in hydrodynamics and actuation so a single policy can generalize across platforms without platform-specific tuning.

Method: Train an adaptive RL policy with partial observability by conditioning on interaction history. Use a teacher-student architecture where a learned module infers a latent representation of platform dynamics. Train in simulation with randomized vessel dynamics using a simple analytical dynamics model; deploy zero-shot to two real platforms without fine-tuning and compare against baselines.

Result: Real-world experiments on two platforms show the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive baselines by up to 58% in position MAE and approaches the accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.

Conclusion: Demonstrates effective cross-platform generalization and zero-shot deployment for AIS trajectory tracking, leveraging latent-dynamics inference and partial observability without requiring high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulators.

Abstract: Autonomous surface vehicles vary widely in hydrodynamic and actuation characteristics, yet most controllers are designed for single-platform deployment. We present an adaptive reinforcement learning approach for trajectory tracking that enables zero-shot cross-platform deployment using a single policy. Since the deployment platform's dynamics are unknown to the policy, we address cross-platform generalization with the standard partial-observability approach of conditioning on interaction history, employing a teacher-student architecture in which a learned module infers a latent representation of the platform dynamics. The policy is trained in simulation under randomized vessel dynamics and is deployed zero-shot to two real-world platforms without any fine-tuning, despite relying on a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator. In real-world experiments on two different platforms, the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error while approaching the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.

</details>


### [148] [Guided Action Flow: Q-Guided Inference for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02092)
*Liuhaichen Yang,Zhuang Jiang,Chenchao Sheng,Zezhi Tang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Guided Action Flow shows that inferring with a frozen flow-matching VLA policy can be improved at test time by a learned action-chunk critic guiding a reverse-time flow sampler; results show notable gains in single-task and multi-task settings, but generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain core bottlenecks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable test-time improvement of flow-matching vision-language-action policies without retraining the base policy, leveraging a critic trained on real rollouts to steer sampling.

Method: Freeze a pretrained SmolVLA policy; train an action-chunk critic using real success/failure rollouts; condition the critic on task descriptions from the language pathway; apply critic gradients only during reverse-time sampling to steer action chunks.

Result: Single-task critic raises success from 68.0% to 82.0% (seed window) and 82.0% to 86.0% (another window). Multi-family task-description critic raises validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%; locked-held-out test gain from 65.0% to 67.5% (positive but modest).

Conclusion: Q-guided inference is feasible for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, but critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance are key bottlenecks limiting larger gains.

Abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action policies generate robot action chunks through an iterative transport process, creating an opportunity for test-time guidance without retraining the base policy. We study this opportunity in Guided Action Flow, an inference-time framework that keeps a pretrained SmolVLA policy frozen and uses a learned action-chunk critic to guide its reverse-time flow sampler. The critic is trained from real success and failure rollouts, can condition on task-description features from the frozen SmolVLA language pathway, and is used only through action gradients during sampling. We evaluate the approach on LIBERO manipulation tasks. A single-task critic improves success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improves validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, while the locked held-out test gain is positive but modest, from 65.0% to 67.5%. These results support the feasibility of Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, while showing that critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain the central bottlenecks.

</details>


### [149] [Choreographing the Way of Water: A Computational Framework for Aquatic Robotic Art](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02174)
*Aswin Ramachandran,Christopher Golling,Sebastian Burmester,Noa Sendlhofer,Jan Kamm,Ruiheng Jiang,Raffaello D'Andrea*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Way of Water introduces a cyber-physical framework and a browser-based Studio to choreograph a fleet of autonomous surface vessels for music-responsive, 3D water performances. It integrates a full control stack and high-level authoring with Sequential Convex Programming for trajectories and MPC for disturbance rejection, validated on large-scale deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenges of nonlinear aquatic fluid dynamics and environmental disturbances while democratizing access to high-performance aquatic robotics for artists by providing an accessible, integrated cyber-physical platform.

Method: Develop the Way of Water Studio (browser-based, timeline-compositing) that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument; implement Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection; deploy a complete cyber-physical stack with a custom holonomic chassis, aquatic-tuned state estimation, LTE/MQTT fleet link, and RTK-GPS time synchronization; enable 3D choreography via laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting.

Result: Validation across two deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera; establishes a foundational reference for the design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.

Conclusion: Presents a scalable, artist-friendly architecture for expressive aquatic robotics, bridging advanced control methods with accessible authoring tools and providing deployment benchmarks for fluidic swarms.

Abstract: Robotic choreography in open water is governed by nonlinear fluid dynamics, which impose significant challenges due to environmental disturbances and nonlinear system dynamics. This paper presents the cyber-physical architecture of Way of Water, a vertically integrated framework that orchestrates a fleet of autonomous surface vessels as a distributed choreographic platform. Moving beyond the surface-pixel paradigm, these vessels use laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend their expressive range from the 2D water plane into the 3D volumetric domain. Our primary contribution is the Way of Water Studio, a browser-based, timeline-compositing authoring paradigm that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument for music-responsive choreography. The Studio encapsulates Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection presented through a visual timeline, broadening access to high-performance aquatic robotics for non-programmer artists. Grounding the Studio is the full cyber-physical stack: a custom holonomic chassis, a state-estimation and control stack tuned for the aquatic domain, and an LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS time synchronization. We report on the system's validation across two distinct deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera, establishing a foundational reference for the design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.

</details>


### [150] [Bridge-WA: Predicting Where and How the World Changes for Robotic Action](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02195)
*Yongjie Bai,Hanting Wang,Mingtong Dai,Qijun Zhong,Yang Liu,Liang Lin*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Bridge-WA is a lightweight world-action model that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors—future tokens, change maps, and motion-flow maps—to condition an action transformer. It removes the teacher at inference and improves task success, progress, and robustness, especially under out-of-distribution visual shifts, without deployment-time dense future-image generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable effective manipulation by anticipating action-relevant scene changes while avoiding the computational burden of large generative world models and dense future rollouts. Prior models overfit to appearance details and are costly; a compact, principled set of priors can steer action generation toward meaningful scene dynamics.

Method: A three-prior distillation approach: (1) future tokens representing intended outcomes, (2) change maps encoding intervention-supportive scene changes, and (3) motion-flow maps indicating local transition directions. A WorldBridge module conditions the action transformer on these priors using multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases. A frozen teacher model predicting future changes is used during training, but is removed at inference time, enabling efficient execution. The framework avoids dense, expensive future-image generation by focusing on relevant scene changes.

Result: Empirical results across VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus, and real-robot evaluations show that Bridge-WA improves task success, progress, and robustness, with notable gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. The method suppresses nuisance appearance factors (background, lighting, distractors), yielding better generalization.

Conclusion: Bridge-WA provides an efficient alternative to heavy generative world models for vision-language-action tasks by distilling action-relevant priors from a teacher, achieving robust generalization and practical deployment without on-the-fly dense future image generation.

Abstract: General-purpose vision-language-action models benefit from large vision-language priors, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating action-relevant scene changes. Existing world-action models often rely on large generative world models or dense future rollouts, which are expensive and spend capacity on visual details weakly coupled to control. We present Bridge-WA, a lightweight world-action framework that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors: future tokens for intended outcomes, change maps for intervention support, and motion-flow maps for local transition direction. A WorldBridge conditions the action transformer on these priors through multi-source attention memories and spatial-temporal biases, while the teacher model is removed at inference. Across VLABench, RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO-Plus and real-robot evaluations, Bridge-WA improves task success, progress, and robustness, with particularly clear gains under out-of-distribution visual shifts. By focusing action generation on where and how the scene will change, Bridge-WA suppresses nuisance appearance factors such as background, lighting, and distractors, leading to better generalization without deployment-time dense future-image generation. Code and visualizations are available at: https://hcplab-sysu.github.io/BRIDGE-WA .

</details>


### [151] [Actuator Reality Shaping for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02205)
*Satoshi Yamamori,Koji Ishihara,Kentaro Minamikawa,Kiyoharu Ohomori,Taiyo Yazaki,Norikazu Sugimoto,Jun Morimoto*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Actuator reality shaping aligns real actuator closed-loop dynamics with an ideal second-order reference, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for RL policies without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge the sim-to-real gap caused by nonlinear, hardware-dependent actuator dynamics by shaping actuators rather than changing the simulator, providing a standardized interface for RL.

Method: Attach a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward–feedback controller to each joint to shape the actuator's response to match a prescribed reference model, decoupling reference-shaping from stabilization and enabling zero-shot deployment. Validate across a single high-gear-ratio servo with external load, a 7-DOF arm, a wheeled-legged robot on slopes, and a humanoid walking scenario.

Result: Substantial reduction in sim-to-real tracking error and improved zero-shot task performance versus standard servo-control and representative baselines; demonstrated transfer across diverse hardware including walking and driving tasks.

Conclusion: Actuator reality shaping provides a reusable, standardized interface for robot learning that enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across diverse hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models.

Abstract: Sim-to-real transfer in robot learning is often limited by discrepancies between the ideal actuator dynamics assumed during policy training and the nonlinear, hardware-dependent behavior of physical motors. While conventional approaches attempt to bridge this gap by increasing simulator fidelity through system identification, domain randomization, or learned actuator models, we introduce an alternative paradigm: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match the real world, our method shapes the closed-loop behavior of physical actuators to match the idealized second-order reference dynamics used in simulation. By equipping each joint with a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward--feedback controller, we decouple reference-response shaping from robust stabilization, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface for reinforcement learning policies. As a result, policies trained only with the prescribed reference model can be deployed zero-shot on real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models. We validate the approach on a single-joint high-gear-ratio servo under external loads and a 7-DOF robotic arm reaching task, where actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servo-control and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot driving over a slope and a humanoid robot walking, suggesting that actuator reality shaping can serve as a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms.

</details>


### [152] [CoFL-S: Spatially Queryable Sector Flow Fields for Local Language-Conditioned Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02222)
*Haokun Liu,Zhaoqi Ma,Yicheng Chen,Wentao Zhang,Masaki Kitagawa,Zicen Xiong,Jinjie Li,Moju Zhao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: CoFL-S introduces a low-level VLN framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field to generate continuous trajectories. It trains on frame-level supervision derived from VLN-CE episodes and evaluates on a continuous-time Habitat benchmark with a shared velocity controller, showing improvements over action-token and action-chunk baselines and real-world zero-shot transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in low-level action representations in Vision-Language Navigation by producing continuous, language-conditioned motion rather than discrete actions, enabling planner-frequency agnostic, closed-loop control and better real-world transfer.

Method: Predict a language-conditioned flow field over the local visible sector and roll out continuous trajectories by integrating the field. Train by converting whole-episode VLN-CE data into frame-level supervision with aligned sub-instructions, actions, trajectories, and dense flow-field targets. Evaluate on a continuous-time Habitat benchmark using a shared velocity-command controller to separate low-level control from planning and enable multi-frequency comparison; assess zero-shot real-world generalization.

Result: CoFL-S outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark. It also demonstrates superior zero-shot real-world closed-loop performance compared to the baselines.

Conclusion: A low-level language-conditioned flow-field framework (CoFL-S) provides robust, continuous motion for VLN, with strong cross-frequency performance in simulation and successful real-world transfer when paired with a shared velocity controller.

Abstract: Vision-Language Navigation has increasingly emphasized high-level instruction reasoning, memory, global map construction, and instruction decomposition, while the low-level action representation remains comparatively underexplored. We propose CoFL-S, a low-level vision-language-action framework that predicts a language-conditioned flow field over the robot's local visible sector and generates continuous trajectories by rolling out the predicted field. To train this low-level representation, we convert each VLN-CE episode, originally a whole-episode instruction paired with an action sequence, into frame-level local supervision with aligned sub-instructions and matched action, trajectory, and dense flow-field targets. For evaluation, we introduce a continuous-time Habitat benchmark that isolates low-level action interfaces from instruction decomposition and executes all methods through a shared velocity-command controller, enabling decomposition-independent closed-loop comparison across different planner frequencies rather than fixed discrete forward-and-turn transitions in VLN-CE. Under matched encoders and training settings, CoFL-S consistently outperforms action-token and action-chunk baselines across planner frequencies in the continuous-time Habitat benchmark, and zero-shot real-world closed-loop deployment further shows its advantage over both baselines beyond simulation.

</details>


### [153] [NEUROSYMLAND: Neuro-Symbolic Landing-Site Assessment for Robust and Edge-Deployable UAV Autonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02277)
*Weixian Qian,Tianyi Yang,Sebastian Schroder,Yao Deng,Jiaohong Yao,Xiao Cheng,Richard Han,Xi Zheng*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment (NEUROSYMLAND) combines probabilistic semantic scene graphs with symbolic safety rules to assess UAV landing regions under perceptual uncertainty, achieving robust, interpretable edge-efficient performance in simulated and hardware-in-the-loop tests and releasing open-source code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-only learning methods struggle with terrain variability and provide limited transparency for safety decisions in autonomous UAV landing; there is a need for interpretable, robust per-frame safety reasoning on resource-constrained edge hardware.

Method: Build a probabilistic semantic scene graph (PSSG) from onboard vision; apply symbolic constraints on terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency to evaluate candidate landing sites; analyze under perceptual uncertainty; emphasize edge-resource efficiency; provide open-source artifacts.
