Result: 72 simulated scenarios yielded 61 successful assessments (better than four baselines at 37–57). 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials measured end-to-end latency, stage times, CPU/GPU, memory, and power. Symbolic reasoning adds negligible latency; main cost is perception and PSSG construction. Demonstrates edge deployment feasibility; open-source release.

Conclusion: NEUROSYMLAND shows feasible, robust, and interpretable landing-site assessment on edge UAV hardware, with an open-source ecosystem to support reproduction and refinement.

Abstract: Safe landing-site assessment in unstructured environments remains a key challenge for autonomous UAV deployment, as vision-only learning approaches often degrade under terrain variability and provide limited transparency in safety decisions. We present NEUROSYMLAND, a neuro-symbolic landing-site assessment system that integrates lightweight perception with explicit safety reasoning. The framework constructs a probabilistic semantic scene graph from onboard visual input and evaluates candidate landing regions using symbolic constraints capturing terrain flatness, obstacle clearance, and spatial consistency, enabling structured reasoning under perceptual uncertainty while maintaining edge-feasible execution. Across 72 simulated landing scenarios spanning diverse terrains, NEUROSYMLAND achieves 61 successful assessments, outperforming four competitive baselines (37-57 successes). To evaluate deployability, we further conduct 100 hardware-in-the-loop trials with randomized initial poses, profiling end-to-end latency, stage-wise execution time, and system-level metrics including CPU/GPU utilization, memory footprint, and power consumption. Results demonstrate improved robustness and interpretability with bounded edge-resource usage. Profiling shows that symbolic reasoning contributes only a small fraction of end-to-end latency, while the main computational cost arises from perception and PSSG construction. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying the landing-site assessment stack on edge-constrained UAV hardware, and all source code, datasets, prompts, and symbolic rule refinement examples are released in an open-source repository

</details>


### [154] [Real-Time Visual Intelligence on Low-Cost UAVs: A Modular Approach for Tracking, Scanning, and Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02298)
*Andrei-Marian Ungureanu,Stelian Spînu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Modular, open-source AI drone platform on DJI Tello with facial detection, recognition, and monocular depth estimation; real-time processing via a Python server and web interface; demonstrates low-cost, embedded AI for personal assistant drones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Show feasibility and accessibility of real-time AI on constrained UAV hardware; enable personal assistant capabilities and pave way for broader research in autonomous UAVs.

Method: Developed a modular architecture on DJI Tello; integrated three AI pipelines (face detection, face recognition, depth estimation); used lightweight models optimized for embedded systems; built web-based control and video monitoring; implemented Python-based processing server; demonstrated robotic capabilities (tracking, indoor scanning, line following with virtual sensors).

Result: Robust performance in real-world conditions; validates deployment of advanced AI on constrained hardware; demonstrates practical autonomous UAV behaviors; supports open-source, low-cost hardware; establishes foundation for future research in military, rescue, and surveillance applications.

Conclusion: Concludes that accessible, affordable, open-source AI-enabled UAVs are feasible and valuable for research and applications, offering a platform for further development.

Abstract: Autonomous drones are rapidly transforming modern warfare and civil applications alike. This paper presents the development of an integrated intelligent drone system designed to serve as a personal assistant. Leveraging the DJI Tello drone platform, we implemented a modular architecture that integrates three core artificial intelligence functionalities: facial detection, facial recognition, and depth estimation from monocular vision. A web-based interface enables seamless drone control and real-time video monitoring, while a Python-based server processes visual data and executes inference pipelines using lightweight neural models optimized for embedded systems. Unlike existing commercial solutions, this system emphasizes accessibility, low-cost hardware, and open-source technologies. The system demonstrates robust performance in real-world conditions, including person tracking, indoor scanning, and autonomous line following using virtual sensors. This project validates the applicability of advanced AI techniques in real-time robotic systems and illustrates the feasibility of deploying them on constrained hardware, providing a foundation for future research in autonomous UAVs for military, rescue, and surveillance missions.

</details>


### [155] [The Moving Eye: Enhancing VLA Spatial Generalization via Hybrid Dynamic Data Collection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02322)
*Jincheng Tang,Yilong Zhu,Zhengyuan Xie,Jiang-Jiang Liu,Jiaxing Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A data-centric hybrid viewing strategy in a dual-arm setup improves spatial generalization for Vision-Language-Action models by reducing shortcut learning, outperforming purely fixed/static viewpoints across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address fragile spatial generalization in VLA models due to shortcut learning and spurious correlations, which persist despite more viewpoints.

Method: Dual-arm setup with one arm manipulating and the other as a mobile environmental camera; compare three data distributions (Fixed, Multi-Fixed, Moving Views); propose a hybrid strategy of continuous camera motion plus diverse static viewpoints to reduce spurious correlations while maintaining training stability.

Result: The hybrid Moving+Static strategy achieves the best performance, enabling generalization to unseen camera poses and object configurations where added static viewpoints fail; benefits across architectures (ACT, Diffusion, Pi0, Gr00t).

Conclusion: Shortcut learning and spatial generalization challenges are universal across VLA architectures. Mixed data strategies systematically mitigate spurious correlations and enhance generalization.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown remarkable promise in generalized robotic manipulation. However, their spatial generalization remains fragile. We argue that simply increasing the number of viewpoints is insufficient. Models often fall into the trap of Shortcut Learning, latching onto spurious correlations (e.g., fixed relative poses between objects or between the camera and robot base) rather than learning true spatial relationships. In this work, we propose a data-centric solution to enhance VLA spatial generalization. We utilize a dual-arm setup where one arm performs manipulation while the other serves as a mobile environmental camera. We systematically evaluate three data distribution patterns: Fixed, Multi-Fixed, and Moving Views. Our findings reveal that a hybrid strategy, combining continuous camera motion with diverse static viewpoints, yields the best performance by substantially reducing spurious correlations while maintaining training stability. Our experiments demonstrate that this strategy mitigates spurious correlations, enabling VLAs to generalize to unseen camera poses and object configurations where simply adding more static viewpoints fails. Crucially, we reveal that the susceptibility to shortcut learning and the struggle with spatial generalization are universal characteristics shared across diverse architectures. Consequently, all evaluated models (ACT, Diffusion, and VLA models including Pi0 and Gr00t) benefit significantly from our mixed data strategy.

</details>


### [156] [HEFT: Heavy-Payload Full-size Humanoid Teleoperation with Privileged Motion Guidance and Windowed Payload Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02332)
*Chenxin Liu,Qingzhou Lu,Guangxiao Yang,Xuanyang Shi,Chenghan Yang,Yanjiang Guo,Jianyu Chen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: HEFT enables robust heavy-payload teleoperation for full-size humanoids via Privileged Motion Guidance and Windowed Payload Curriculum, demonstrated on a 1.75 m, 65 kg L7 robot with payloads up to 24 kg.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the challenge of validating full-size humanoids under real payload interaction, where larger inertia and tight balance margins increase sensitivity to VR-tracker noise, drift, and retargeting, and where payload potential is underutilized.

Method: Introduce HEFT with Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG) to reconstruct physically plausible references from deployable noisy VR data, and Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps to train robust heavy-payload tracking; deployed on the L7 humanoid (175 cm, 65 kg).

Result: Demonstrated tracking of turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24 kg.

Conclusion: HEFT offers a viable framework for scalable heavy-payload humanoid teleoperation by mitigating noise/drift and leveraging payload capabilities through PMG and WPC on full-size platforms.

Abstract: General motion tracking and teleoperation offer a promising path to scalable humanoid skill acquisition, yet most existing frameworks are validated on compact platforms or without real payload interaction, leaving full-size humanoids with real payloads largely unexplored. Scaling to full-size humanoids introduces two compounding challenges: their larger inertia and tighter balance margins make tracking highly sensitive to noise, drift, and retargeting errors from commodity VR trackers, while their payload potential remains largely underutilized. We present HEFT, a heavy-payload full-size humanoid teleoperation framework that addresses both challenges. HEFT learns from deployable noisy VR references with physically plausible reconstructed references through Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG), and uses a Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps to acquire robust heavy-payload tracking. We deploy HEFT on L7, a 175cm, 65kg humanoid. The robot tracks motions including turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24kg.

</details>


### [157] [ACID: Action Consistency via Inverse Dynamics for Planning with World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02403)
*Gawon Seo,Dongwon Kim,Suha Kwak*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ACID: a decision-time planning framework enforcing cycle action consistency via an inverse dynamics model, improving planning reliability and reducing compute across diverse action-conditioned world models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current planning costs only penalize terminal-state error, neglect intermediate realizability; predicted trajectories may diverge during rollout, reducing policy performance and efficiency.

Method: Introduce cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the original conditioned action. Integrate per-step residual into planning cost with a scale-invariant adaptive weight, making planning cost more robust to model uncertainty. Evaluate across four world models and six tasks, including rigid/deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation.

Result: ACID consistently improves planning performance and matches baseline accuracy with substantially less planning compute across four world models and six tasks.

Conclusion: Cycle-consistent action reasoning yields more reliable and efficient decision-time planning; the adaptive per-step residual weighting helps balance realism vs accuracy; the approach is broadly applicable across action-conditioned world models.

Abstract: Decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models has become a popular paradigm for embodied control. However, the standard planning cost judges a candidate solely by how close its predicted terminal state lies to the goal, leaving the realizability of the intermediate transitions unchecked -- a predicted trajectory can look convincing while the environment rollout drifts away from it. In this paper, we propose ACID, a decision-time planning framework that introduces cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the one that was conditioned on. We fold this per-step residual into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight. Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks spanning rigid and deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation, ACID consistently improves planning and matches the baseline's accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

</details>


### [158] [LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02417)
*Boyang Sun,Jiajie Li,Yung-Hsu Yang,Chenyangguang Zhang,Tim Engelbracht,Sunghwan Hong,Cesar Cadena,Marc Pollefeys,Hermann Blum*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Presents LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator for robots that predicts the next target camera pose based on current RGB input and a natural-language intent, addressing multi-hypothesis and varying semantic granularity in active perception.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language-conditioned camera motion as an underexplored primitive for autonomous perception; viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intents and can vary in granularity, necessitating models that jointly handle language, vision, and 3D camera control.

Method: LIME combines an autoregressive observation-gain decoder with a continuous flow-matching pose head to jointly predict the next view (what it should reveal) and a set of target SE(3 poses. It learns from mined multi-intention supervision in egocentric video by pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative poses, enabling multi-hypothesis target views.

Result: Empirical evaluation across tasks shows LIME can learn to actively select camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception and improving downstream performance.

Conclusion: Vision-language camera-motion generation is a viable approach for intent-driven active perception in robotics; LIME demonstrates effective multi-intention pose planning and can leverage passive video supervision to learn useful camera motions.

Abstract: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

</details>


### [159] [WorldSample: Closed-loop Real-robot RL with World Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02431)
*Yuquan Xue,Le Xu,Zeyi Liu,Zhenyu Wu,Zhengyi Gu,Xinyang Song,Bofang Jia,Ziwei Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: WorldSample: a real-synthetic loop for real-robot RL that uses a post-trained world model to generate high-fidelity synthetic transitions from real rollouts, combined with Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate augmentation. It improves policy success and data efficiency while reducing hallucination and maintaining world-model fidelity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce the high interaction costs of real-robot RL and overcome demonstration-coverage limitations by enabling efficient learning from augmented synthetic transitions that reflect real-world dynamics.

Method: Ground real rollouts to train a world model; generate synthetic transitions from the world model; apply Policy-Paced Learning to select and schedule augmented data, mitigating value overestimation and hallucination noise.

Result: Policy success rate improves by 28% and training steps reduce by 59% compared with baselines; world-model visual fidelity improves by 19.4 dB PSNR and 0.47 SSIM over demonstration-only post-training.

Conclusion: The real-synthetic WorldSample loop with PPL enhances both policy performance and world-model fidelity on contact-rich, precise robot manipulation tasks, validating efficient RL in real-robot settings.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can overcome the demonstration-coverage limitation of imitation learning (IL) by allowing robots to improve through trial-and-error interaction beyond the states observed in demonstrations. However, deploying RL on real robots remains constrained by high interaction costs, since each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path. To address this challenge, we propose WorldSample, a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, world-model generation, and policy improvement. Grounded on real rollouts, WorldSample generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions through a post-trained world model, which greatly lowers the visual hallucination. Specifically, rather than simply using these transitions as real-world experience, WorldSample introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate the training process through sample selection and scheduling, balancing useful augmentation against value overestimation and mitigating the hallucination-induced noise. Experiments on robot manipulation tasks involving contact-rich and precise tasks show that WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% while reducing training steps by 59% compared with baselines. Furthermore, WorldSample improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB in PSNR and 0.47 in SSIM over demonstration-only post-training, validating the effectiveness of the real-synthetic loop for both policy and world model performance.

</details>


### [160] [Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02466)
*Junhao Shi,Siyin Wang,Xiaopeng Yu,Li Ji,Jingjing Gong,Xipeng Qiu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP) decouples physical competence from semantic alignment in Vision-Language-Action models. It uses a two-stage approach: (1) self-supervised inverse dynamics on cheap unlabeled interaction data to learn transferable motor priors, and (2) a lightweight, language-grounding stage with minimal expert data. On SIMPLER, TAP matches models trained with 1M+ expert trajectories using far less labeled data and shows robust real-world performance on WidowX under camera perturbations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLA models are limited by the scarcity of expert demonstrations, and there is a conceptual gap between learning how to move (physical competence) and learning what to do (semantic alignment). The authors propose to separate these objectives, arguing that language supervision is mainly needed for alignment rather than control. A decomposition enables leveraging abundant unlabeled interaction data to learn physical priors.

Method: Two-stage TAP framework. Stage 1: self-supervised inverse dynamics on unlabeled interactions (including off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play) to learn transferable motor priors. Stage 2: lightweight grounding in language using a small amount of expert data to align priors with task instructions.

Result: On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on more than 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data; achieves a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations (baselines drop to 0%), demonstrating robust, transferable physical representations.

Conclusion: Task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI by decoupling physical competence learning from semantic grounding and exploiting cheap unlabeled data for priors.

Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations -- triplets of observations, instructions, and actions that are costly to collect at scale. We argue that this bottleneck stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: acquiring physical competence (how to move) and acquiring semantic alignment (what to do). Crucially, only the latter requires language supervision. Building on this Decomposition Hypothesis, we propose Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP), a two-stage framework that first learns transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data -- including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play -- via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. A lightweight second stage then grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, yielding a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI.

</details>


### [161] [Learning Agile Intruder Interception using Differentiable Quadrotor Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02472)
*Michael Anoruo,Xiaoyu Tian,Abhishek Rathod,Timothy Naudet,Thomas Canchola,Eric Sturzinger,Kshitij Goel,Wennie Tabib*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A differentiable quadrotor policy gradient method learns interception using 3D direction to the intruder, enabling monocular-sensor applicability and outperforming point-mass baselines by ~30% at speeds up to 10 m/s.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world interception with monocular cameras lacks access to precise relative position or distance to the intruder. Existing DRL approaches assume such information, creating a gap for monocular-sensor deployment.

Method: Analytical policy gradient approach with differentiable quadrotor dynamics. The policy uses the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor state as inputs, enabling agile interception up to 10 m/s.

Result: The proposed method outperforms baselines that use simplified point-mass dynamics by an average of 30% in interception performance.

Conclusion: A differentiable-quadrotor policy gradient framework effectively leverages directional cues from monocular sensing to achieve agile interception, surpassing point-mass-based baselines.

Abstract: This paper presents a methodology for learning a control policy to intercept an intruder using the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor state. Prior deep reinforcement learning approaches assume either relative position or distance to the intruder is available, but this information is not readily accessible in real-world applications that employ passive, monocular camera sensors. Instead, we propose a solution that leverages an analytical policy gradient method using differentiable quadrotor dynamics to learn agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s. The proposed approach outperforms baseline methods that utilize simplified point mass dynamics by an average of 30%.

</details>


### [162] [QuadRocket: An Aerial Robotic Testbed for Adaptive Thrust-Vector Control of Rocket-Like Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02474)
*Pedro Santos,Joel Reis,Paulo Oliveira,Carlos Silvestre*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A low-cost quadrotor-based rocket prototype (QuadRocket) validates thrust-vector control for launch-like systems using a mounted, axial-symmetric rigid-body model, adaptive backstepping, and dynamic-surface attitude control; validated in simulation and indoor experiments with promising tracking and disturbance rejection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a safe, low-cost testbed to explore thrust-vector control strategies for launch-vehicle-type systems, addressing non-minimum-phase behavior and integrating attitude/actuation dynamics while preserving axial symmetry and decoupling yaw from thrust vector direction.

Method: Model the platform as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored thrust along its longitudinal axis; use a reduced-attitude representation on the two-sphere to exploit symmetry and decouple yaw; derive an adaptive backstepping controller with a control-point transformation to mitigate non-minimum-phase behavior; design a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller for thrust-vector tracking that accounts for actuation dynamics without differentiating virtual signals; implement in simulation and validate experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena.

Result: The approach achieves almost global trajectory tracking under unknown constant disturbances; effective disturbance rejection; experimental validation confirms tracking accuracy and the proposed architecture’s suitability as a versatile thrust-vector testbed.

Conclusion: QuadRocket offers a versatile, low-risk platform for validating thrust-vector control in robotic vehicles, enabling accurate trajectory tracking and disturbance compensation, and supporting the development of thrust-vector strategies for launch-like systems.

Abstract: This paper presents QuadRocket, a quadrotor-based rocket prototype that provides a low-cost, low-risk platform for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicle-type systems. The prototype consists of a cylindrical main body mounted on top of a quadrotor through a universal joint, forming a flying inverted pendulum with non-negligible inertia. For control design, the coupled system is modeled as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored force applied along its longitudinal axis. A reduced-attitude representation on the two sphere is adopted to explicitly exploit the vehicle's axial symmetry and to decouple yaw from the thrust-vector direction. On this model, we derive an adaptive backstepping controller that achieves almost global trajectory tracking in the presence of unknown constant disturbances, while a control-point transformation mitigates non minimum-phase behavior. The quadrotor is then treated as a thrust vector actuator, and a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller is designed to track the desired thrust-vector, accounting for actuation dynamics and avoiding explicit differentiation of virtual control signals. The complete architecture is evaluated in simulation and validated experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena. Results demonstrate accurate trajectory tracking, effective disturbance compensation, and confirm the suitability of the QuadRocket as a versatile testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles.

</details>


### [163] [Controllable Sim Agents with Behavior Latents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02496)
*Juanwu Lu,Junyu Zhu,Ziran Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Introduces Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable, per-channel latent-driven traffic-simulation framework with soft eligibility gates, achieving competitive realism on Waymo data and demonstrating interpretable steering and safety controls to mitigate reward hacking.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need realistic agents that imitate logged behavior and are steerable along interpretable axes to test autonomous systems, isolate variables, and reproduce edge cases without real-world risk.

Method: Infer per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update. Condition a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained with a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. Introduce soft eligibility gates (smooth exponential decay) to replace hard thresholds, preserving gradient signals near thresholds.

Result: On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, achieves competitive realism and exposes per-channel controllability not present in higher-ranked imitators. Steering based on speed/acceleration yields monotone responses with no stall-related reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and improved with soft eligibility. Demonstrates steerable map compliance under a context-residual return; highlights that steering metrics must be interpreted alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid confounds.

Conclusion: CNeVA provides a controllable, gradient-friendly framework for realistic traffic imitation that enables interpretable steering and safety controls, while underscoring the necessity of coupling steering metrics with guardrails to prevent reward hacking and ensure physical plausibility.

Abstract: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that imitate logged behavior and can also be steered along interpretable axes. Such controllability enables engineers to isolate variables, reproduce specific edge cases, and test autonomous systems without real-world risk. We introduce Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable simulated-agent framework that learns to infer a per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update, conditioning a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. To tackle scarcity in reward signals, we propose soft eligibility gates that replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay, preserving the gradient signal for near-threshold agents. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA attains competitive realism on the benchmark while exposing per-channel controllability that the higher-ranked imitation models lack. Speed- and acceleration-based steering produces monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with the introduction of soft eligibility. We manage to achieve steerable map compliance under a context-residual return measure. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that steering metrics must be read alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.

</details>


### [164] [Embodied.cpp: A Portable Inference Runtime of Embodied AI Models on Heterogeneous Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02501)
*Ling Xu,Chuyu Han,Borui Li,Hao Wu,Shiqi Jiang,Ting Cao,Chuanyou Li,Sheng Zhong,Shuai Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A portable C++ runtime (Embodied.cpp) enables unified, multi-rate, latency-first deployment of embodied AI models across heterogeneous hardware, demonstrated on VLA and WAM benchmarks with efficiency gains and preserved accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fragmentation across model stacks, backends, and robot glue code hinders practical deployment of embodied AI on edge devices; a common runtime is needed to support closed-loop control, diverse hardware, and extensible I/O.

Method: Architectural decomposition into five layers (input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins, deployment adapters), enabling modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible operators/IO with a single backend abstraction; evaluated on HY-VLA, pi0.5, and a LingBot-VA Transformer block WAM.

Result: VLA deployments achieved 100.0% and 91.0% task success; WAM benchmark reduces block memory from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB, indicating improved deployment efficiency while maintaining accuracy across diverse embodied models.

Conclusion: Embodied.cpp provides a practical, portable runtime that unifies deployment of embodied models across diverse architectures and hardware, enabling efficient end-to-end performance in real-world robotic settings.

Abstract: Embodied AI models now span vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs), but practical deployment remains fragmented across model-specific Python stacks, backend assumptions, and robot-side glue code, especially on heterogeneous edge devices. Existing inference runtimes are designed mainly for request-response serving and therefore do not satisfy the runtime contract of embodied deployment: multi-rate execution inside closed-loop control, latency-first batch-1 inference on heterogeneous hardware, and extensible embodied interfaces beyond fixed token I/O. We present Embodied.cpp, a portable C++ inference runtime for embodied models. Based on an architectural analysis of representative VLA models and WAMs, Embodied.cpp captures a shared execution path and organizes it into five layers: input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins, and deployment adapters. The runtime provides modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible operator and I/O support, enabling deployment across heterogeneous devices, robots, and simulators through one backend abstraction. We evaluate Embodied.cpp on two VLA models, HY-VLA and pi0.5, and on a preliminary WAM benchmark using a LingBot-VA Transformer block. The VLA deployments achieve successful closed-loop execution with 100.0% and 91.0% task success rates, respectively. The WAM benchmark reduces block memory from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB. These results show that Embodied.cpp improves deployment efficiency while preserving high accuracy across diverse embodied model architectures.

</details>


### [165] [VT-WAM: Visual-Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02503)
*Shuai Tian,Yupeng Zheng,Yuhang Zheng,Songen Gu,Yujie Zang,Yuxing Qin,Weize Li,Haoran Li,Wenchao Ding,Dongbin Zhao*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VT-WAM is a Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly predicts future visuals, tactile deformation, and actions in a flow-matching framework, using novel attention mechanisms to bridge visual and tactile signals and emphasize tactile evidence during contact.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many manipulation policies rely on sparse or invisible tactile cues; existing visual-tactile methods often predict actions without modeling tactile dynamics. There is a need to integrate visual, tactile deformation, and action generation for contact-rich manipulation.

Method: Proposes VT-WAM with (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention connecting a first-frame visual anchor to temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) that biases action queries toward tactile evidence during contact. The model is trained within a unified flow matching framework to predict future visuals, tactile deformations, and actions.

Result: Evaluated on six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, VT-WAM achieves a 71.67% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%. Ablations show both tactile deformation modeling and contact-phase tactile attention guidance are important for task performance.

Conclusion: Jointly modeling visual, tactile deformation, and action generation with the proposed attention mechanisms yields improved performance in contact-rich manipulation, demonstrating the value of tactile dynamics and contact-aware attention in visual-tactile world models.

Abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to react to local deformation, pressure, slip, and friction, yet these cues are temporally sparse and often invisible in visual observations. Existing visual-tactile policies usually feed tactile observations directly into action prediction, but rarely model tactile deformation dynamics during action generation. In this paper, we introduce VT-WAM, a Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly learns future visual prediction, tactile deformation prediction, and action prediction within a unified flow matching framework. In particular, VT-WAM introduces (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention to bridge a first-frame visual anchor with temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) to encourage action queries to rely on tactile evidence during contact phases. Across six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, VT-WAM achieves a 71.67% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%. Ablations demonstrate that modeling tactile deformation dynamics and guiding contact-phase tactile attention are both important for contact-rich tasks. Project website: https://vt-wam.github.io/.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [166] [Multilayer Q-Matrix-Embedded Neural Network for Cognitive Diagnosis (M-QCDNet): Structure-Aware Deep Learning Architecture for Psychometric Interpretability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01278)
*Yiyao Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: M-QCDNet: a multilayer Q-matrix–embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis that uses a Q-matrix as a prior, with an L2-based regularization to enforce alignment and new interpretability metrics; aims for interpretable, actionable AI in education.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge psychometric interpretability and neural flexibility; ensure mastery profiles align with cognitive theory; enable early detection of learning difficulties and targeted interventions.

Method: Develop a multilayer neural network whose item-skill structure is guided by a Q-matrix; train with a loss incorporating an L2 penalty to penalize skills misaligned with the Q-matrix; introduce interpretable alignment-based metrics to quantify correspondence between predicted skill activations and item-level skills.

Result: Claims interpretable skill activations aligned to the Q-matrix, introduces alignment-based metrics, and demonstrates practical classroom benefits for early detection and mastery-based interventions; no quantitative results are provided in the abstract.

Conclusion: Embeds diagnostic validity into model design to bridge psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

Abstract: The research proposes a multilayer Q-matrix-embedded neural network for cognitive diagnosis (M-QCDNet), which integrates the structural interpretability of cognitive diagnostic models (CDMs) with the deep learning neural network (NN). M-QCDNet structures the item-skill relationship using the Q-matrix as a structural prior, ensuring latent mastery profiles remain interpretable and consistent with cognitive theory, followed by the proposed loss function with an L2 penalty to penalize skills not aligned with the Q-matrix and to balance predictive performance and structural alignment. Corresponding evaluation matrices, the interpretable alignment-based metrics that quantify the degree to which predicted skill activations correspond to item-level skills, were further developed. M-QCDNet offers practical benefits for classroom practice, enabling early detection of learning difficulties and supporting mastery-based interventions. By embedding diagnostic validity into model design, M-QCDNet bridges psychometric transparency and neural flexibility, advancing interpretable, fair, and actionable AI for cognitive diagnostics.

</details>


### [167] [I\textsuperscript{2}RiMA: Spectral Riemannian Representation with Temporal Attention for Mental Stress Detection based on EEG Signals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01279)
*Cheng He,Kunyu Peng,Shangen Han,Jinming Ma,Jinhong Ding,Likun Xia*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A frequency-aware, intra-inter Riemannian attention architecture for EEG stress detection that preserves channel-wise geometry and spectral cues, uses data-driven frequency clustering, and employs intra-inter slice attention to capture local spectral dynamics and global temporal context, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with low complexity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-subject EEG stress detection is hindered by subject-dependent, frequency-specific patterns. Traditional Riemannian methods focus on time-domain covariance and overlook neural oscillations; standard temporal tokenization may disrupt inter-slice coherence. There is a need to preserve frequency-resolved geometry and capture both local and global temporal cues.

Method: Construct spatial covariance matrices at each frequency, map to SPD tangent space to preserve channel geometry and frequency cues. Introduce frequency cluster aggregation to form compact, data-driven spectral clusters aligned with EEG rhythms and reduce redundancy. Apply an intra-inter slice attention module to integrate local slice-level spectral dynamics with global temporal context across EEG sequences.

Result: Empirical evaluation on three datasets shows the proposed method consistently outperforms five strong baselines, achieving up to 82.78% balanced accuracy. The model is lightweight (1.60M parameters) and computationally efficient (31.95M FLOPs).

Conclusion: The approach successfully exploits frequency-resolved Riemannian geometry and attention mechanisms to enhance EEG-based stress detection, delivering strong performance gains with a compact, efficient architecture.

Abstract: Cross-subject EEG stress detection remains challenging because discriminative stress-related patterns are both subject-dependent and frequency-specific. Conventional Riemannian methods model spatial covariance mainly in the time domain, overlooking neural oscillations that are critical for high-level cognitive state decoding, while standard temporal tokenization often fragments inter-slice temporal coherence. To address these limitations, we propose \method{}, an Intra-Inter Riemannian Manifold Attention Network for EEG-based stress detection. \method{} constructs spatial covariance matrices independently at each frequency point and maps them to the SPD tangent space, preserving channel-wise geometry together with frequency-specific discriminative cues. It further introduces frequency cluster aggregation to select informative spectral components and reduce redundancy by forming compact, data-driven frequency clusters aligned with EEG rhythms. Finally, an intra-inter slice attention module adaptively integrates local slice-level spectral dynamics and global temporal context across EEG sequences. Experiments on three datasets show that \method{} consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 82.78\% balanced accuracy while remaining efficient with only 1.60M parameters and 31.95M FLOPs.

</details>


### [168] [Fixed-Set Robustness in Programming by Example: Example Corruption and Semantic Partition Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01280)
*Yuan Si,Jialu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adversarial worst-case corruption in finite PBE version spaces is studied; a defense (Version-Space Partition Aggregation, VPA) is proposed, but robustness gains are limited and highly task-dependent, with many realistic settings showing no improvement and some tasks being driven to zero accuracy by adaptive attackers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand a neglected failure mode in PBE: an adversary who observes the synthesizer and selects corrupted examples to maximally degrade the produced program, highlighting a potential robustness gap beyond stochastic noise models.

Method: Formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces; implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL; introduce VPA that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures; evaluate on curated/generated DSL tasks, SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE baselines.

Result: Finds a bounded and partly negative robustness dimension: low-margin PBE tasks are vulnerable to adversarial corruption; VPA helps only when semantic partitions yield clear vote margins, which often fails on realistic tasks. Across benchmarks, evidence shows boundary effects: some tasks flip under small budgets; adaptive attackers can drive VPA accuracy to zero on public SyGuS slices; Playgol shows some positive improvements, while a small prompt-based harness shows similar patterns.

Conclusion: The defense is not a universal solution; adversarial robustness in PBE is bounded and highly sensitive to task properties. Semantic partitioning can help but only under favorable margin conditions; more robust defenses and a deeper understanding of margin structure are needed to address adversarial corruption in practical PBE systems.

Abstract: Programming-by-example systems infer programs from a small set of input-output examples. Robust PBE work usually models wrong examples as samples from a stochastic noise process and then minimizes an expected or empirical loss. This paper studies a different failure mode: an adversary who sees the synthesizer and chooses the examples whose corruption most damages the returned program. We formalize fixed-set worst-case corruption for finite PBE version spaces, implement exact-within-bounded-pool and heuristic corruption searches for a string-transformation DSL, and introduce version-space partition aggregation (VPA), a defense that synthesizes on disjoint example groups and votes by semantic signatures. The central claim is deliberately bounded and partly negative: low-margin PBE tasks have an adversarial robustness dimension that random-typo and noisy-PBE evaluations miss, while semantic partition aggregation helps only when the clean semantics keep a partition vote margin, which often fails on realistic tasks. Evidence from curated/generated DSL tasks, accepted public SyGuS PBE_SLIA slices, SYNTRA Playgol v2, and noisy-PBE objective baselines supports that boundary. One curated edit flips all 8 spike tasks while 200-trial typo, DSL-pool, and distance-matched random controls succeed on 10.3%, 11.0%, and 16.7%; generated margin-1 rows flip under budget 1 yet VPA recovers them; on public SyGuS the vote margin is near one, so an adaptive attacker drives VPA accuracy to zero; accepted public SyGuS slices move across exact-within-pool budget boundaries; and Playgol shows positive paired-bootstrap gaps against typo and same-pool random controls on the 141 accepted rows. A small exact-output prompt harness over 20 controlled margin-1 tasks shows the same qualitative clean-to-attacked pattern across local and API models, while it is treated as a scope check, not a broad LLM benchmark.

</details>


### [169] [Domain Knowledge Based Temporal-Spatial Graph Convolution Network for ECG Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01282)
*Wenting Ma,Zhipeng Zhang,Xiaohang Yuan,Ningwei Xie,Yuxin Xie,Xiaolin Wang,Meng Guo,Xingang Chai,Zhenjie Yao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel domain-knowledge based graph convolution network (DK-GCN) for ECG recognition using landmark-based domain knowledge and a double-stream graph to model intra- and inter-cycle relations, achieving state-of-the-art F1 on a 9-class ECG dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address interpretability and performance gaps in AI for specialized ECG analysis by leveraging domain-specific landmarks (PRQST) and graph-based relational modeling rather than pure end-to-end CNNs.

Method: Construct a double-stream directed graph: a spatial graph connecting key ECG landmarks (PRQST) to capture positional relationships, and a temporal graph connecting adjacent cycles to capture cross-cycle dependencies; use a domain knowledge-informed GCN for ECG recognition on extended sequences.

Result: On the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset (9-class classification): average F1 score 88.1%; rare-category F1 score 76.3%; both metrics surpass state-of-the-art models, with domain knowledge enhancing performance especially for rare categories.

Conclusion: Incorporating domain knowledge via a DK-GCN improves ECG recognition performance and interpretability, particularly for underrepresented (rare) classes.

Abstract: In light of strides in Arti cial Intelligence (AI) and its wide spread application, challenges persist in the interpretability of AI models, particularly within specialized domains like healthcare, such as electro cardiograph (ECG) recognition. Rather than relying solely on end-to-end convolutional neural networks, this paper introduces a novel approach using a domain knowledge-based graph convolution network for ECG recognition. Key landmarks points of PRQST, vital to ECG interpreta tion, are incorporated as domain knowledge. The double-stream directed graph is employed to model both intra and inter ECG cycles. Speci cally, spatial directed graphs capture the positional relationships among key points, while temporal directed graphs delineate temporal dependencies between adjacent cycles in extended ECG sequences. Experimental re sults on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset, which speci cally classify ECG into nine categories, prove the e cacy of the proposed model. The overall average F1 score is 88.1%, the average F1 score of rare categories is 76.3%, both outperform the state-of-the-art models. The introduction of domain knowledge did enhance the detec tion performance, especially for rare categories.

</details>


### [170] [Scaling Laws for Grid-Based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search in High Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01283)
*Matthew J Liu,Wei Hang Zheng,Vidhan Purohit,Siqi Xie,Chieh-En Li,Jerry Li,Noah Flynn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Grid-based multiprobe ANN search shows stable d-scaling and near-linear N-scaling with lower indexing costs, outperforming other methods in high-dimensional, rebuild-heavy settings; potential relevance to efficient transformer architectures; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To systematically characterize the scaling behavior of grid-based ANN methods, specifically multiprobe grid, across dataset size N and dimensionality d, and to assess its competitiveness relative to graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based ANN methods.

Method: Systematic experiments varying N and d on datasets (GloVe embeddings), evaluating multiprobe grid against alternative ANN methods, measuring throughput and indexing cost; identifying a d-scaling crossover and analyzing its implications; code provided.

Result: Multiprobe grid maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent across d, while graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods degrade in throughput with increasing d. It exhibits near-linear query scaling in N and lower indexing cost compared to competing ANN methods. The results indicate grid-based methods can be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings, and may inform cost analyses for efficient transformer architectures.

Conclusion: Grid-based multiprobe grid is robust to dimensionality and offers favorable indexing costs, making it a promising option for high-dimensional ANN workloads and for cost-aware design of transformer-based models; code is available for replication.

Abstract: Grid-based approaches to approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search have been absent from modern scaling analyses. We present a systematic characterization of a multiprobe grid algorithm with respect to dataset size $N$ and dimensionality $d$. Our experiments reveal a previously unreported $d$-scaling crossover on the GloVe embedding family, in which multiprobe grid search maintains an approximately constant dimensional scaling exponent while other graph-, tree-, and partitioning-based methods exhibit degrading throughput. The advantage comes with near-linear query scaling in $N$, but also with lower indexing cost than competing ANN methods. Our results suggest that grid-based methods such as multiprobe grid may be competitive in rebuild-heavy or high-dimensional settings where indexing cost and dimensional robustness dictate performance. More broadly, recent work has formalized self-attention as an ANN operation. Thus, the $N$- and $d$-scaling properties of ANN algorithms may guide cost analysis of efficient transformer architectures. Code is available at: https://github.com/weiz345/MultiProbeANN.

</details>


### [171] [IonSense-QKG: A Quantum-Readiness Metadata Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery Dataset Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01286)
*Sakthi Prabhu Gunasekar,Prasanna Kumar Rangarajan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IonSense-QKG provides a metadata framework to assess and rank lithium-ion battery datasets for near-term quantum-classical ML, enabling query-based discovery and reproducible artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Datasets vary widely in chemistry, modality, scale, labels, and preprocessing; such variability gates the feasibility of hybrid quantum-classical workflows. A transparent quantum-readiness scoring system guides dataset selection.

Method: Extend the EV-Battery-IonSense index with quantum-relevant metadata (task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements); enumerate candidate quantum encodings, estimate qubit range, and assess NISQ feasibility; introduce a Quantum Readiness Score as a dataset-selection heuristic; provide query-based discovery tools and a released artifact with metadata tables, scoring scripts, and utilities.

Result: A framework and artifact for discovering and ranking lithium-ion battery datasets by quantum readiness, enabling identification of datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and benchmarking; reproducible data-centric foundation for quantum battery analytics.

Conclusion: IonSense-QKG reframes dataset selection as a data-management problem for quantum analytics; the Quantum Readiness Score is a heuristic for resource guidance, not a claim of quantum advantage.

Abstract: Public lithium-ion battery datasets are increasingly used for state-of-health estimation, remaining-useful-life prediction, anomaly detection, electrochemical diagnostics, second-life analytics, and battery safety research. However, these datasets vary substantially in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, sequence structure, access status, and preprocessing complexity. These differences directly affect whether a dataset is feasible for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine-learning workflows.
  This paper presents IonSense-QKG, a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery dataset discovery. Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the proposed framework enriches public battery dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata, including task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, and NISQ feasibility. A transparent Quantum Readiness Score is introduced to rank datasets as candidate resources for future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarks. The score is intended as a dataset-selection heuristic, not as evidence of quantum advantage.
  The framework demonstrates query-based discovery over enriched metadata to identify datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and future battery-health benchmarking. The released artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples. IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.

</details>


### [172] [A Novel Machine Learning Approach for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification from DNA Methylation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01307)
*Paulo R. Ferreira,Lucas Coutinho Freitas,Laís dos Santos Gonçalves,William Borges Domingues,Lucas Petitemberte de Souza,Mariana B. Michalowski,Vinicius F. Campos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A method combining Sparse Random Projection and multinomial logistic regression improves methylation-based CNS tumor classification, achieving higher accuracy and robustness across cohorts and multiclass levels than the current state-of-the-art.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation in methylation-based CNS tumor classification.

Method: Dimensionality reduction via Sparse Random Projection followed by multinomial logistic regression. Evaluation mirrors the reference classifier's experimental setup: 2,801-sample reference cohort with stratified 3-fold CV; independent 1,104-sample clinical cohort evaluated at 91-class level and at the broader methylation class family level.

Result: Mean accuracy of 96% on the reference cohort; 86% (91-class level) and 93% (family level) on the independent cohort, outperforming state-of-the-art figures of 82% and 88% respectively, with absolute gains of ~4–5 percentage points.

Conclusion: Stronger methodological practice yields consistent, clinically meaningful improvements in CNS tumor classification reliability over the prior state-of-the-art.

Abstract: NA methylation profiling has become a powerful approach for central nervous system (CNS) tumor classification, yet important challenges remain regarding cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation. In this work, we propose a novel and methodologically rigorous machine-learning approach for methylation-based CNS tumor classification that combines Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction with multinomial logistic regression for classification. We evaluate the proposed approach in the same general experimental setting established by a widely used reference classifier. On the 2,801-sample reference cohort, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 96\% under stratified 3-fold cross-validation. On the independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, it reaches 86\% accuracy at the 91-class level and 93\% when predictions are evaluated at the methylation class family level. These results improve upon the corresponding state-of-the-art reference figures of 82\% class-level concordance and 88\% family-level concordance, yielding absolute gains of approximately 4 and 5 percentage points, respectively. This improvement is clinically relevant: in a diagnostic setting, a 5-point increase in correct tumor classification can directly affect cancer subtype assignment and, in turn, influence treatment selection and downstream clinical decision-making. Our results show that the proposed model, grounded in stronger methodological practice in machine learning, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art across evaluation settings and can materially improve the reliability of CNS tumor classification.

</details>


### [173] [From Approximation to Emergence: A Theory of Deep Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01311)
*Zhilin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A proof-oriented synthesis that unifies classical DL foundations with modern phenomena, offering a coherent narrative and framework to study how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many DL results are isolated; a unified theory is needed to map, relate, and explain diverse phenomena from approximation and optimization to emergence and alignment.

Method: Literature synthesis organized by the object controlled, the assumptions needed, and the phenomena they leave unexplained; rigorous exposition rather than empirical results.

Result: A monograph delivering a rigorous map of DL theory, covering approximation, optimization, generalization, overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence; emphasizes coherence and gaps.

Conclusion: Deep learning theory is powerful yet incomplete, increasingly focused on emergent phenomena driven by scale, data, architecture, and training; the book provides a framework for researchers and practitioners to navigate the field.

Abstract: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. From Approximation to Emergence develops a unified, proof-oriented account of modern deep learning theory, tracing a path from the classical foundations of approximation, optimization, and generalization to the contemporary mechanisms of overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence. Rather than presenting isolated results, the book organizes a broad literature into a coherent research narrative: each theory is examined through the object it controls, the assumptions that make it valid, and the phenomena it leaves unexplained. Written for researchers, graduate students, and mathematically trained practitioners, this monograph offers a rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands today: powerful, incomplete, and increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.

</details>


### [174] [Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01313)
*Christopher Ellis,Shreyas Chaudhari,Mei-Yu Wang,Leighton Barnes,Giulia Fanti,José M. F. Moura*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NightVision uses black-box API access to infer LLM architecture (hidden dimension, depth, parameter count) despite restrictive APIs, via common prompting, spectral analysis, and TTFT timing; evaluated on 32 open-source LLMs with notable accuracy; implication: APIs don't fully obscure model architecture.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prior work showed that access to top-k logits and logits bias can reveal architectural details of LLMs; current commercial APIs restrict to single logit and remove logits bias exposure; question: can architectural details still be inferred under these restrictions?

Method: NightVision employs a novel common-set prompting technique that reveals log probabilities for the same output tokens across prompts, enabling spectral analysis to infer hidden dimension; uses end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to infer depth and parameter count; extensive experiments on 32 open-source LLMs with ablations to study token-budget scaling and model properties.

Result: Hidden dimension estimated within 23% average relative error across models (9% for MoE models); depth and parameter count within 53% for models larger than 3B parameters; robust ablations show performance scales with token budget and model characteristics.

Conclusion: Current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restrictive to fully obfuscate architectural details of their underlying models, raising concerns about information leakage and security.

Abstract: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

</details>


### [175] [Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01365)
*Paimon Goulart,Chansong Lim,Nícolas Roque dos Santos,Yue Dong,Sheldon Peterson,Jia Chen,Evangelos E. Papalexakis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A proof-of-concept multi-modal system for railway-crossing safety that fuses images and official accident history to predict expert-aligned FRA-style safety scores; uses a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model; achieves macro F1 of 0.757 for HIGH/LOW risk, RMSE 0.078, and correlation 0.492, with qualitative expert-aligned results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve crossing safety assessment by leveraging both visual cues from imagery and structured historical data (accident reports), aiming to produce safety scores that align with expert judgment and FRA scoring.

Method: Develop a multi-modal pipeline that ingests images and structured data, process via a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) architecture, and optimize jointly for (i) risk classification (HIGH vs LOW) via macro F1 and (ii) regression to FRA-based safety scores via RMSE and correlation. The workflow includes data preparation, multimodal fusion, training with possibly modality-specific routing heads, and evaluation against expert/ FRA-aligned baselines.

Result: Macro F1 for HIGH/LOW risk: 0.757. FRA-aligned safety score predictions: RMSE = 0.078; correlation with FRA scores = 0.492. Qualitative results indicate alignment with domain experts.

Conclusion: Feasible proof-of-concept for multi-modal safety assessment at railway crossings. Demonstrates that combining visual data with historical accident information can yield predictions that align with expert judgment and FRA scoring, but further work is needed on data diversity, calibration, robustness, and interpretability to enable practical deployment.

Abstract: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

</details>


### [176] [How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01391)
*Maria Elkjær Montgomery,Christian Igel,Mikkel Odgaard,Martin Sillesen,Mads Nielsen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Explores how numeric values are encoded in transformer models for EHR data by comparing discrete, continuous, and hybrid strategies across synthetic arithmetic tasks and real clinical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine how encoding numerics affects precision, stability, and flexibility in EHR-oriented transformers and identify practical default approaches.

Method: Systematic empirical study using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded in real-world EHR data and real clinical prediction tasks; compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies; evaluate numeric precision, optimization stability, and task performance as a function of dataset size.

Result: Explicit value-concept interaction models excel on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architecture allows; hybrid token-based encodings with pre-projection binning offer robustness and broad applicability; optimal number of bins follows a dataset-size–driven power law; models tend to perform “good enough” numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic; clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.

Conclusion: Hybrid token-based encodings are a practical default for EHR transformer models, balancing precision, stability, and deployability better than pursuing maximal numeric precision.

Abstract: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

</details>


### [177] [NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01401)
*Mengyu Li,Guoyao Shen,Chad W. Farris,Xin Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that combines large-scale self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning to diagnose AD, MCI, and related dementias. It achieves strong cross-cohort performance (ADNI and OASIS) and enables probability-based opportunistic screening.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate MRI-based differentiation of AD, MCI, and related dementias is challenging due to subtle and heterogeneous disease-related brain changes; there is a need for robust, generalizable, multi-task learning approaches that leverage large-scale pretraining and clinically relevant objectives.

Method: The approach integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with three tasks—hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and image reconstruction—followed by gated fusion fine-tuning for final diagnosis. Evaluation spans ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening.

Result: NeuroBridge achieved up to 88.17% accuracy for AD vs controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS, with the largest gains in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. It demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, a systematic association between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening.

Conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning enhances neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond single-task approaches. NeuroBridge offers a robust, scalable framework for dementia assessment and opportunistic MRI-based screening.

Abstract: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

</details>


### [178] [Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01408)
*Chenxing Liang,Yuchao Lin,Andrii Kryvenko,Wendi Yu,Chuan Li,Jianwen Xie,Xiaofeng Qian,Shuiwang Ji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SpinGTP generalizes from scalar GTP to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH) to recover antisymmetric interactions in E(3)-equivariant networks, achieving complete expressivity with scalable complexity, matching full CGTP performance on benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CGTP offers complete expressivity but is computationally expensive (O(L^6)); GTP is more scalable but misses antisymmetric paths, limiting expressivity. There is a need for a complete, scalable, high-order equivariant basis for large-scale 3D atomistic simulations.

Method: Generalize from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH) to exploit their algebraic properties, thereby recovering antisymmetric interactions and enabling parity-odd components in the tensor product basis while preserving the asymptotic efficiency of GTP.

Result: Empirical evaluation on Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20 shows SpinGTP achieving accuracies comparable to full CGTP, with particularly strong gains in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries due to explicit antisymmetric path modeling.

Conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order E(3)-equivariant modeling in large-scale 3D atomistic systems by incorporating spin-weighted harmonics to capture antisymmetric interactions.

Abstract: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

</details>


### [179] [The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01415)
*Daniel Thi Graviet,Lovre Pesut,Ivan Dagelic,Vedran Jukic,Ivan Burazin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Substrate choice for execution environments in coding-agent RL causes large variance in startup and run-time costs; optimizing substrates during training yields nontrivial efficiency gains at scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Execution infrastructure is often treated as a background system in RL training. Measuring and optimizing overhead from rollouts can reveal practical improvements for post-training efficiency, especially since large-scale training compounds small per-rollout gains.

Method: Empirical comparative study across four substrates (single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes containers, and cloud VMs). Evaluates cold-start latency and projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories to quantify overhead and scalability implications.

Result: Found up to 110× variation in cold-start latency and about 1.8× spread in projected worker-hours across substrates for the same workload, indicating substantial substrate-driven differences in training efficiency.
