Conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should integrate substrate optimization into the training pipeline, treating execution substrates as a co-optimized component rather than only deployment plumbing.

Abstract: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

</details>


### [180] [Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01417)
*Robert Milletich,Justin Downes,Steve Goley,Newel Hirst*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CIF/CIT reduce split-selection bias in tree methods but incur computational costs; in downstream prediction benchmarks, CIF performs strongly as a top-k feature-ranking method, with runtime sensitive to adaptive stopping and threshold search; potential risk of missing informative features in sparse high-p scenarios; overall CIF is a competitive top-k ranking method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether conditional inference trees/forests can serve as reliable top-k feature-ranking tools for downstream prediction, balancing bias reduction against computational cost.

Method: Empirical evaluation using real-data benchmarks across classification and regression tasks, runtime ablations to quantify the impact of adaptive stopping and threshold search, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments (sparse high-p simulations) to assess feature sampling effects. Nodewise significance tested via Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo permutation p-values under complete permutation null.

Result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With fixed Bonferroni correction, adaptive stopping and number of thresholds searched are the main drivers of runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0–8.4x and 1.9–10.8x, respectively, while downstream score changes are ≤0.011. Sparse high-p simulations show that forest feature sampling can miss informative features in many split decisions.

Conclusion: CIF is a strong top-k feature-ranking method for downstream prediction across the evaluated benchmarks, though practitioners should account for runtime costs and potential missed features in sparse settings.

Abstract: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

</details>


### [181] [On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01444)
*Atsuki Yamaguchi,Szymon Palucha,Léo Bijar,Aline Villavicencio,Nikolaos Aletras*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Moderate pruning of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models can reduce memory while preserving in-domain utility in biomedicine, with limited impact on reliability; extreme pruning raises hallucination risk. In cross-domain settings, both utility and reliability deteriorate rapidly, underscoring that safe compression is highly task- and domain-dependent and that relying solely on utility is insufficient for high-stakes deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap between memory-efficient MoE pruning and the reliability of model outputs, particularly in high-stakes biomedical domains where hallucinations can have serious consequences.

Method: Empirically evaluate four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks in both in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings to measure utility and reliability.

Result: Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility with no immediate reliability decline; hallucination risks rise at extreme pruning. In cross-domain settings, both utility and reliability rapidly degrade, indicating strong domain dependence for safe compression.

Conclusion: Pruning efficacy is task- and domain-dependent; evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

</details>


### [182] [Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01449)
*Sergei Kucherenko,Nilay Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid neural architecture GRs-KAN: integrates differentiable R-functions with Kolmogorov-Arnold Network to encode geometric constraints and discontinuities, improving regression performance and interpretability; multiple variants (additive, multiplicative, agnostic) with up to 67% RMSE reduction and automatic priors selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Incorporate explicit geometric or logical priors into neural regression models to handle discontinuities and complex boundaries by combining smooth learned structure with analytic geometric constraints via differentiable R-functions.

Method: A two-branch hybrid: KAN branches learn smooth nonlinear structure while differentiable R-functions encode geometry through R-conjunctions/disjunctions. Variants include additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch weighting. Geometry-prior constraints implemented analytically and trainable; tested on regression tasks with circular/rectangular supports.

Result: Significant performance gains over standard KAN in regression with discontinuities, with up to 67% reduction in test RMSE and improved boundary localization. Added interpretability due to explicit geometric representation. The agnostic variant can determine whether geometric priors are beneficial.

Conclusion: Integrating analytic geometric priors via R-functions into KANs yields improved accuracy and interpretability for regression tasks with discontinuities; a flexible framework that can automatically decide the utility of priors and adaptively weight branches.

Abstract: We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

</details>


### [183] [Token Geometry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01455)
*Kathan Shah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ember is a memory-efficient optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that reduces optimizer-state memory from Adam-scale to O(V+D), scales across batch size and parameter count, reveals that token optimization follows a simple 1D ray, and enables a lightweight, open-source distributed implementation compatible with ZeRO/FSDP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Language models use an embedding table and an LM-head as the read/write interface between discrete tokens and continuous representations. Optimizing these interfaces is memory-intensive and may exhibit distinct gradient geometry from dense weights. The work seeks to exploit this geometry to improve training efficiency and Pareto performance across finetuning, RL, and pretraining with minimal optimizer-state.

Method: Introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that requires O(V + D) VRAM and avoids the need to shard token-table optimizer states. Provide theoretical and empirical analysis of token optimization trajectories as a simple 1D ray. Demonstrate scalability across batch size and parameter count. Open-source the distributed Ember implementation that integrates with ZeRO/FSDP.

Result: Ember achieves memory-efficient optimization for embedding/LM-head matrices, enabling improved Pareto trade-offs in supervised fine-tuning, RL, and pretraining with only kilobytes of optimizer state. Empirical results show Ember scales with batch size and parameter count, and token optimization follows a 1D ray trajectory rather than a complex nonconvex surface. The work also provides a principled view on the limited set of optimizers needed for Transformer training and delivers a distributed, open-source implementation compatible with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups.

Conclusion: The study argues that the token-embedding/LM-head optimization problem lies in a narrow optimizer space and that Ember offers a practical, scalable solution that reduces memory overhead while preserving or improving performance across major training paradigms; this paves the way for broader, more memory-efficient exploration of large language model training.

Abstract: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

</details>


### [184] [Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01474)
*Haemin Park,Diego Klabjan,Martin W. Braun,Xiuqi Li,Balakrishnan Ananthanarayanan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedCGNM and FedHOO address class-imbalance in federated learning by a class-grouped normalized momentum optimizer and an X-armed-bandit rate tuner; they achieve convergence and empirical gains on long-tailed benchmarks and chip-defect data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In FL, extreme class imbalance harms minority-class performance; privacy and client heterogeneity prevent standard centralized balancing.

Method: FedCGNM partitions classes into a small number of groups by minimum within-group variance; maintains a momentum per group; normalizes each group's momentum to unit length; update direction is the sum of the normalized group momenta. Theoretical convergence analysis accounts for time-varying resampling rates. FedHOO is an X-armed-bandit algorithm leveraging federated parallelism to efficiently optimize two-rate combinations per client at linear cost.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset shows FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines; FedHOO yields additional gains in small-scale federations.

Conclusion: The design equalizes gradient magnitudes across groups and mitigates noise in rare-class gradients; it provides convergence guarantees and practical improvements, with FedHOO enhancing rate optimization in small federations.

Abstract: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

</details>


### [185] [How to Allocate Your Tokens? Scaling Laws with Training Steps and Batch Size](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01487)
*Fabian Schaipp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a three-term scaling law that separates model size, training data, and batch size (via training steps and batch size); shows it recovers optimal batch-size scaling and enables robust fitting with fewer runs, and derives suboptimal-batch-size scaling aligned with prior critical-batch-size findings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the dependence of training efficiency and final performance on batch size by explicitly modeling how training data is consumed (steps) and how batch size interacts with data size; aim for data-efficient extrapolation of scaling laws for planning large-scale training.

Method: Propose a three-term scaling law that includes model size and training data, with an explicit split of data into training steps and batch size. Fit the law on a large collection of training runs to recover the scaling of the optimal batch size, and show it can be robustly fit using suboptimal batch sizes. Extend the framework to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes and verify consistency with known critical-batch-size findings.

Result: The law recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size; it can be robustly fitted using many suboptimal batch-size runs, reducing the total number of runs required; it enables deriving scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes and aligns with prior empirical results on the critical batch size.

Conclusion: The three-term law offers a data-efficient, robust framework for understanding and predicting how model size, training data, and batch size jointly influence training dynamics and efficiency, with practical implications for planning experiments and resources.

Abstract: We propose a scaling law that takes into account model size and training data while explicitly splitting the latter into training steps and batch size (called three-term law). Fitting the proposed law on a large set of training runs, we find that it correctly recovers the scaling of the optimal batch size. Moreover, because it makes use of training runs with suboptimal batch size, our proposed law can be robustly fit with a significantly smaller amount of training runs. We further show that the three-term law can be used to derive scaling laws for suboptimal batch sizes, and that it matches previous empirical findings related to the critical batch size.

</details>


### [186] [Don't Let Gains FADE: Breaking Down Policy Gradient Weights in RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01490)
*Juliette Decugis,Sean O'Brien,Francis Bach,Gabriel Synnaeve,Taco Cohen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unifies advantage-based RL objectives via a two-axis gradient decomposition and introduces FADE, a self-adaptive gradient scheduler that improves LLM post-training performance and diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address training instability and diversity collapse in RL post-training for LLMs; clarify which advantage to use and when.

Method: Decompose any advantage into positive/negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes: sign axis (affecting entropy and weight geometry) and difficulty axis (balance between hard-problem focus and sample efficiency). Propose FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy) that reads training dynamics to automatically schedule the gradient weight.

Result: FADE achieves earlier peak pass@1 at 20k steps for 7B models and 2k steps for 32B models, and attains the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME, outperforming static baselines.

Conclusion: Adaptive, self-tuning advantage scheduling clarifies when to emphasize exploration versus exploitation, improving sample efficiency and diversity; the unifying framework helps decide which advantage to use and when.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training dramatically improves LLM reasoning, but suffers from training instability and diversity collapse. Advantage functions offer an appealing fix: they reshape the training objective, reweight which rollouts drive learning, and are trivial to implement. Yet a proliferation of methods makes it unclear which advantage to use and when. We cut through the confusion with a unifying framework that decomposes any advantage into its positive and negative gradient mass along two orthogonal axes. On the sign axis, imbalanced updates collapse either entropy or weight geometry. On the difficulty axis, hard-problem focus sharpens signal but costs sample size. Both trade-offs shift during training: exploration favors balance and hard focus; exploitation favors suppression and medium focus. This motivates FADE (Focal Advantage with Dynamic Entropy), a self-adapting advantage that reads training dynamics to schedule the gradient weight automatically. FADE reaches peak pass@1 20k steps earlier than the best static baseline at the 7B scale and 2k steps earlier at the 32B , while achieving the best accuracy-diversity trade-off across all pass@k on LiveCodeBench and AIME.

</details>


### [187] [Unveiling the Non-Monotonic Effect of Privacy on Generalization under Byzantine Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01492)
*Thomas Boudou,Batiste Le Bars,Nirupam Gupta,Aurélien Bellet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Generalization error in Byzantine-robust distributed learning with local DP is regime-dependent; strong privacy improves generalization, while weak privacy can hurt it, supported by stability bounds and experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resolve whether the robustness-privacy-generalization trilemma extends to generalization, showing it depends on privacy regime; explain non-monotonic behavior via algorithmic stability bounds under LDP; provide empirical validation.

Method: Theoretical analysis deriving matching lower and upper bounds on algorithmic stability for Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP; regime-specific proofs for high-noise and low-noise settings; empirical experiments.

Result: High-noise (strong privacy) regime: increasing privacy reduces generalization error; low-noise (weak privacy) regime: increasing privacy degrades generalization; there is a non-monotonic dependence on privacy; bounds explain the behavior; experiments corroborate.

Conclusion: Generalization error behavior is regime-dependent; the robustness-privacy trade-off is not universal; offers guidelines for privacy settings in Byzantine-robust distributed learning; prompts future work on additional regimes and practical implications.

Abstract: Recent work has established a fundamental trilemma between Byzantine robustness, local differential privacy (LDP), and optimization error in distributed learning. We show that this trilemma does not universally extend to generalization error, but instead depends critically on the privacy regime. Specifically, in the high-noise regime (strong privacy), we prove that increasing privacy reduces the generalization error, i.e., there is no tension between robustness and privacy. In the low-noise regime (weaker privacy), however, the tension between robustness and privacy reappears and increasing privacy indeed degrades generalization. Our theory explains this surprising non-monotonic behavior of the generalization error via matching lower and upper bounds on the algorithmic stability of Byzantine-robust distributed learning under LDP constraints. We corroborate and further analyze these theoretical findings with empirical evaluations.

</details>


### [188] [Towards Learning Representations of Policies in Two-Player Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01498)
*Kevin Wang,Kevin Yang,Arjun Prakash,Amy Greenwald*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Study learning policy embeddings in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games, proposing datasets of policies, SSL-based embeddings, and downstream evaluation tasks; experiments on Kuhn and Leduc Poker show embeddings capture useful behavioral structure and enable downstream tasks; code provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable systematic learning and evaluation of policy representations in imperfect-information games, and assess the effectiveness of self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques for such representations.

Method: Three-part approach: (1) design methods to create datasets of policies for a given game; (2) develop SSL-based methods to learn policy embeddings; (3) define downstream tasks to evaluate embedding quality. Empirical evaluation on Kuhn and Leduc Poker.

Result: Embeddings learned via basic SSL methods contain useful behavioral information; the study is among the first to systematically compare SSL techniques for policy representations in games; code released for extension.

Conclusion: Policy representations for imperfect-information games can be learned with SSL, enabling meaningful downstream tasks; results are preliminary but promising, suggesting avenues for richer SSL methods and broader game domains.

Abstract: We investigate the problem of learning useful policy representations (embeddings) in two-player zero-sum imperfect-information games. We make three contributions: First, we introduce methods of creating datasets of policies for a given game. Second, we propose methods to learn policy representations. Third, we introduce downstream tasks to evaluate the effectiveness of such representations.
  We evaluate each dataset method, embedding method, and downstream task on Kuhn and Leduc Poker. Although our methods are very basic, we demonstrate that useful behavioral representations are present in the learned embeddings. To our knowledge, this work is among the first to systematically compare self-supervised learning techniques for learning policy representations in games. Our code is available at https://github.com/VitamintK/ssl-project for others to extend.

</details>


### [189] [The risk of KV cache compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01520)
*Lukas Haverbeck,Carmen Amo Alonso,Andres Felipe Posada-Moreno,Sebastian Trimpe,Marco Pavone*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Characterizes the minimax risk of KV cache compression for transformer inference on long sequences using the cache's intrinsic compressibility; provides principled design guidelines under causal masking, and a practical algorithm with empirical validation on LongBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the computational bottleneck of softmax attention over large KV caches by compressing the cache efficiently while offering theoretical guarantees, bridging gaps where worst-case impossibility results offer little guidance.

Method: Theoretical minimax analysis of KV cache compression under causal masking, expressed via the cache's intrinsic compressibility; derivation of design principles that map to prefill and autoregressive decoding; development of a practical algorithm based on these principles.

Result: Characterizes when accurate compression is possible through minimax risk bounds tied to intrinsic compressibility; yields minimax-optimal design principles for prefill and autoregressive steps; presents a practical algorithm achieving these guarantees and reports promising LongBench performance in targeted experiments.

Conclusion: Provides a principled, theory-backed pathway for practical KV cache compression with guarantees, connecting compression theory to design choices and delivering a workable algorithm validated on benchmarks.

Abstract: Transformer inference on long sequences is expensive because softmax attention repeatedly reads from a large KV cache. The prevalent approach to this bottleneck is KV cache compression, which replaces the full cache with a compact summary. Despite its practical importance, the design of such summaries is largely driven by empirical experimentation. On the theoretical side, existing results show that KV cache compression can be impossible in the worst case, but offer little systematic guidance for designing algorithms in regimes where accurate compression is possible. We bridge this gap by characterizing the minimax risk of KV cache compression in terms of the intrinsic compressibility of a cache, revealing when and how accurate compression is possible. These results yield novel design principles for KV cache compression under causal masking that map efficiently to prefill and autoregressive decoding while achieving minimax-optimal risk. We instantiate these principles in a practical algorithm and report promising performance on LongBench in targeted experiments. Overall, our results provide a principled avenue for practical KV cache compression with theoretical guarantees.

</details>


### [190] [Multi-Head Recurrent Memory Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01523)
*Jiatong Li,Samuel Yeh,Sharon Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A memory-augmented LLM for long contexts suffers from a retention bottleneck due to monolithic memory blocks. The paper introduces Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free architecture that partitions memory into independent heads with stage-wise select-then-update. A lightweight instantiation, MHM-LRU, uses a least-recently-updated policy ensuring uniform head usage with no token overhead. Empirical results show substantial gains in memory retention and end-to-end accuracy across very long contexts (100K–1M tokens), including a jump from <30% to 73.96% retention on RULER-HQA at 896K tokens. The approach generalizes across models, scales, and task types, suggesting architectural memory design as a practical solution for reliable long-context operation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address reliability degradation of recurrent memory agents as context length increases, caused primarily by memory retention failures when memory is stored as a single text block, leading to overwrites during updates.

Method: Introduce Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), partitioning memory into independent heads with a stage-wise select-then-update rule; at each step, only one head is updated while others are shielded. Propose MHM-LRU, a lightweight, training-free instantiation using least-recently-updated head selection, with zero token overhead.

Result: MHM-LRU substantially improves retention and end-to-end accuracy across long context ranges (100K–1M tokens); on RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, retention increases from <30% to 73.96%; gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types.

Conclusion: Architectural memory design, particularly multi-head partitioning with selective updates, is an effective, cost-efficient path to reliable long-context recurrence, with MHM-LRU offering a practical instantiation that improves both retention and accuracy.

Abstract: Recurrent memory agents extend LLMs to arbitrarily long contexts by iteratively consolidating input into a fixed-size memory window. Despite their scalability, these agents exhibit a well-documented reliability problem: end-to-end performance degrades systematically as context length grows. We diagnose this failure by decomposing performance into two factors--memory capture and memory retention--and quantitatively confirm that retention is the dominant bottleneck. Retention collapses because existing designs maintain memory as a monolithic text block, forcing every update to risk overwriting previously retained content. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a general, training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads governed by a stage-wise select-then-update strategy. At each step, exactly one head is selected for update while the remaining heads are structurally shielded from overwriting, shifting the burden of retention from model behavior to architectural design. As a lightweight instantiation, we introduce Least-Recently-Updated MHM (MHM-LRU), which guarantees uniform head utilization with zero additional token overhead. Extensive experiments on long-context benchmarks show that MHM-LRU substantially improves both retention and end-to-end accuracy across the 100K--1M token range, where baselines degrade sharply. On RULER-HQA at 896K tokens, MHM-LRU improves the memory retention rate from less than 30% to 73.96%. These gains generalize across model families, scales, and task types, positioning architectural optimization as a practical and cost-efficient path toward reliable long-context recurrent memory.

</details>


### [191] [Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01528)
*Abdullah Al Tasim,Wei Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage learning pipeline estimates local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and uses it in a reinforcement learning controller to improve trajectory tracking of small multirotors in boundary-layer turbulence, achieving substantial performance gains and graceful degradation under strong winds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve robustness of small multirotor flight in atmospheric boundary layer turbulence by compensating wind disturbances with learned wind state estimation integrated into an RL controller.

Method: Stage 1: wind estimator via an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer to recover the horizontal wind vector (RMSE 0.40 m/s, direction error 3.2°) and generalize to vertical ascent; Stage 2: a proximal policy optimization controller that consumes the estimator’s output (frozen) to reduce horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind PD baseline across mean winds 4–12 m/s, winning 100% of evaluation episodes; a three-way ablation separates kinematic contribution (wind-free) from wind-perception contribution, with the latter increasing with wind speed; tested on out-of-distribution winds (13–15 m/s) where the baseline fails catastrophically.

Result: Wind estimator achieves RMSE 0.40 m/s and direction error 3.2°, with a vertical ascent skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. The PPO controller using the frozen wind estimator reduces horizontal tracking error by 48% across 4–12 m/s mean winds, with 100% evaluation win-rate. Ablation shows wind-perception component contributes more at higher winds; performance degrades gracefully for 13–15 m/s winds where the wind-blind baseline fails.

Conclusion: A two-stage approach that first estimates local wind from onboard data and then leverages that estimate in an RL controller enables significantly improved and robust trajectory tracking in turbulent boundary-layer winds, with a growing reliance on wind perception at higher winds and good generalization to vertical ascent profiles and out-of-distribution conditions.

Abstract: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

</details>


### [192] [Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01537)
*Hongbo Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Certified sensing clock derived from audited equivariant world models to schedule sensing; drift-aware deployment; reduces tail event violations; recognized limits in short-horizon regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable reliable timing of sensing by translating validity horizons of world-model predictions into a practical clock for when to re-sense.

Method: Audit an equivariant world model to derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals; show that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware (on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate validity) and that calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes provide deployed guarantees; validate on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model; use a cue-conditioned theorem-bed bench to isolate scheduling rules; compare to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling; assess deployment distribution performance.

Result: The clock controls hold-out interval-simultaneous certificate violations across seeds and data shards; the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to matched-budget scheduling; in short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA, empirical conformal horizons align with the deployed clock; partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.

Conclusion: Presents a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method; explicitly refrains from claiming spectral clocks universally outperform non-spectral schedulers.

Abstract: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

</details>


### [193] [Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01548)
*Ege Onur Taga,Yilin Zhuang,M. Emrullah Ildiz,Petros Mol,Abhimanyu Das,Karthik Duraisamy,Samet Oymak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LLM-guided evolutionary feature engineering discovers dataset-specific preprocessing and feature-generation Python programs, boosting accuracy and interpretability for both time-series and tabular data, often substantially.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automate feature engineering for structured data using large language models and evolutionary search to tailor preprocessing to each dataset, improving downstream model performance and interpretability.

Method: Transformations are encoded as Python programs with a fit/transform interface suitable for direct insertion into ML pipelines. An evolutionary loop refines candidate programs using dataset context, summary statistics, and validation feedback. Two instantiations: EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series forecasting; EFE-Tab evolves compact, interpretable feature programs for tabular prediction.

Result: EFE-Time yields average forecasting performance gains of at least 3% (across metrics such as MASE, WQL, MAE), with gains up to 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset, and compatibility with Chronos-2. EFE-Tab yields improvements or parity with existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods, notably enhancing classical decision trees while preserving interpretability.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can enhance both accuracy and interpretability for structured data through automated feature preprocessing and feature engineering, applicable across time-series and tabular domains.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

</details>


### [194] [X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01553)
*Leyan Li,Rennong Yang,Zhenxing Zhang,Liping Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects topology into Transformer attention logits, enabling topology-aware, multi-hop graph learning within standard transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph data exhibit sparse, structured, multi-scale interactions. Vanilla self-attention is dense and topology-agnostic, limiting efficiency and interpretability for graphs. A simple, interpretable mechanism to constrain attention by topology is desirable.

Method: Propose X-LogSMask: apply a logarithmic transform to the symmetrically normalized adjacency to gate attention logits. Each attention head uses a different power of the normalized adjacency, giving a defined structural radius per head and enabling multi-hop propagation within a single layer. Interprets a standard Transformer encoder as one-step message passing on a complete graph, positioning X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative.

Result: Empirically strong performance across 20 node/edge/graph benchmarks, with state-of-the-art results on 13 datasets. Maintains competitiveness in a lightweight one-layer configuration. Code released at the provided GitHub URL.

Conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention effective for graph learning without modifying the Transformer architecture, offering topology-aware gating and interpretability.

Abstract: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

</details>


### [195] [Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01571)
*Aria Masoomi,Mahsa Bazzaz,Adel Javanmard,Vahab Mirrokni*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a geometric framework for chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in transformer hidden states, defines an effective dimension d_ρ to quantify trajectory complexity, and links spectral properties to task difficulty. Demonstrates that kinematic trajectory features can predict solution correctness early, with strong empirical results on MATH500 (0.93 AUC for easy-vs-hard, and early correctness detection from ~20% of tokens).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To uncover the internal geometry of CoT reasoning, relate trajectory shape to task hardness and solution quality, and enable potential early-stopping and accuracy improvements by monitoring hidden-state dynamics.

Method: Model CoT as discrete curves in Rd and analyze them via spectral (eigenvalue spectrum), positional, and kinematic functionals. Define effective dimension d_ρ to quantify trajectory complexity. Investigate the relationship between eigenvalue spectrum flatness and task difficulty. Extract kinematic features (mean position, positional dispersion, initial/current hidden states, mean velocity/speed, speed dispersion) to predict correctness before generation completes. Validate on MATH500 math problems.

Result: The effective dimension d_ρ distinguishes task difficulty with high discriminative power (0.93 AUC for easy vs hard). Kinematic features can predict correctness from as little as 20% of generated tokens. Correctness signatures generalize across questions of varying difficulty, indicating the trajectory shape reliably encodes task hardness and solution quality.

Conclusion: Geometric analysis of CoT trajectories provides a principled window into task hardness and solution quality, suggesting practical early-stopping cues and insights into how model reasoning unfolds internally.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

</details>


### [196] [BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01600)
*Zewen Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces CAF-based Boundaries_Sync protocol to quantify inter-agent coupling in LLMs; finds text and image communication drive homogenization under certain settings, with group size and model heterogeneity modulating the effect; coupling is prompt-driven and controllable, with implications for multi-agent design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand whether inter-agent communication among LLMs leads to output convergence or diversification, and quantify it with a scalable, interpretable metric.

Method: Controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls) measuring coupling via CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline for text and image channels; ablations (no-communication, prompt perturbations); varying group sizes (K=3,5); cross-model replication; analysis indicating coupling is driven by prompt context (stateless) and exhibits monotonic convergence.

Result: Text communication homogenizes outputs (CAF=0.803 [0.740,0.873]); image communication similarly homogenizes (CAF=0.834 [0.811,0.858]); group size shifts: K=5 homogenizing, K=3 tending toward diversification (CAF>1); cross-model replication shows wide CAF range (0.034–0.803) with model artifacts; coupling is stateless and driven by prompt context, yielding monotonic convergence.

Conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level; has direct implications for designing robust multi-agent systems and mitigation strategies against unwanted homogenization or diversification.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

</details>


### [197] [SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01609)
*Saoud Aldowaish,Yashwanth Karumanchi,Kai-Chen Chiang,Mohammed Ayman Habib,Finn Murphy,Rishen Cao,Morteza Fayazi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SINA is an open-source image-to-netlist generator that converts IC/PCB schematic images into machine-readable netlists using a complete pipeline (component detection, connectivity labeling, OCR for designators, and VLM-based assignment) with crossing-wire detection; achieves 96.67% netlist accuracy, ~2.7x better than prior approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unlock machine-readable knowledge from schematic images and enable AI-driven EDA in analog and mixed-signal domains, addressing generalization gaps across IC and PCB schematics and improving component connectivity interpretation.

Method: A fully automated pipeline combining deep learning for component detection, connected-component labeling for inferring connectivity, OCR for component reference designators, and a Vision-Language Model for assigning designators; specialized crossing-wires detection to distinguish connections from wire crossings; validation via graph isomorphism; open-source implementation.

Result: Netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, outpacing state-of-the-art methods by 2.72x.

Conclusion: SINA demonstrates generalizable IC- and PCB-level schematic-to-netlist conversion with high accuracy, enabling simulations, verification, and AI-model training; open-source resource with potential for broader adoption, though performance depends on dataset diversity and schematic style variations.

Abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

</details>


### [198] [MKGR: Multimodal Knowledge-Graph Representation Learning for Cold-Start Protein-Protein Interaction Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01627)
*Wenbo Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multimodal framework for cold-start PPI prediction that fuses region-aware protein sequences with four protein-centered knowledge graphs via graph attention, a bridge reconstruction objective, and a pair-level gating mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cold-start PPI prediction where proteins have no observed PPI edges during training; network topology alone is insufficient, necessitating integration of sequence information and rich biomedical knowledge.

Method: 1) Region-aware sequence encoding for context-rich protein representations; 2) Graph attention encoders for four modalities: protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, protein-lncRNA; 3) Bridge reconstruction objective to recover shared protein-entity associations and regularize graph learning; 4) Pair-level gating module to adaptively fuse sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair.

Result: On two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings, method consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

Conclusion: Multimodal integration of sequence context and diverse protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, with bridging regularization and adaptive fusion, enhances cold-start PPI prediction and improves generalization to unseen proteins.

Abstract: Accurate protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction is central to functional genomics, disease mechanism discovery, and drug development. A difficult setting arises when candidate interactions include proteins that have no observed PPI edges during training, where models relying on network topology alone often lose useful context. This paper presents \method, a multimodal representation framework for cold-start PPI prediction. \method\ combines region-aware protein sequence encoding with four protein-centered biomedical knowledge graphs, including protein-drug, protein-disease, protein-miRNA, and protein-lncRNA associations. The sequence branch extracts contextual representations from structurally informed sequence regions, while graph attention encoders learn modality-specific protein embeddings from sparse biomedical associations. A bridge reconstruction objective regularizes graph learning by recovering shared protein-entity associations, and a pair-level gating module adaptively integrates sequence and graph evidence for each candidate protein pair. Experiments on two benchmark datasets under novel-old and novel-novel cold-start settings show that \method\ consistently outperforms competitive sequence, network, and knowledge-graph baselines across ACC, F1, AUC, AUPR, and MCC.

</details>


### [199] [DeadPool: Resilient LLM Training with Hot-Swapping via Zero-Overhead Checkpoint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01646)
*Haotian Xie,Junlin Chen,Mingkai Zheng,Lishan Yang,Zhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DeadPool is a fault-tolerance system for large-scale LLM training that achieves zero overhead during failure-free execution and rapid recovery under node failures by hot-swapping failed workers with spares using in-memory checkpointing and a dynamic communicator reconstruction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing fault-tolerance approaches for LLM training trade off between per-iteration overhead during normal operation and recovery latency after failures, especially with permanent node failures; a solution that minimizes both is highly desirable for scaling LLM training.

Method: Two core ideas: (1) off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing for spatial redundancy to enable rapid reuse of memory state; (2) runtime communicator reconstruction protocol to swap in spare nodes for failed ones without terminating the job; these are overlapped with computation to incur zero overhead in failure-free execution; memory state can be rebuilt from in-memory checkpoints to minimize recomputation after permanent failures.

Result: Empirical evaluation up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and LLMs up to 65B params shows zero overhead during normal execution and hot-swapping recovery completes in under 40 seconds.

Conclusion: DeadPool demonstrates that zero-overhead failure-free operation and very low recovery cost are compatible for large-scale LLM training, effectively addressing the Pareto frontier between overhead and recovery latency.

Abstract: State-of-the-art large language model (LLM) training takes tens of thousands of graphics processing units (GPUs) for months and encounters failures across the software and hardware stack. Existing fault-tolerance mechanisms either impose non-trivial overhead during failure-free execution or suffer from prolonged recovery latency, particularly under scenarios where a small subset of compute nodes experience permanent failures. %The tradeoff between failure-free overhead and recovery latency forms a space forms a Pareto frontier We present DeadPool to simultaneously address both optimization objectives. DeadPool incorporates a fault-tolerance mechanism that restores LLM training via hot-swapping, namely by replacing failed nodes with spare nodes without terminating the complete job. The hot-swapping of DeadPool is enabled by two ideas: First, it exploits an off-critical-path in-memory checkpointing mechanism for spatial redundancy. Second, it introduces a communicator reconstruction protocol that replaces failed nodes with spare nodes at runtime. DeadPool efficiently overlaps the in-memory checkpointing with computation, thus introducing zero overhead during error-free execution. Upon permanent node failures, DeadPool can rebuild memory states with minimal recomputation by leveraging in-memory checkpoints. We evaluate DeadPool across scales (up to 512 NVIDIA A100 GPUs) and LLMs (up to 65B parameters), and observe zero checkpoint overhead with hot-swapping recovery completing in under 40 seconds. These results show that DeadPool simultaneously achieves both zero-overhead error-free execution and extremely low recovery cost.

</details>


### [200] [CALM: Interpretable Cross-Modal Alignment for Biomarker Discovery from Unpaired Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01656)
*Jueqi Wang,Zachary Jacokes,John Darrell Van Horn,Kevin A. Pelphrey,Michael C. Schatz,Archana Venkataraman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CALM learns interpretable cross-modal associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from disjoint populations by projecting to a shared latent space; it generalizes to unseen paired data and reveals pathway-ROI links in autism, enabling use of unimodal datasets for cross-modal brain disorder studies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Lack of large paired neuroimaging-genetics datasets; existing work relies on unimodal data. CALM aims to leverage large unimodal repositories to study cross-modal brain–genetic interactions in neuropsychiatric disorders.

Method: CALM uses linear projections to map neuroimaging ROIs and genetic pathways into a common latent space. It optimizes to align class-conditional latent distributions and enforce group separability, yielding interpretable ROI–pathway associations. Trained on unimodal data, CALM generalizes to unseen paired datasets and its associations are analyzed for stability.

Result: CALM outperforms state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines on generalization to unseen paired data. It shows stability of learned associations against a paired baseline. In autism-spectrum disorder experiments, CALM identifies immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions, aligning with established literature.

Conclusion: CALM enables leveraging large unimodal repositories to study cross-modal brain–genetic interactions across disparate datasets, providing interpretable ROI–pathway links and robust generalization to unseen paired data.

Abstract: The interaction between brain structure and genetic influences is key to understanding neuropsychiatric disorders. However, most large-scale datasets are unimodal, providing either neuroimaging or genetics data. We propose CALM, a framework that learns interpretable associations between brain ROIs and genetic pathways from completely disjoint populations. CALM aligns the two modalities in a shared latent space via linear projections that simultaneously match the class-conditional latent distributions and ensure group separability. These projections provide interpretable pathway--ROI associations. When trained on unimodal imaging and genetics datasets, CALM generalizes to an unseen paired dataset, outperforming several state-of-the-art methods and ablation baselines. We also demonstrate stability of the learned associations against a paired baseline. Our experiments on autism spectrum disorder reveal immune and metabolic pathways linked to specific cortical regions and are consistent with established literature. Thus, CALM opens the door to leveraging large unimodal repositories for studying cross-modal interactions in brain disorders across disparate datasets.

</details>


### [201] [Message Passing Based Two-Timescale Bayesian Learning for Joint Channel and Memory Hardware Impairments Tracking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01660)
*Wei Xu,An Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel two-timescale Bayesian deep learning framework jointly tracking channels and hardware impairments in massive MIMO, using RGRU modeling for intra-slot memory and Turbo-OAMP/DAMP with EP for iterative inference across fast-varying channels and slow-varying impairment parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hardware impairments induce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling that degrade channel estimation in massive MIMO; a joint, timescale-aware approach is needed to robustly track both the channel and the slowly drifting hardware impairments.

Method: Model intra-slot impairment memory with Residual Gated Recurrent Unit (RGRU); formulate a multi-slot factor graph with fast-varying Markov prior for the channel and slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior for impairment parameters. Use a two-module intra-slot graph: (1) channel-tracking via Turbo-OAMP for sparse channel estimation; (2) impairments-calibration via DAMP; exchange extrinsic information through Expectation Propagation (EP) between modules; inter-slot messages have closed-form updates.

Result: The framework achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators across various online impairment scenarios and SNRs, demonstrating robust joint tracking of channels and impairments.

Conclusion: A scalable, timescale-aware Bayesian framework with RGRU modeling and Turbo-OAMP/DAMP inference yields improved channel estimation under hardware impairments in massive MIMO.

Abstract: Hardware impairments in massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) receivers introduce inter-symbol memory and inter-element coupling, severely degrading channel estimation. This paper employs a residual recurrent gated unit (RGRU) to model the intra-slot memory of the hardware impairments and proposes a message-passing-based two-timescale Bayesian deep learning (MP-TTBDL) framework for joint channel and impairment tracking. Owing to small-scale fading, the wireless channel varies rapidly across slots, whereas hardware impairments drift slowly due to hardware aging and environmental variations. To capture these distinct physical timescales, a fastvarying Markov prior and a slow-varying Gaussian Markov prior are assigned to the sparse channel and the network parameters, respectively. Based on a multi-slot factor graph formulation, a message-passing algorithm is developed. Specifically, the inter-slot messages admit closed-form updates, while the intra-slot factor graph, due to its complex recurrent structure, is partitioned into a channel tracking module and an impairments calibration module. The channel tracking module performs sparse channel estimation via turbo orthogonal approximate message passing (Turbo-OAMP), and the impairments calibration module updates the impairment parameters via a specially designed deep approximate message passing (DAMP) procedure, with the two modules iteratively exchanging extrinsic information through expectation propagation (EP) until convergence. Simulation results show that the proposed framework robustly achieves lower channel estimation error than conventional compensators followed by channel estimation across different online impairment scenarios and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions.

</details>


### [202] [Revisiting Decentralized Online Convex Optimization with Compressed Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01665)
*Hao Zhou,Xiaoyu Wang,Chang Yao,Mingli Song,Yuanyu Wan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (FTRL)–type algorithms are proposed for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication. They leverage dual updates to adapt average consensus with compression. The full-information variant matches existing regret bounds; the bandit variant improves regret and communication costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce communication bottlenecks in decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) with streaming data by leveraging FTRL machinery and compression, extending to the bandit setting.

Method: Introduce two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compression. Use dual update structure to unify consensus with compressed communication. First algorithm targets full-information feedback and achieves regret bounds comparable to state-of-the-art OGD-based methods. Second algorithm handles bandit feedback, yielding improved regret bounds and lower communication costs compared to previous bandit approaches.

Result: Full-information algorithm attains regret bounds matching existing OGD/FTRL benchmarks. Bandit algorithm achieves significantly better regret and reduced communication costs than prior work.

Conclusion: FTRL-based D-OCO with compression offers a cleaner algorithmic design and tighter analyses, connecting dual averaging with compressed consensus. It extends the effectiveness of FTRL to both full-information and bandit settings in decentralized online learning.

Abstract: Decentralized online convex optimization (D-OCO) is a popular framework for distributed applications with streaming data. To tackle the communication bottleneck, previous studies have investigated D-OCO with compressed communication and proposed several algorithms that are variants of online gradient descent (OGD). However, for D-OCO with exact communication, the best existing algorithms are variants of follow-the-regularized-leader (FTRL). In this paper, for the first time, we propose two FTRL-type algorithms for D-OCO with compressed communication. Compared with OGD-type algorithms, our algorithms are more elegant in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. The key insight is that the dual update mechanism of FTRL allows us to make a simple application of the technique for average consensus with communication compression. More specifically, our first algorithm considers the full-information setting, and can match the existing regret bounds. Our second algorithm is designed for the bandit setting, and can significantly improve both the regret bounds and communication costs of existing algorithms.

</details>


### [203] [UniWind: Toward Unified Day-Ahead Wind Power Forecasting via Physics-Informed State Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01670)
*Ronghui Xu,Tongxin Wu,Guozhen Zhang,Yihan Li,Chenjuan Guo,Bin Yang,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: UniWind combines physics-informed priors with latent state routing to improve day-ahead wind power forecasts, achieving strong accuracy and cross-farm robustness across 20+ real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the entanglement of meteorological effects with site-specific operational states in wind power forecasts and the limited cross-site generalization of purely physical or purely data-driven models.

Method: Physical Prior Estimator: site-conditioned monotonic warping + shared physical power curve; Physical upper-bound constraint as soft envelope. Latent State Encoder: models operating-state embeddings. State-aware Power Corrector: knowledge-guided supervised state routing with bounded, state-specific experts to transform the physical prior into final forecasts.

Result: Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on >20 real-world datasets demonstrate accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

Conclusion: Physically guided state routing yields accurate, robust day-ahead wind power forecasts and improved cross-site generalization compared to baseline models.

Abstract: Day-ahead wind power forecasting is essential for cost-effective power-system operation. It is primarily driven by future meteorological conditions while retaining temporal dependencies in power generation. In practice, observed wind-farm power often entangles physically available power with local environmental effects and latent operational states, such as shutdowns and curtailment. Existing physical models provide useful constraints but adapt poorly across wind farms, whereas data-driven models can capture rich correlations but often conflate meteorological effects with state-induced deviations. In this study, we propose UniWind, a wind power forecasting model based on physics-informed state routing. UniWind first employs a Physical Prior Estimator to construct a site-calibrated physical prior by combining site-conditioned monotonic warping with a shared physical power curve. It further applies a physical upper-bound constraint to shape this prior as a soft envelope of available wind power generation. UniWind then proposes a Latent State Encoder to model operating-state embeddings and transforms the physical prior into final power forecasts through a State-aware Power Corrector, which uses knowledge-guided supervised state routing and bounded, state-specific expert correction. Full-shot and cross-farm zero-shot experiments on more than 20 real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of UniWind.

</details>


### [204] [SCAPE: Accurate and Efficient LLM Training with Extreme Sparse Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01678)
*Mingkai Zheng,Junlin Chen,Haotian Xie,Zhao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCAPE is a sparsified, first-moment-based distributed optimizer that enables aggressive gradient sparsification for LLM pre-training without sacrificing model quality, achieving notable wall-clock and per-step speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Communication becomes the dominant cost in data-parallel and sharded LLM training. Classic sparsification on raw gradients can destabilize Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, while quantization has limited theoretical savings and incur runtime overhead. A method that preserves optimizer stability while reducing communication is highly desirable.

Method: SCAPE derives sparsification masks from first-moment statistics (AdamS) rather than raw gradients, distributes mask generation across workers to match optimizer sharding, and delays applying masks by one step to allow overlap between computation and mask synchronization. It reconstructs second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer to avoid extra collectives, and is implemented in Megatron-LM. Evaluations train GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 GH200 GPUs; targets 90% and 99% sparsity respectively.

Result: SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under very high sparsity (90% for GPT-345M and 99% for Llama-500M). It achieves up to 43.3% end-to-end wall-clock time reduction on Llama-500M and up to 3.26x speedup per step on Llama-1.8B, compared to dense AdamS (and with quality comparable to dense AdamW/AdamS).

Conclusion: SCAPE demonstrates that first-moment-based sparsification with careful mask distribution and synchronization can dramatically reduce communication in LLM pre-training while preserving model quality, enabling substantial training-time improvements across model scales.

Abstract: Communication increasingly dominates the cost of Large Language Model (LLM) pre-training, especially under data-parallel and sharded training schemes, where gradient synchronization and parameter reconstruction overhead increase with model size and system scale. Existing communication-reduction methods either sparsify raw gradients, which can be unstable for modern Adam-style optimizers at high sparsity, or quantize communication, whose savings are fundamentally bounded by bit width and often incur additional runtime overhead. We present SCAPE, a communication-efficient distributed optimizer for LLM training that exploits the stability of AdamS's first-moment to enable aggressive sparsification without loss of LLM quality. Instead of constructing masks from raw gradients, SCAPE derives them from first-moment-based statistics, partitions mask generation across workers to align with optimizer sharding, and delays mask usage by one step so that mask synchronization can overlap with computation. SCAPE also reconstructs the quantities required for second-moment updates from a single synchronized sparse buffer, avoiding an additional collective. We implement SCAPE in Megatron-LM and evaluate its convergence by pre-training GPT-345M on OpenWebText and Llama-500M on SlimPajama-6B using 32 NVIDIA GH200 GPUs on TACC Vista. In both models, SCAPE preserves training stability, validation loss, and downstream task accuracy under 90\% and 99\% sparsity. For Llama-500M, SCAPE reduces end-to-end pre-training wall-clock time by up to 43.3\% while maintaining model quality comparable to dense AdamW and AdamS. For Llama-1.8B, SCAPE achieves up to 3.26$\times$ speedup per step compared to dense AdamS.

</details>


### [205] [WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01686)
