Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

</details>


### [231] [Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01943)
*Giacomo Cappiello,Filippo Caruso,Xing Liang,Dimitrios Makris*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks applied to NLP tasks (COVID tweet sentiment analysis and SMS spam classification) show comparable accuracy to classical models and improved transfer performance, with distinct learning dynamics suggesting enhanced representational capacity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess feasibility and potential benefits of quantum machine learning (QML) in natural language processing, focusing on sentiment analysis and transfer learning for text classification using hybrid quantum circuits.

Method: Vectorize text with TF-IDF and feed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits; evaluate on a COVID-19 tweet sentiment dataset; apply transfer learning to an SMS spam dataset; compare accuracy and learning dynamics (validation loss/accuracy).

Result: Hybrid models achieve accuracy comparable to classical baselines for sentiment analysis and exhibit distinct learning dynamics implying richer representations; in transfer learning for spam detection, hybrids outperform classical models, achieving 81% accuracy on the spam class versus 66% for the classical baseline (a 15-point gain).

Conclusion: The results support the feasibility of quantum-classical hybrids for NLP tasks and suggest potential generalization and representational benefits as quantum hardware improves.

Abstract: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

</details>


### [232] [A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01958)
*Koki Konishi,Masataka Ushiku,Yuta Saito*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A/B testing can incur higher algorithm selection errors than offline evaluation due to lack of positive correlation between estimates; introducing a hypothetical middle algorithm to induce correlation enables online evaluation to match offline performance with less A/B data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explain a counterintuitive gap where offline evaluation may outperform A/B testing in terms of selection accuracy, and to reduce online experimentation cost by leveraging correlation in estimates.

Method: Introduce a stepwise estimator using a hypothetical middle algorithm (A, M, B). At each step, reuse shared offline data to evaluate performance differences, applying offline evaluation techniques to induce positive correlation among comparisons. Derive the optimal middle algorithm by variance minimization and perform bias-variance analysis.

Result: The estimator achieves variance reduction via induced correlation and, on real-world data, attains the same algorithm-selection error rate as existing approaches while using only half the A/B testing data.

Conclusion: Inducing positive correlation through a staged, middle-algorithm approach reconciles offline and online evaluation for more reliable algorithm selection, reducing data requirements; theoretical and empirical results support the approach, with potential extensions to broader settings.

Abstract: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

</details>


### [233] [Probabilistic Low-Voltage Peak Load Forecasting with Time Series Foundation Models Evaluated on Application-Oriented Metrics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01966)
*Benedikt Kaas,Manuel Treutlein,Hannes Benedikt Gerber,Oliver Neumann,Cheewan Phatthanakhuha,Oliver Resch,Ralf Mikut,Veit Hagenmeyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Time series foundation models (notably Chronos-2) improve short-term net load forecasts for 200 real-world low-voltage feeders, with strong robustness to missing weather covariates and a novel peak-focused metric for grid planning decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for accurate, uncertainty-aware short-term low-voltage load forecasts that capture peak behavior and are evaluated against grid-relevant criteria.

Method: Extensive empirical evaluation of 200 real-world feeders comparing Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2, and TabPFN-TS against six baselines; ablation by removing weather covariates; introduction of an application-oriented metric linking forecast quality to peak planning costs and risk.

Result: Chronos-2 yields the strongest performance among the tested models; all time series foundation models adapt to higher uncertainty when weather data are omitted; the new metric demonstrates practical implications for the trade-off between cost reduction and minimizing failure risk in grid asset planning and operation.

Conclusion: Time series foundation models are effective for short-term low-voltage load forecasting and peak prediction, offering robust performance under missing weather information; the proposed metric connects forecasting to grid planning decisions, highlighting operational value.

Abstract: Low-voltage load forecasting is an important component in current and future energy systems with a high degree of electrification and decentralized generation. However, current forecasting methods require significant manual effort, often lack uncertainty estimation and proper peak prediction, and they are often not adequately evaluated in terms of grid requirements. In the present study, we provide an extensive evaluation of short-term net load forecasts of 200 real-world low-voltage feeders with a focus on the rapidly evolving time series foundation models. Our study compares Chronos-Bolt, Chronos-2 and TabPFN-TS to six baseline models and demonstrates superior performance, in particular for Chronos-2. An ablation study, in which weather covariates are omitted, shows that time series foundation models adapt to increased uncertainty, despite the importance of weather information. A novel application-oriented metric links the model's forecasting capabilities in peak prediction to the trade-off in grid asset planning and operation between cost reduction and minimizing the risk of failure.

</details>


### [234] [Do Newer Lightweight CNNs Perform Better Under Resource Constraints? A Controlled Multigenerational Study of Architecture, Initialization, Training Budget, and Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01984)
*Tasnim Shahriar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A benchmarking study of nine lightweight CNN packages across CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet shows EfficientNetV2-S achieves top accuracy on CIFAR datasets, while EfficientNet-B0 offers a strong trade-off with near-best accuracy and substantially fewer parameters and GMACs; latency varies by hardware; no universal winner; design gains are selective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To critically evaluate claims of deployment efficiency and predictive performance in lightweight CNNs by benchmarking them under a unified protocol across datasets and hardware, and to examine whether improvements translate to real-world latency and resource usage.

Method: 9 lightweight CNN packages evaluated across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet using a shared downstream protocol. Metrics collected include top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on NVIDIA L4 GPU and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA memory, and Pareto frontiers. Analyses include pretrained vs randomly initialized vs trained-from-scratch conditions, and hardware-aware latency comparisons.

Result: EfficientNetV2-S records the highest top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 (97.57%) and CIFAR-100 (86.98%). RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet (79.87%). EfficientNet-B0 is within 0.22pp (CIFAR-10), 0.85pp (CIFAR-100), and 1.79pp (Tiny ImageNet) of the best results while using ~79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. EfficientNet-B0 appears on every accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMACs and is the fastest under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, MobileNetV3-Small leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S on accuracy by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points (with nonzero confidence intervals for fixed trained models). EfficientNet-B0’s scratch training from random initialization lags behind its pretrained counterpart by 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points after 100 epochs, despite fivefold longer training time. SqueezeNet1.1 uses the fewest parameters and shows the lowest peak CUDA allocation but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ between the L4 GPU and CPU environments, indicating GMACs alone do not predict real-world inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains.

Conclusion: Newer CNN lightweight designs do not universally outperform earlier architectures; EfficientNet-B0 emerges as the most consistently competitive option in intermediate budgets, but hardware and training regime (pretrained vs random) strongly modulate gains. Real-world latency is not fully captured by GMACs, underscoring the need for hardware-aware benchmarking.

Abstract: Newer lightweight convolutional neural networks are often presented as improving predictive performance and deployment efficiency, but such claims require controlled evaluation. This study compares nine lightweight CNN model packages across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet under a shared downstream protocol. We report top-1 accuracy, macro F1, top-5 accuracy, parameter count, FP32 storage, GMACs, batch-size-1 latency on an NVIDIA L4 and AMD Ryzen 5 5500U CPU, peak PyTorch CUDA allocated tensor memory, and point estimate Pareto frontiers. EfficientNetV2-S achieves the highest observed top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at 97.57% and 86.98%, while RepViT-M1.0 leads Tiny ImageNet at 79.87%. EfficientNet-B0 remains within 0.22, 0.85, and 1.79 percentage points of the best result on the three datasets while using approximately 79% fewer parameters and 86% fewer GMACs than EfficientNetV2-S. It also appears on every evaluated accuracy and resource Pareto frontier, making it the most consistently competitive intermediate-budget option. MobileNetV3-Small has the lowest GMAC count, is the fastest model under both CPU thread settings, and records higher observed accuracy than MobileNetV4-Conv-S on all three datasets. Under random initialization, it leads MobileNetV4-Conv-S by 2.55, 1.76, and 0.99 points, with paired test-set intervals excluding zero for the fixed trained models. EfficientNet-B0 remains 3.29, 10.10, and 17.54 points below its pretrained counterpart after 100 epochs of scratch training, despite requiring about five times the recorded training time. SqueezeNet1.1 has the fewest parameters and lowest peak CUDA allocation, but substantially weaker accuracy. Latency rankings differ sharply between the L4 and CPU environments, showing that GMACs alone do not predict measured inference performance. Overall, newer designs provide selective rather than universal gains

</details>


### [235] [Liquid Latent State Dynamics for Interpretable Turbofan Degradation Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01986)
*Weizhi Nie,Weijie Wang,Yuting Su*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A liquid latent dynamics model for aircraft engine health monitoring disentangles degradation and operating-condition latent spaces, yielding improved sensor forecasting and a more interpretable degradation axis, while RUL regression remains stronger with standard GRU baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the lack of a coherent, exposeable degradation process in multivariate prognostics by explicitly separating health evolution from operating-condition variation.

Method: Encode a history window into a latent state, evolve it with a liquid transition model, and decode future sensor observations. Factorize the latent state into degradation and condition components. Train with supervision signals for degradation (remaining useful life, monotonic risk, latent-consistency) and with auxiliary losses to discourage operating-condition leakage (condition prediction, decorrelation). Evaluate on C-MAPSS FD001–FD004.

Result: Sensor forecasting RMSE improves from 0.2438 (GRU baseline) to 0.2266, with the largest gains on multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state aligns with degradation speed, achieving an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct RUL regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating the proposed representation currently functions better as an interpretable degradation-world model than as a calibrated lifetime regressor.

Conclusion: Liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling, yielding a clearer degradation axis and improved forecasting, though direct RUL estimation may still favor traditional sequence models.

Abstract: Multivariate time-series models for prognostics are often evaluated by point prediction accuracy, yet their internal states rarely expose a coherent degradation process. We study liquid neural networks as latent dynamics models for aircraft engine health monitoring on the C-MAPSS benchmark. The proposed model encodes a history window into a latent state, evolves that state with a liquid transition model, and decodes future sensor observations. To separate health evolution from operating-condition variation, the latent state is factorized into degradation and condition components. Remaining useful life, monotonic risk, and latent-consistency losses supervise the degradation component, while condition prediction and decorrelation losses discourage operating-condition leakage. Across FD001--FD004, the full disentangled model improves overall sensor forecasting RMSE from 0.2438 for a GRU baseline to 0.2266, with the largest gains on the multi-condition subsets FD002 and FD004. The learned degradation state also forms a clearer temporal degradation axis, reaching an average state-speed Spearman correlation of 0.5960. Direct remaining-useful-life regression remains stronger for the GRU baseline, indicating that the proposed representation is currently more effective as an interpretable world model for degradation dynamics than as a calibrated lifetime regressor. These results suggest that liquid latent dynamics can bridge predictive maintenance forecasting and inspectable health-state modeling.

</details>


### [236] [Fast and Accurate Anomaly Detection in Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02046)
*Emanuele Mele,Massimo Cafaro,Angelo Coluccia,Italo Epicoco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unsupervised time-series anomaly detector using Haar discrete wavelet and a designed t-test; theoretical grounding and strong empirical performance across 343 datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address label scarcity and class imbalance in anomaly detection; reduce dependence on labeled anomalies and lower false positives in unsupervised settings; provide a principled statistical approach.

Method: Apply Haar discrete wavelet transform to time-series data and develop a tailored t-test on the resulting coefficients; provide theoretical justification for the test; validate experimentally.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised baselines across a large suite of 343 datasets, demonstrating robust anomaly detection capability.

Conclusion: Introduces a principled unsupervised framework for time-series anomaly detection with both theoretical support and broad empirical validation; suitable for deployment in safety-critical contexts.

Abstract: Anomaly detection is a critical and evolving field in Machine Learning, with applications targeting different domains such as cybersecurity, finance, healthcare, manufacturing and IoT (Internet of Things) systems. Traditionally, anomaly detection algorithms have been designed using both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms. The fundamental challenge in real-world anomaly detection scenarios is related to the inherent class imbalance (anomalies are typically rare) and, for supervised methods, to the scarcity of labelled anomalous data. Indeed, labelling is both expensive and time-consuming. Conversely unsupervised methods do not require labelling, but may suffer from high false positive rates when deployed in safety-critical applications. In this work we introduce a novel unsupervised algorithm for anomaly detection in time series based on the Haar discrete wavelet and a suitably designed $t$-test. We establish the theoretical foundation of the proposed $t$-test and, through extensive experimentation across 343 datasets, demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised and self-supervised benchmarks.

</details>


### [237] [A Memory Efficient Unified Algorithm for Online Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02050)
*Yuval Ran-Milo,Angelos Assos,Elad Hazan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An online learning approach for stabilizing unknown linear dynamical systems (LDS) with sublinear regret, parameterized by instability complexity k. Proposes a unified algorithm achieving O~(k) parameters, proves a matching lower bound (k filters) for filter-based predictors, and validates the theory with experiments showing improved performance under a fixed budget.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Stabilize general unknown LDS from streaming observations via online prediction while keeping memory and computation aligned with intrinsic instability, not full state dimension. Identify a complexity measure (k) that captures feasible stabilization regimes.

Method: Develop a unified online predictor applicable to all LDS (including non-diagonalizable and complex/exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count ~ O~(k). Establish regret guarantees (sublinear) and a matching lower bound. Provide empirical evaluation on high-dimensional systems comparing with prior methods at equal parameter budgets.

Result: Proves sublinear regret with memory footprint adapting to k; shows any filter-based predictor requires at least k filters; empirical results demonstrate superior performance over prior methods for the same parameter budget on a high-dimensional system.

Conclusion: Instability complexity k effectively governs stabilization feasibility. The proposed online algorithm achieves near-optimal parameter efficiency (~k) with sublinear regret and supports non-diagonalizable and complex explosion modes. A matching lower bound confirms the necessity of k; experiments confirm practical advantage.

Abstract: Motivated by the challenge of stabilizing a general unknown linear dynamical system (LDS) from observations, we study the natural prerequisite of online prediction. Our goal is to achieve sublinear regret with a memory footprint that adapts to the intrinsic complexity of the dynamics rather than the full hidden -- state dimension. We focus on the practically central regime of systems with low instability complexity -- eigenvalues outside the real stable interval that do not decay rapidly, together with non-semisimple modes-potentially embedded in an otherwise stable real spectrum of much higher dimension; we write $k$ for this count. This regime is the primary setting in which stabilization is plausible: we show that many systems with high instability complexity cannot be stabilized without exponentially large controls. Thus, prediction is meaningful for stabilization precisely when the instability complexity is small. Within this regime, we introduce a unified online algorithm that handles every LDS (including non-diagonalizable systems with complex or exploding modes) with a learnable parameter count of $\widetilde{O}(k)$. Finally, we prove a lower bound showing that $k$ is a valid complexity measure: any filter-based predictor needs at least $k$ filters. Experiments corroborate our theory: on a high-dimensional system, our predictor sharply outperforms prior methods at an equal parameter budget.

</details>


### [238] [Beyond the Performance Illusion: Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization for Spatially Correlated Domains](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02055)
*Prathamesh Patil,Arpit Jain,Aswanth Krishnan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spatiotemporal correlations in data break i.i.d. splits, causing data leakage and hidden stratification; introduce SASP for structure-aware partitioning and CDRO for curriculum-based distributionally robust optimization; together improve generalization, calibration, and reveal failure modes under non-random splits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional random data splits assume i.i.d. data, which is violated in spatially/temporally correlated domains, leading to overoptimistic performance and undiscovered failures.

Method: 1) Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP): creates validation splits with reduced spatiotemporal leakage while maintaining class balance. 2) Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO): a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust optimization to stabilize learning under the stricter splits.

Result: Across multiple benchmarks, the SASP/CDRO combination yields better generalization, improved confidence calibration, and reveals failure modes hidden by random-split evaluation.

Conclusion: A unified framework with SASP and CDRO provides more reliable evaluation and training for spatially correlated data, mitigating leakage and hidden stratification and exposing robustness limitations of standard methods.

Abstract: Performance evaluation in AI systems commonly assumes that random dataset splits produce independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) subsets. We show that this assumption often breaks down in spatiotemporally correlated domains such as aerial surveillance, precision agriculture, and medical imaging, leading to two systematic failures: data leakage, where correlated samples span training and validation splits and inflate performance estimates, and hidden stratification, where errors on minority subpopulations are obscured by aggregate metrics. To address these issues, we propose a unified evaluation and training framework for spatially correlated data. We introduce Structure-Aware Stratified Partitioning (SASP), which constructs validation splits that reduce spatiotemporal leakage while preserving meaningful class balance, and Curriculum Distributionally Robust Optimization (CDRO), a curriculum-based relaxation of distributionally robust training that stabilizes optimization under these stricter splits. Across multiple benchmarks, this combination yields consistently improved generalization, more reliable confidence calibration, and exposes failure modes that remain hidden under conventional random-split evaluation.

</details>


### [239] [SA-HGNN: Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network for EEG-Based Depression Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02063)
*Yang Li,Pan Hu,Yan Zhang,Wenfan Yang,Tao Wu,Lianbo Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN) to model hierarchical depression-related brain networks for EEG-based depression recognition using three modules: sample-adaptive graph construction, hyperbolic graph convolution, and attention pooling; demonstrates superior performance and robustness to noise on public EEG datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Depression-related brain networks exhibit inherent hierarchical structure that is difficult to capture with Euclidean GNNs. Personalized topology construction and a hyperbolic geometry framework can better model hierarchical connectivity and improve EEG-based depression recognition, especially in noisy data.

Method: Three-module architecture: (1) Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction to dynamically build personalized brain network graphs; (2) Hyperbolic Graph Convolution to exploit hyperbolic geometry for latent hierarchical relationships; (3) Attention Pooling to filter noisy EEG channels and reduce interference with hierarchical topology. Evaluated on public EEG datasets across resting-state and task paradigms under robustness to noise.

Result: The method achieves superior performance across resting-state and task-related paradigms, and demonstrates robustness to noise while effectively capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in depression-related brain networks.

Conclusion: SA-HGNN effectively captures authentic hierarchical topology in depression-affected brain networks and improves EEG-based depression recognition with adaptive graph construction, hyperbolic message passing, and noise-aware pooling.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely used to capture spatial functional connectivity patterns to improve electroencephalography (EEG)-based depression recognition performance. However, the functional connectivity of brain networks in patients with depression exhibits an inherent hierarchical structure, making it difficult to capture accurate connection patterns. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel model named Sample-Adaptive Hyperbolic Graph Neural Network (SA-HGNN), which aims to accurately extract the authentic hierarchical structure of depression-affected brain networks. Specifically, the proposed model comprises three core modules. First, a Sample-Adaptive Graph Construction module dynamically constructs personalized brain network topologies to capture more complex spatial relationships within the brain network. Second, hyperbolic graph convolution is employed to overcome the representation bottlenecks of Euclidean space, leveraging hyperbolic geometry to precisely capture latent hierarchical relationships within the brain network. Finally, an Attention Pooling module adaptively filters out highly redundant noise channels in EEG signals, effectively mitigating the interference of inherent noise on the authentic hierarchical topology. Extensive experiments on public EEG datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method across resting-state and task-related paradigms, validating its robustness to noise and efficacy in capturing abnormal functional connectivity patterns in brain networks of patients with depression.

</details>


### [240] [kNNGuard: Turning LLM Hidden Activations into a Training-Free Configurable Guardrail](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02072)
*Mahmoud Abdelfattah,Hamid Nasiri,Peter Garraghan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: kNNGuard is a training-free guardrail that leverages LLM activation and embedding spaces via multi-layer kNN fusion on a small bank of 50 prompts to detect unsafe or off-topic prompts, achieving strong F1 with low latency and easy domain adaptation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce reliance on fine-tuning-based classifiers, which often generalize poorly and incur high inference costs, by providing a fast, adaptable guardrail that can operate without gradient updates.

Method: Use an off-the-shelf LLM to extract hidden activations for a small bank (≈50) of safe/unsafe prompts; compute multi-layer kNN scores in activation-space and embedding-space; fuse scores for final classification without gradient updates; adapt domain by updating the labeled bank (fast, requires ≈10 seconds).

Result: Demonstrates competitive or superior F1 across six domains compared with fine-tuned guardrails; achieves 2.7× speed-up over the best comparable guardrail and ≈10× faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier; low-latency integration and analysis of prompts, layers, and system prompts.

Conclusion: A training-free, activation-space kNN fusion approach yields effective, low-latency guardrails with rapid domain adaptation, suitable for production LLM pipelines without retraining.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in domains requiring guardrails to detect unsafe, off-topic, or adversarial prompts. Existing guardrails predominately rely on fine-tuning to build classifiers, which often suffer from low generalization and high inference latency. We present kNNGuard, a training-free guardrail that utilizes the activation space of an off-the-shelf LLM. Given a small bank of 50 safe and unsafe prompts, kNNGuard extracts hidden activations and performs multi-layer kNN fusing activation-space and embedding-space scores for classification. Across six domains spanning topical and security prompts, kNNGuard achieves competitive or superior F1 compared to fine-tuned state-of-the-art guardrails while running 2.7x faster than the best comparable guardrail, and 10x faster than a fine-tuned safety classifier without gradient updates or fine-tuning. Domain adaptation requires only updating the labeled bank, which can be constructed in under 10 seconds and several orders of magnitude faster than established guardrails. We also analyze the impact of system prompts, layer selection, and integration into production LLM pipelines as a configurable, low-latency guardrail.

</details>


### [241] [Fourier Neural Operators for Rayleigh-Bénard Convection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02088)
*Chelsea Maria John,Thibaut Lunet,Sebastian Götschel,Andreas Herten,Stefan Kesselheim,Daniel Ruprecht*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Improved Fourier Neural Operator for 2D Rayleigh–Bénard convection predicts time increments, achieving higher accuracy than a baseline FNO while remaining compact and fast; accuracy is still limited by training data resolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enhance accuracy and efficiency of neural-operator surrogates for time-evolving PDEs (Rayleigh–Bénard convection) and investigate how predicting time increments affects generalization to finer meshes.

Method: Modify the Fourier Neural Operator architecture to predict time increments (differences) rather than full solution fields; keep a compact model (≈314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and evaluate inference speed (~7 ms); train on 2D RB convection data and compare against standard FNO benchmarks.

Result: The time-increment FNO yields higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline, while maintaining a compact size and fast inference; performance is on par with previous benchmarks. FNOs can generalize to finer meshes, but accuracy remains constrained by the resolution of the training data.

Conclusion: Predicting time increments with FNOs is a viable strategy to boost accuracy and efficiency for 2D RB convection, but ultimate accuracy is limited by the resolution of the available training data; data quality and resolution are critical for further gains.

Abstract: We propose an improved Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for modeling two-dimensional Rayleigh-Bénard convection by predicting time increments instead of full solutions, achieving higher accuracy than a standard FNO baseline. The resulting model is compact (314k parameters, 1.26 MB) and fast (7 ms inference), while maintaining similar accuracy as demonstrated in previous benchmarks. We show that although FNOs generalize to finer meshes, accuracy remains limited by the resolution of the training data.

</details>


### [242] [Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02104)
*Jian Xu,Delu Zeng,John Paisley,Qibin Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian latent-quality modeling with judge-specific biases and a top-k aware active acquisition improves top-k identification under constrained comparisons for LLM judges; bias-rectification helps cheap/mid-tier judges while frontier judges are already accurate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs used as cheap, scalable judges are noisy and biased (verbosity, position effects) so naive vote aggregation yields rankings driven by presentation rather than true quality. The goal is reliable top-k identification under a fixed comparison budget.

Method: Model judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior to let data determine bias per judge. Introduce a top-k–aware active acquisition rule that selects the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about top-k membership, not full ranking.

Result: On a benchmark with 16 LLMs (open and proprietary families), naive aggregation yields wrong top-k under bias; the bias-aware model recovers the true top-k. The top-k–aware acquisition achieves this with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-optimal (global-uncertainty). Bias is real but heterogeneous: cheap/mid-tier judges show strong verbosity bias corrected by the model (recall improves from ~0.5–0.6 to 0.84–1.0), while frontier judges show little bias and require minimal adjustment.

Conclusion: Bias-aware judging is essential for accurate top-k identification under budget constraints. Modeling judge biases yields substantial gains for lower-quality judges, while advanced judges already rank accurately; activesense acquisition focusing on top-k membership reduces costs significantly.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

</details>


### [243] [Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02124)
*Varshith Roy Kotla*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Negative evaluation: rolling split-conformal volatility of RF residuals for per-driver slip prediction yields essentially zero precision/recall and high false alarms; exchangeability violated; no improvement over a simple baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether a conformal-prediction-based volatility signal can serve as a reliable pre-incident warning for traction loss in racing, addressing limitations of conventional post-adhesion-control strategies.

Method: Train per-driver Random Forest to predict slip; monitor volatility of non-conformity residuals; apply Rolling Split Conformal Prediction to detect anomalies; include vehicle speed as an explicit feature; evaluate on all laps (not just fastest) using timestamped FIA incident labels and track-limits deletions; compare against a static 95th-percentile threshold baseline.

Result: Across 19 drivers and 55,563 samples, the detector achieved mean precision ≈ 0 and mean recall ≈ 0 for 14 ground-truth incidents, flagging ~15.3% of samples as anomalous (high false-alarm rate). The 95th-percentile baseline performs no better. Ljung-Box tests (p < 0.001) indicate residual autocorrelation; exchangeability assumption of split conformal prediction is violated for every driver.

Conclusion: This is a rigorously documented negative finding. Likely causes include non-exchangeability/non-stationarity in residuals and inadequate features. A genuinely predictive version would require addressing the violated assumptions (e.g., time-varying calibration, hierarchical modeling, richer predictive features, or alternative anomaly definitions) and a dataset with sufficient events and stable temporal structure.

Abstract: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

</details>


### [244] [ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02137)
*Yilie Huang,Wenpin Tang,Xun Yu Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART) learns a continuous-time clock for score-based diffusion sampling, yielding adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. ART-RL extends this with a Gaussian-policy formulation, proving optimizer-level equivalence with ART, and derives practical actor–critic updates. Empirically, ART‑RL improves sample quality over fixed schedules and generalizes across budgets and pipelines, while requiring only a change to the timestep grid.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed, hand-crafted timestep schedules in discretized reverse-time diffusion are suboptimal. An adaptive, learnable time warp can allocate steps where the dynamics require higher resolution, potentially improving sample quality and efficiency.

Method: Frame scheduling as a continuous-time control problem: learn the speed of the sampling clock so a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in diffusion time. Use a leading-order Euler error surrogate as the objective. Solve via ART-RL, a randomized formulation with Gaussian policies; prove equivalence to ART at the optimizer level; develop policy evaluation/improvement and trajectory-based moment identities to enable actor–critic updates.

Result: Across controlled low-dimensional tasks and image generation, ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets. The learned timesteps generalize broadly, transferring across budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces without retraining.

Conclusion: Adaptive, learnable time-warping for diffusion sampling yields principled, effective timestep allocation with strong empirical gains and broad generalization, and it can be integrated into existing samplers by modifying only the timestep grid.

Abstract: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

</details>


### [245] [Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02140)
*Anna Karnysheva,Dietrich Klakow,Ji-Ung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Pre-training enhances molecular structure awareness in CLMs; ring substructures emerge even in random models; fine-tuning concentrates on task-relevant substructures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reveal which chemically meaningful substructures are encoded by CLMs trained on SMILES and to assess how pre-training and downstream fine-tuning shape these representations.

Method: Systematic probe of 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models; analysis of layer-wise encodings; examination of effects of fine-tuning on two chemical downstream tasks.

Result: Pre-training generally improves substructure awareness, especially in upper layers; randomly initialized models already capture ring structures in the first layer; fine-tuning preferentially affects substructures relevant to the specific task.

Conclusion: Findings support that pre-training enhances chemical structure awareness in CLMs, and that fine-tuning guides representations toward chemically theory-consistent, task-relevant substructures.

Abstract: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

</details>


### [246] [Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02142)
*Debopriya Ghosh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-model ML pipeline using ADNI data to detect early Alzheimer's; employs data imputation, SMOTE-based balancing, feature selection, a stacking ensemble, and an ANN; aims to identify a superior classifier and potential biomarkers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early detection of Alzheimer's disease enables timely intervention and better management; leveraging ADNI data across clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging measures to identify biomarkers.

Method: Handle missing data via iterative imputation; address class imbalance with Borderline SVM-SMOTE; perform wrapper-based and embedded feature selection; split data into training/testing with feature scaling; build a stacking ensemble of Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM; train an artificial neural network on the same dataset; evaluate using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.

Result: The study trains and compares multiple models, reporting performance to identify the best classifier for early AD detection and to highlight features (biomarkers) that drive predictions.

Conclusion: A composite ML framework is proposed to optimize early AD detection and to pinpoint biomarkers that may aid early diagnosis, with the expectation of improved clinical decision support.

Abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

</details>


### [247] [Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02166)
*Di Wu,Huan Liu,Zhixiang Chi,Yuanhao Yu,Konstantinos N. Plataniotis,Yang Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) models neural network weight spaces as dynamic graphs to capture sequential inference dynamics, and INR2JLS enables joint latent-space classification of Implicit Neural Representations, achieving ~10% accuracy gain on CIFAR-100-INR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-dimensional weight spaces and the lack of modeling of layer-by-layer sequential processing hinder effective analysis and downstream tasks; dynamic graphs offer a principled way to encode temporal evolution of neural parameters during inference.

Method: Propose Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder to process time-evolving neural graphs, preserving the sequential nature of inference; develop INR2JLS to map Implicit Neural Representations into a joint latent space for downstream classification tasks.

Result: The approach yields significant improvements, surpassing state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR benchmark.

Conclusion: Dynamic graph-based representations of neural parameters, together with DNG-Encoder and INR2JLS, effectively support analysis and downstream tasks for INRs, demonstrating strong performance gains and potential for broader applicability.

Abstract: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

</details>


### [248] [Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02182)
*Jijie Zhang,Zhe Ren,Quan Zhang,Dandan Guo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DALorRA introduces a variational Bayesian sparse framework that performs data-adaptive, low-rank adaptation by stochastic masking of LoRA rank components to calibrate uncertainty, achieving well-calibrated LLMs without sacrificing reasoning accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Task-specific fine-tuning of LLMs often leads to overconfident predictions, hindering trustworthy deployment. The work shifts uncertainty quantification from dense parameter space to the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) space by enforcing Bayesian regularization at the rank level.

Method: Proposes Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a variational Bayesian sparse approach that imposes stochastic masking on LoRA rank dimensions during training, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity; during inference, the masking induces ensemble-like calibration.

Result: Extensive experiments show that DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs without reducing reasoning accuracy.

Conclusion: DALorRA effectively controls model capacity at the rank level, providing reliable uncertainty quantification and calibration for LoRA-based fine-tuning without compromising performance.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

</details>


### [249] [Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02187)
*Xavier Martínez-Luaña,Alba Gude-Santos,Manuel Fernández-Veiga,Rebeca P. Díaz-Redondo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that fuses privacy-enhancing coded computing with robust aggregation and lightweight verification, applicable to both federated and decentralized settings; shows improved privacy and resilience to active adversaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distributed ML faces privacy leakage and malicious manipulation, with no unified defense across federated and decentralized paradigms. A practical, model-agnostic framework is needed to secure learning while preserving accuracy.

Method: Proposes GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary models, integrated with paradigm-specific defenses: (i) for federated learning, robust aggregation to mitigate malicious participants; (ii) for decentralized learning, approximate decode-and-compare and group testing for lightweight verification and adversary isolation. An explicit attack-driven evaluation implementing representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows that combining GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries in both settings.

Conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing, when paired with suitable adversary-resistance strategies, offers a practical, deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning across federated and decentralized paradigms.

Abstract: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

</details>


### [250] [An Optimisation Framework for the Well-Conditioned Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02194)
*Joseph Webb,Sadok Jerad,Coralia Cartis*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DSGNAR is a scalable second-order optimization framework for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that addresses ill-conditioning in training, delivering unprecedented accuracy and speed across nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, and high-dimensional PDEs (including Burgers' equation and high-dimensional Poisson).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PINNs often underperform compared to classical solvers due to severely ill-conditioned loss landscapes; a robust, scalable second-order optimization method is needed to close the gap in accuracy and speed.

Method: Introduce DSGNAR (Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton with Adaptive Ratio): combines a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton model with adaptive regularization and adaptive step-length control to stabilize optimization; demonstrates robustness across architectures, precisions, and hyperparameters; validated on nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes problems.

Result: Achieves relative L2 errors as low as 3e-16 in double precision; five orders of magnitude improvement on Burgers' equation; up to eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem; single-precision results near round-off with Burgers' equation reaching 4.75e-7 in under 10 seconds; framework is faster and more accurate than state-of-the-art and robust to settings.

Conclusion: DSGNAR substantially mitigates optimization-induced limitations in PINNs, enabling ultra-high accuracy and fast convergence across diverse PDE problems; code is publicly available.

Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising route to solve partial differential equations, yet they have struggled to reach the precision of classical solvers. The obstacle is increasingly understood to be one of optimisation, owing to the severely ill-conditioned loss landscape. We present $\textbf{DSGNAR}$: Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton with Adaptive Ratio, a scalable second-order optimisation framework that confronts this ill-conditioning and, in doing so, obtains unprecedented accuracy and speed. $\textbf{DSGNAR}$ couples a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton model with a novel strategy that carefully controls both regularisation and step length. Across a suite of problems spanning nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes, the framework greatly improves on the state of the art: able to attain relative $\ell_2$ errors as low as $3\times10^{-16}$ in double precision, improve contemporary results by five orders of magnitude on the canonical Burgers' equation, and as much as eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, while remaining markedly faster. We further show that, in single precision, solutions at the limit of round-off error can be obtained very quickly: Burgers' equation to $\ell_2^{\text{rel}} = 4.75 \times 10^{-7}$ in under ten seconds. The framework is also robust to the choice of architecture, arithmetic precision, and initial hyperparameters.
  The code is available at https://www.github.com/wephy/physics-informed-neural-networks

</details>


### [251] [Online Resource Allocation with Continuous Random Consumption: Regret under Degeneracy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02196)
*Jiawei Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: We study online resource allocation with continuous reward and size distributions, defining an active weighted-mass exponent p that governs regret via mass near acceptance cutoffs. For p>1, regret is at least T^{1/2-1/(2p)}; a sample-path marginal policy matches this up to polylog factors. For p=1, regret is polylog (O((log T)^2)). Examples show p can be 1 or 2, and the policy achieves o(sqrt(T)) regret without fluid non-degeneracy or dual uniqueness assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Characterize fundamental regret limits and design robust online allocation policies when rewards and sizes are stochastic and scalable by type-specific vectors, even when the fluid relaxation is degenerate or the dual is non-unique.

Method: Introduce active weighted-mass (p) to quantify near-cutoff mass of value-to-size ratios; derive lower bounds for regret based on p; construct a sample-path marginal policy achieving matching upper bounds up to polylog factors; analyze in two distributional examples to illustrate p values (p=1, p=2).

Result: Regret lower bound: for p>1, at least T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}; upper bound via the sample-path marginal policy matches order up to polylogs; for p=1, regret O((log T)^2); in general, the policy achieves o(sqrt(T)) regret across the regularity class, without requiring fluid non-degeneracy or dual uniqueness.

Conclusion: The active weighted-mass framework ties regret to p, yielding near-optimal online policies under broad distributional settings and degeneracies. The results unify different distributional dependencies (e.g., p=1 or p=2 cases) and show robustness of performance without strong regularity assumptions.

Abstract: We study online resource allocation when both rewards and consumption sizes may be continuously distributed. Requests arrive sequentially and must be accepted or rejected irrevocably under fixed resource capacities. Each request belongs to one of finitely many observable types; conditional on an observable request type, both the reward and the scalar size are random, and the realized size scales a fixed type-specific resource-consumption vector. The model allows the deterministic fluid relaxation to be degenerate.
  We show that additive regret is governed by the size-weighted mass of requests whose value-to-size ratios lie near the active acceptance cutoffs. We formalize this quantity through an active weighted-mass exponent p. When p > 1, this cutoff mass is thin, and the problem is genuinely hard: every online policy must incur regret of order at least $T^{1/2 - 1/(2p)}$, and this holds for every p > 1. A sample-path marginal policy matches this lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors; and when p = 1, so that the mass grows linearly near the cutoff, it attains $O((\log T)^2)$ regret. For example, if the size and the value-to-size ratio are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 1; if instead the size and the reward are independent and uniformly distributed, then p = 2. Thus the policy achieves $o(\sqrt{T})$ regret throughout this regularity class without any fluid non-degeneracy assumption, allowing both primal degeneracy and dual non-uniqueness.

</details>


### [252] [Self-explainable Operator Learning for Discovering Spatial Patterns in Functional Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02203)
*Mojgan Alishiri,Amirhossein Arzani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A self-explainable operator-learning framework that expresses operators as linear combinations of generalized functional linear models via integral equations, enabling localized, domain-decomposed explanations embedded in the model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural operator models are opaque; there is a need for intrinsically interpretable mechanisms that reveal how input regions influence outputs in physics-informed learning.

Method: Rewrite operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations; exploit additive decomposability to partition the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals linking input regions to outputs.

Result: Operator emphasizes regions with strong feature gradients and provides physically meaningful explanations; qualitative agreement with post-hoc explainability methods; demonstrated on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics.

Conclusion: Embedding explainability into the operator structure yields a mathematically transparent, physically interpretable framework that can foster trust and support informed data-driven analysis of complex physical systems.

Abstract: Operator learning has emerged as a powerful tool for modeling complex physical systems in functional spaces. However, their neural network-based architectures make them opaque models, obscuring the reasoning behind their predictions. In this work, we introduce a self-explainable operator learning framework that overcomes this challenge by reformulating operator learning as a linear combination of generalized functional linear models expressed through integral equations. Exploiting the additive decomposability of these integral equations, we divide the input domain into subdomains and compute localized integrals to evaluate the contribution of each region to the final prediction. This decomposition enables direct interpretability where the model explains both inputs and outputs by linking specific input regions to corresponding output patterns, thereby revealing which spatial features drive predictions. We demonstrate the framework on function-to-scalar and function-to-function mappings in fluid flow problems involving blood flow and unsteady aerodynamics. The results show that the operator most often prioritizes regions with strong feature gradients, providing physically meaningful insight into the model's decision-making process. Comparisons with established post-hoc explainability methods demonstrate qualitative agreement while highlighting the key advantage of the proposed approach: explainability is embedded directly within the operator structure itself and does not require an external tool. Therefore, our framework provides a mathematically transparent and physically interpretable approach to uncover relationships within data, fostering trust in machine learning for scientific applications by enabling more informed data-driven analysis of physical systems.

</details>


### [253] [HERMES: A Multi-Granularity Labeling Substrate for Pre-training Data Mixtures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02266)
*Ziyun Qiao,Yue Min,Ruining Chen,Yujun Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hierarchical, data-derived labeling substrate (HERMES) enables coarse-to-fine data mixing via a Learned Semantic Transform plus 3-stage residual vector quantization, creating ~130k granularity cells. The substrate (not the mixer) is the contribution, showing macro-task gains at coarse granularity with a pre-trained 1B-parameter, 25B-token model, and diminishing gains at finer granularity due to shrinking candidate pools.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current data-mixing methods assume pre-partitioned corpora and rely on fixed-label taxonomies that fix semantics at a single granularity. The bottleneck lies in the labeling system; a reusable, multi-resolution substrate could unlock more expressive data mixing.

Method: Apply a Learned Semantic Transform to documents, followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization to annotate each document into a coarse-to-fine code. Prefix length controls granularity up to ~130k cells. Evaluate interplay of Stage-2 rules with equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality, using a 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training setup and 16-task macro-average metrics.

Result: At coarse granularity, the labeling framework sits on a plateau comparable to KMeans-family clustering. At one prefix, a Stage-2 rule yields a +0.0253 macro-average improvement across 16 tasks; at the next finer level, the improvement vanishes as candidate pools contract roughly 5×. This demonstrates that the label substrate, rather than the mixer, can drive data-mixing performance and that granularity tuning materially affects results.

Conclusion: HERMES reframes data mixture design from selecting among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy. The learned labeling substrate enables flexible granularity control and can uncover interaction effects that fixed-label pipelines cannot test; its primary contribution is the labeling substrate rather than any single clustering method.

Abstract: Most data-mixing methods assume the corpus has already been partitioned into groups, and the choice of those groups determines what a mixer can express. Existing labels, including provenance, topic or format taxonomies, and flat embedding clusters, commit to one semantic axis at one granularity; changing the resolution rebuilds the labels. We argue the bottleneck is the label system, not the mixer, and provide a hierarchical one. HERMES is a data-derived labeling substrate: a Learned Semantic Transform followed by 3-stage residual vector quantization annotates each document once into a coarse-to-fine code whose prefix length controls granularity up to approximately 130k cells. At coarse granularity HERMES sits at a plateau with KMeans-family methods on standard clustering metrics, so the contribution is the substrate, not the clusterer. On 1B-parameter, 25B-token pre-training, the hierarchy exposes an interaction fixed-granularity pipelines cannot test: at one prefix length, a combined Stage-2 rule contrast, equal-subbucket coverage versus size-proportional within-bucket quality top-30%, lifts a 16-task capability macro-average by +0.0253; at the next finer level, the same rule loses its measurable edge as candidate pools contract approximately 5x. HERMES reframes data mixture design from choosing among fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-derived granularity hierarchy.

</details>


### [254] [Generalization in offline RL: The structure is more important than the amount of pessimism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02288)
*Max Weltevrede,Matthijs T. J. Spaan,Wendelin Böhmer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In offline RL for contextual MDPs, generalization hinges on symmetry-consistent pessimism rather than the mere amount of pessimism; a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. Data-augmentation (DA) can help enforce symmetry, implemented as a consistency loss during policy extraction rather than standard offline training; validated with IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalization in offline RL is limited by how pessimism interacts with the problem's symmetries and by dataset coverage. Understanding the role of the pessimism structure—especially symmetry—can clarify when pessimism helps or hinders generalization in CMDPs.

Method: Theoretical analysis showing that non-symmetric mild pessimism can underperform compared to symmetric pessimism. Link pessimism structure to dataset coverage in offline RL. Propose enforcing symmetry via a data-augmentation approach implemented as a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than training on augmented data alone. Empirically validate using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

Result: The theory shows that symmetry matters for generalization under pessimism; empirically, a symmetric, possibly stronger pessimism generalizes better than a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric one. DA with a consistency loss during policy extraction improves performance in the rotationally symmetric reacher setup for IQL and CQL.

Conclusion: Successful generalization in CMDPs hinges on symmetry-aligned pessimism. Enforcing symmetry through DA, via a consistency loss during policy extraction, provides a practical and effective route to improve offline RL generalization, corroborated by experiments on a rotationally symmetric reacher.

Abstract: While pessimism counteracts overestimation bias in offline reinforcement learning (RL), being overly conservative has been associated with hindering certain forms of generalization. However, in this paper we demonstrate that being overly pessimistic does not inherently prevent optimal generalization in contextual MDPs (CMDPs). Instead, we argue successful generalization depends not on the amount of pessimism, but whether the pessimistic structure respects the underlying symmetries of the optimal solution. We prove that a mildly pessimistic, non-symmetric value function can generalize worse than an overly pessimistic, symmetric one. In offline RL, the structure of the pessimism is determined by the structure of the dataset coverage. As such, enforcing a symmetric value function can be non-trivial, and might require techniques such as data augmentation (DA). Inspired by our theoretical results, we argue that DA can best be applied through a consistency loss during policy extraction, rather than the common practice of (regular) offline training on an augmented dataset. This is empirically validated using IQL and CQL on a rotationally symmetric reacher environment.

</details>


### [255] [Optimizing Visual Generative Models via Distribution-wise Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02291)
*Ruihang Li,Mengde Xu,Shuyang Gu,Leigang Qu,Fuli Feng,Han Hu,Wenjie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Distribution-wise rewards for RL-based visual generation improve diversity and perceptual quality by aligning training with data distribution; introduces a subset-replace trick for efficiency and applies RL to merge coefficients to mitigate train–inference inconsistency, with substantial FID-50K gains across SiT and EDM2.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reward hacking and reduced diversity are common with sample-wise RL rewards; aligning the training signal with the actual data distribution can reduce mode collapse and artifacts, while keeping computation tractable.

Method: Introduce distribution-wise reward that accounts for the data distribution of generated samples; propose a subset-replace strategy to approximate this reward by updating only a small subset of a reference set; apply RL to optimize post-hoc model merging coefficients to mitigate train–inference inconsistency caused by SDE in regular RL.

Result: Significant improvements in FID-50K: SiT improves from 8.30 to 5.77; EDM2 improves from 3.74 to 3.52. Qualitative evaluation shows improved perceptual quality with preserved sample diversity.

Conclusion: Distribution-aware rewards better align training with real data, reduce mode collapse and reward hacking, and are scalable via the subset-replace approach; RL-assisted post-hoc merging addresses train–inference inconsistencies and yields robust gains across base models.

Abstract: Conventional reinforcement learning strategies for visual generation typically employ sample-wise reward functions, yet this practice frequently results in reward hacking that degrades image diversity and introduces visual anomalies.
