To address these limitations, we present a novel framework that finetunes generative models using distribution-wise rewards, ensuring better alignment with real-world data distributions. Unlike rewards that evaluate samples individually, distribution-wise reward accounts for the data distribution of the samples, mitigating the mode collapse problem that occurs when all samples optimize towards the same direction independently. To overcome the prohibitive computational cost of estimating these rewards, we introduce a subset-replace strategy that efficiently provides reward signals by updating only a small subset of a generated reference set. Additionally, we apply RL to optimize post-hoc model merging coefficients, potentially mitigating the train-inference inconsistency caused by introducing stochastic differential equation (SDE) in regular RL practices. Extensive experiments show our approach significantly improves FID-50K across various base models, from 8.30 to 5.77 for SiT and from 3.74 to 3.52 for EDM2. Qualitative evaluation also confirms that our method enhances perceptual quality while preserving sample diversity.

</details>


### [256] [One More Time: Revisiting Neural Quantum States from a Reinforcement Learning Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02292)
*Juan Agustín Duque,Sergio García Heredia,Vinicius Hernandes,Eliška Greplová,Thomas Spriggs,Aaron Courville,Anna Dawid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO) introduces a trust-region approach for neural quantum states (NQS) that clips updates in amplitude and phase, avoids matrix inversions, and reuses samples, achieving stable, scalable optimization and improved wall-clock convergence over Adam, minSR, and SPRING, demonstrated up to a 1.5B-parameter RWKV-7 model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive NQS offer exact Born-distribution sampling but optimization methods are underdeveloped: Adam is scalable but ignores geometry; stochastic reconfiguration is principled but costly and fragile at scale. A principled, scalable, geometry-aware optimization is needed.

Method: Formulate variational energy minimization as an advantage policy-gradient problem over the Born distribution and introduce Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO). PWO is a trust-region algorithm that clips probability-ratio changes in the amplitude channel and phase increments in the phase channel, avoids explicit matrix inversion, reuses samples across updates, and combines first-order scalability with theoretical guarantees.

Result: PWO improves stability and wall-clock convergence compared to Adam, minSR, and SPRING across Ising and frustrated J1-J2 spin systems in 1D and 2D. Demonstrates NQS optimization at scale on a 1.5B-parameter RWKV-7 model, indicating feasibility of large-scale NQS training.

Conclusion: PWO provides a principled, scalable training paradigm for autoregressive NQS, marrying trust-region theory with practical sampling strategies to enable stable optimization and efficient convergence at large model scales.

Abstract: Neural quantum states (NQS) provide a flexible and scalable framework for approximating quantum many-body wavefunctions. Among NQS parameterizations, autoregressive models are especially attractive because they enable exact, independent sampling from the Born distribution, avoiding the autocorrelation and mixing issues of Markov chain methods. Yet their optimization remains comparatively underexplored: Adam is a scalable method but ignores function space geometry, while stochastic reconfiguration is principled but costly and numerically fragile in large models. To address this gap, we show that variational energy minimization can be viewed as an advantage policy-gradient problem over the Born distribution, motivating trust-region optimization for NQS training. We introduce Proximal Wavefunction Optimization (PWO), a principled trust-region algorithm that clips probability-ratio changes in the amplitude channel and phase increments in the phase channel. PWO avoids explicit matrix inversion, reuses samples across multiple updates, and combines the scalability of first-order optimization with theoretical guarantees. Across Ising and frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ one- and two-dimensional spin systems, PWO improves stability and wall-clock convergence over Adam, minSR, and SPRING. Finally, we fine-tune a $1.5$B-parameter RWKV-7 model, demonstrating NQS optimization at a scale over three orders of magnitude beyond prior work.

</details>


### [257] [Self-Gating Attention for Efficient Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02344)
*Dezheng Wang,Tong Chen,Wei Yuan,Congyan Chen,Shihua Li,Hongzhi Yin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Self-Gating Attention (SGA) introduces a shared learnable matrix and an input-dependent residual to compute attention scores, replacing standard query/key projections, yielding linear-time and memory complexity in the look-back length while maintaining competitive forecasting performance across diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard self-attention in time-series forecasting has quadratic complexity with respect to the look-back length, hindering scalability in resource-constrained or high-throughput settings. Observations show that attention maps often contain redundant patterns due to repetitive temporal patterns and stable correlations in real-world series, motivating a more efficient mechanism.

Method: SGA represents attention scores with a shared learnable matrix plus an input-dependent residual component, eliminating the need for query and key projections. This yields linear time and score-matrix memory with respect to the look-back length. The mechanism is plug-and-play and integrated into multiple forecasting backbones, and its performance is compared against standard self-attention and lightweight variants on nine real-world datasets.

Result: SGA achieves faster inference with linear complexity and memory while maintaining competitive forecasting performance relative to state-of-the-art attention mechanisms, validated on nine public datasets spanning electricity, finance, weather, medical monitoring, human activity, and climate records.

Conclusion: SGA provides a deployment-oriented, efficient attention mechanism for time-series forecasting, delivering substantial inference speedups with competitive accuracy and serving as a practical plug-and-play option for scalable forecasting systems.

Abstract: Transformer architectures have shown strong potential in time series forecasting, where multi-head self-attention is widely used to capture temporal dependencies across historical timestamps. However, standard self-attention has quadratic time and memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. This cost may limit its use in resource-constrained or high-throughput forecasting systems, where fast and memory-efficient inference is important. Through qualitative and quantitative analyses, we observe that self-attention maps in time series forecasting often contain redundant patterns across different timestamps. This phenomenon can be related to the repeated temporal patterns and relatively stable temporal correlations in many real-world time series. Motivated by this observation, we propose Self-Gating Attention (SGA), a plug-and-play attention mechanism that represents the attention score with a shared learnable matrix and an input-dependent residual component. The shared matrix captures common attention patterns, while the residual component captures input-dependent variations. In this way, SGA avoids the query and key projections used in standard attention score computation, leading to linear time and score-matrix memory complexity with respect to the look-back length. We integrate SGA into several forecasting backbones and compare it with standard self-attention and lightweight attention variants on nine publicly available real-world datasets covering electricity, finance, weather, medical monitoring, human activity, and climate records. The results show that SGA improves inference efficiency on public benchmarks while maintaining competitive forecasting performance against state-of-the-art attention mechanisms. These benchmark results provide deployment-oriented evidence.

</details>


### [258] [DecompRL: Solving Harder Problems by Learning Modular Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02390)
*Juliette Decugis,Fabian Gloeckle,Francis Bach,Taco Cohen,Gabriel Synnaeve*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DecompRL: an RL method that decomposes problems into modular sub-functions, recombines multiple implementations, and achieves large gains in cost-efficiency and solvability on code-generation benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard strategies like repeated sampling or RL with verifiable rewards struggle when the base policy has near-zero probability of producing a correct solution, due to an enormous search space. A modular decomposition aims to reduce the effective search space by solving smaller, independently solvable sub-tasks.

Method: Introduce DecompRL, an RL algorithm that learns to decompose tasks into a hierarchy of modules and generate implementations for each module. Recombining k implementations across n modules yields up to k^n candidate solutions. The approach shifts computation from expensive GPU inference to cheap CPU evaluation, reducing GPU token cost by ~50x. Evaluated on LiveCodeBench and CodeContests with Qwen 2.5 7B and Code World Model 32B, it outperforms standard and diversity-focused RL baselines beyond 1e5 tokens per problem, solving problems unreachable by standard generation.

Result: DecompRL outperforms baselines beyond 1e5 tokens per problem, solving problems standard generation cannot reach, and reduces GPU token cost by approximately 50x by enabling CPU-based evaluation of many modular combinations.

Conclusion: Modular decomposition shifts the bottleneck from GPU inference to CPU evaluation, enabling scalable exploration of large solution spaces and solving more complex tasks in code generation than traditional generation or sampling-only approaches.

Abstract: How can Large Language Models (LLMs) solve problems they currently cannot? Repeated sampling scales test-time compute but GPU cost grows linearly with attempts, while reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards improves single-attempt accuracy at the expense of sample diversity. Both strategies ultimately fail when the base policy has near-zero probability of producing a correct solution: no amount of sampling or gradient signal can overcome a search space that is simply too large. We take a different approach: rather than sampling harder, we make the task easier by decomposing problems into smaller, independently solvable sub-functions whose implementations can be recombined. Since off-the-shelf models are not trained for this modular generation, we introduce DecompRL, an RL algorithm that explicitly learns to decompose and implement hierarchical code structures. Recombining $k$ implementations of $n$ modules yields up to $k^{n}$ candidate solutions, shifting the bottleneck from GPU inference to cheap CPU evaluation and cutting GPU token cost by $\sim$50$\times$. On LiveCodeBench and CodeContests (Qwen~2.5~7B, Code World Model~32B), DecompRL outperforms standard and diversity-optimized RL baselines beyond $10^5$ tokens per problem, solving problems that standard generation cannot reach.

</details>


### [259] [Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02423)
*Zhuowei Chen,Liwei Chen,Christian Schunn,Raquel Coelho,Xiang Lorraine Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NeuFS shifts AFSL sample selection from output-level signals to neuron activation patterns, enabling diverse and informative few-shot samples and reducing hallucinations; it outperforms baselines, with ablations showing neuron signals beat external embeddings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AFSL methods rely on output-level signals (e.g., entropy, test-time embeddings) which may miss internal model dynamics and knowledge gaps leading to suboptimal sample selection and hallucinations.

Method: Represent each unlabeled sample via neuron activation patterns; employ dual-criteria selection: (1) diversity of neuron-pattern coverage for broad sample coverage; (2) neuron-consensus to identify informative and challenging samples that LLMs tend to hallucinate; evaluate on reasoning and text classification across three datasets; conduct ablation studies.

Result: NeuFS outperforms existing AFSL baselines on both reasoning and text classification tasks; ablations indicate internal neuron activations provide a more principled and effective selection signal than external embeddings.

Conclusion: Neuron-aware sample selection is a principled and effective AFSL strategy; leveraging internal neuron dynamics yields superior identification of valuable annotations and demonstrations.

Abstract: Active Few-Shot Learning (AFSL) adapts LLMs to specialized domains by identifying the most valuable unlabeled samples for annotation and use as few-shot demonstrations, effectively reducing human annotation costs while promoting high performance. However, existing methods typically rely on output-level signals for sample identification, such as predictive entropy or semantic similarities with test-time data based on external embeddings, which often overlook models' internal dynamics, which could pinpoint specific knowledge gaps. To bridge this gap, we propose NeuFS, a Neuron-Aware Active Few-Shot Learning framework that shifts the selection paradigm from output-level proxies to models' internal dynamics. NeuFS utilizes neuron activation patterns to represent sample directly, and includes a dual-criteria selection strategy that: (1) ensures few-shot sample diversity with neuron patterns for broader example coverage, while (2) prioritizing on identifying informative and challenging few-shot samples LLMs tend to hallucinate by quantifying neuron consensus. Experiments on three datasets demonstrate that NeuFS excels in both reasoning and text classification tasks, outperforming existing AFSL baselines. Ablation studies further highlight that internal neuron activations provide a more principled and effective selection signal than external embeddings, validating the superiority of the proposed NeuFS.

</details>


### [260] [QFedAgent: Quantum-Enhanced Personalized Federated Learning for Multi-Agent Activity Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02426)
*Quoc Bao Phan,Tuy Tan Nguyen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hybrid quantum-classical personalized federated learning (QFedAgent) for multi-agent activity recognition uses a variational quantum circuit fusion module to model sensor interactions, achieving ~10x parameter reduction and competitive accuracy (97.7%) on OPPORTUNITY under non-IID partitions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the degradation of conventional FL due to heterogeneous, non-IID multimodal sensor streams and the high parameter/communication cost of classical fusion modules in multi-agent robotic sensing.

Method: Proposes QFedAgent, a hybrid quantum-classical FL framework with a variational quantum circuit fusion module that encodes accelerometer–gyroscope interactions via quantum state encoding and entanglement; dramatically reduces fusion parameters (72 quantum rotation params vs ~33k in an MLP) and enables personalization within FL.

Result: Demonstrates ~10x reduction in parameter count and achieves 97.7% mean test accuracy on OPPORTUNITY with subject-based non-IID partitions, indicating parameter-efficient quantum fusion remains competitive with conventional federated baselines.

Conclusion: Quantum fusion in a personalized FL setting can be competitive for activity recognition with substantial parameter savings; promising for reducing communication/computation, but empirical validation across more datasets and hardware feasibility considerations remain needed.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed devices without sharing raw data, making it suitable for privacy-sensitive robotic sensing applications. However, multi-agent systems generate heterogeneous and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) multimodal sensor streams that degrade conventional FL algorithms, while classical fusion modules introduce substantial parameter overhead and communication cost. This paper proposes QFedAgent, a hybrid quantum-classical personalized FL framework for multi-agent activity recognition. The approach integrates a variational quantum circuit fusion module that models accelerometer--gyroscope interactions through quantum state encoding and entanglement, requiring only 72 quantum rotation parameters versus 33K in classical multi-layer perceptron-based fusion, achieving approximately 10x total parameter reduction. Experiments on the OPPORTUNITY dataset under subject-based non-IID partitions demonstrate 97.7% mean test accuracy, confirming that parameter-efficient quantum fusion remains competitive with conventional federated baselines.

</details>


### [261] [Extreme Adaptive Transformer for Time Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02437)
*Sanjeev Shrestha,Hui Liu,Yifan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Exformer, an Extreme-Adaptive Transformer for time-series forecasting that explicitly models extreme events to improve short-horizon (3-day) forecasts in hydrology. Uses three sparse attention components—Local, Stride, Extreme—to capture different temporal dependencies and extreme-event interactions, achieving state-of-the-art results on four real-world datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hydrologic time series are highly skewed with rare but impactful extreme events; standard Transformers treat all time points equally and may underrepresent extremes, leading to poorer forecasts for floods and other extremes.

Method: Introduce Extreme-Adaptive Transformer (Exformer) with an extreme-adaptive attention mechanism comprising three sparse components: Local (short-term), Stride (periodic), and Extreme (event-aware between normal and extreme patterns). The model focuses on sparse attention to capture relevant dependencies while emphasizing extreme events.

Result: Empirical evaluation on four real-world hydrologic streamflow datasets shows superior 3-day forecasting performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Explicitly incorporating extreme-aware attention improves Transformer-based forecasting for imbalanced time series with rare but consequential events.

Abstract: Time series forecasting remains challenging when the underlying data contain rare but critical extreme events. This issue is particularly important in hydrologic forecasting, where streamflow distributions are often highly skewed and extreme peaks can have substantial impacts on flood monitoring, water resource management, and early warning systems. Although Transformer-based forecasting models have achieved strong performance by modeling long-range temporal dependencies, they typically treat all time points uniformly and may therefore underrepresent rare extreme patterns. In this paper, we propose the Extreme-Adaptive Transformer (Exformer), a forecasting framework designed to explicitly model temporal dependencies involving both normal and extreme events. Exformer introduces an extreme-adaptive attention mechanism composed of three sparse components: Local, Stride, and Extreme. The Local and Stride components capture short-term and periodic temporal dependencies, respectively, while the Extreme component selectively models event-aware dependencies between normal and extreme streamflow patterns. Experiments on four real-world hydrologic streamflow datasets show that Exformer achieves superior 3-day forecasting performance compared with state-of-the-art baselines. Our findings demonstrate that explicitly incorporating extreme-aware attention improves the forecasting capacity of Transformer models on imbalanced time series with rare but consequential events.

</details>


### [262] [Understanding the Robustness of Distributed Self-Supervised Learning Frameworks Against Non-IID Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02447)
*Xuanyu Chen,Nan Yang,Shuai Wang,Dong Yuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: D-SSL robustness under non-IID data: MIM is more robust than CL; robustness grows with network connectivity; FL is not less robust than decentralized learning; MAR loss improves MIM via local-global alignment; theory supported by experiments across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the theoretical gap on how distributed self-supervised learning frameworks cope with data heterogeneity (non-IID) and to guide algorithm design.

Method: Theoretical analysis of D-SSL robustness under non-IID settings; comparative study of MIM vs CL; analysis of the effect of average network connectivity; introduction of MAR loss; extensive empirical validation across architectures and distributed configurations.

Result: MIM-based pre-training is more robust to heterogeneous data than CL; robust performance increases with average connectivity; FL achieves robustness comparable to DecL; MAR loss enhances MIM with local-to-global alignment and performs well in experiments.

Conclusion: Provides a theoretical foundation for designing future D-SSL algorithms; MAR loss is a practical refinement aligned with the theory and validated empirically.

Abstract: Recent research has introduced distributed self-supervised learning (D-SSL) approaches to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled decentralized data. However, D-SSL faces the critical challenge of data heterogeneity, and there is limited theoretical understanding of how different D-SSL frameworks respond to this challenge. To fill this gap, we present a rigorous theoretical analysis of the robustness of D-SSL frameworks under non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) settings. Our results show that pre-training with Masked Image Modeling (MIM) is inherently more robust to heterogeneous data than Contrastive Learning (CL), and that the robustness of decentralized SSL increases with average network connectivity, implying that federated learning (FL) is no less robust than decentralized learning (DecL). These findings provide a solid theoretical foundation for guiding the design of future D-SSL algorithms. To further illustrate the practical implications of our theory, we introduce MAR loss, a refinement of the MIM objective with local-to-global alignment regularization. Extensive experiments across model architectures and distributed settings validate our theoretical insights, and additionally confirm the effectiveness of MAR loss as an application of our analysis.

</details>


### [263] [Neuron-Aware Data Selection for Annotation-Free LLM Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02460)
*Zhuowei Chen,Xiang Lorraine Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neuron-OPSD is a data-centric, annotation-free self-distillation framework for LLMs that uses internal neuron activations to guide training-data selection and teacher-context construction, enabling on-policy distillation without ground-truth labels and improving in-domain performance while preserving cross-domain generalization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Post-training LLMs without real-world interaction or labeled data is challenging, particularly in specialized domains with costly annotations. Prior annotation-free approaches rely on model outputs (and majority voting) but suffer out-of-domain degradation (SFT- and GRPO-based) and calibration issues with reward-based RL. A data-centric strategy that leverages internal activations could improve data quality and context for training without external supervision.

Method: Proposed Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation (Neuron-OPSD): a data-centric framework that uses internal neuron activations to guide training-data selection and to construct the teacher's context. The model is trained via on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution, with no ground-truth labels at any stage.

Result: Across specialized-domain benchmarks, Neuron-OPSD improves in-domain task performance, preserves cross-domain generalization, and mitigates calibration collapse relative to prior annotation-free baselines. It is particularly suited for settings where online interaction or external supervision is costly or infeasible and remains distinct from offline RL that relies on logged reward signals.

Conclusion: Neuron-OPSD provides a robust annotation-free self-distillation framework that leverages internal neuron signals to guide data curation and teacher-context construction, enabling on-policy distillation with strong in-domain gains and stable cross-domain generalization, without external supervision.

Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) without real-world interaction feedback or human-labeled supervision remains challenging, particularly in specialized domains where expert annotations are costly to obtain. Recent annotation-free self-evolution methods address this by using the model's own outputs as supervision signals, constructing a teacher via additional context and aggregating predictions across multiple rollouts through majority voting to produce pseudo-labels. However, these approaches are not without drawbacks: SFT- and GRPO-based variants suffer out-of-domain performance degradation, while reward-based on-policy RL inflates calibration error. In this paper, we propose Neuron On-Policy Self-Distillation (Neuron-OPSD), a data-centric framework for annotation-free self-distillation that leverages internal neuron activations to guide both training-data selection and teacher context construction. The model is then trained via on-policy distillation from the teacher distribution, requiring no ground-truth labels at any stage. Across specialized-domain benchmarks, Neuron-OPSD improves in-domain task performance while preserving cross-domain generalization and mitigating calibration collapse over prior annotation-free baselines. This framework is particularly relevant to settings where online interaction or external supervision is costly or infeasible, and is conceptually distinct from offline RL approaches that rely on logged, reward-labeled trajectories.

</details>


### [264] [Beyond Adam: SOAP and Muon for Faster, Label-Efficient Training of Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02499)
*Gil Harari,Yoel Zimmermann,Ola Tangen Kulseng,Laura Zichi,Chuin Wei Tan,Marc L. Descoteaux,Boris Kozinsky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Matrix-structured optimizers (Muon, SOAP, SOAP-Muon) significantly improve training of ML interatomic potentials (NequIP, Allegro) over Adam, with SOAP and SOAP-Muon being consistently strong; Muon yields limited gains; benefits amplify under partial force supervision; optimizer choice is a key design axis for MLIPs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the underexplored role of optimizers in MLIPs and quantify potential gains in convergence speed and final accuracy using recent matrix-structured optimizers.

Method: Systematic experimental comparison applying Muon, SOAP, and SOAP-Muon optimizers to NequIP and Allegro MLIPs; evaluate convergence speed and final accuracy under both full and partial force supervision.

Result: SOAP and SOAP-Muon emerge as robust and consistently strong optimizers; Muon provides partial gains relative to Adam; overall improvements exceed Adam in convergence speed and final accuracy, with larger gains under partial force supervision.

Conclusion: Optimizer choice is a crucial design axis for MLIPs. Matrix-structured optimizers, especially SOAP-based variants, offer robust performance gains and should be considered in MLIP training, particularly when force data is partially available.

Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become a hallmark of AI for scientific simulation. While efforts on new architectures and datasets have led to increasingly accurate and general models, the choice of optimizer for training has largely remained unexplored, defaulting to Adam and its variants in the community. Here, we implement and systematically compare a class of recently proposed matrix-structured optimizers, including Muon, SOAP, and the hybrid SOAP-Muon, for training NequIP and Allegro MLIP models. We find that these optimizers can substantially outperform Adam in both convergence speed and final accuracy. SOAP and SOAP-Muon emerge as robust and consistently strong methods, while Muon only provides partial gains relative to Adam. The improvements are particularly pronounced under partial force supervision. Our results indicate that optimizer choice is an overlooked yet impactful design axis for MLIPs.

</details>


### [265] [DemoPSD: Disagreement-Modulated Policy Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02502)
*Yunhe Li,Hao Shi,Wenhao Liu,Mengzhe Ruan,Hanxu Hou,Zhongxiang Dai,Shuang Qiu,Linqi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DemoPSD introduces selective teacher guidance for on-policy self-distillation by blending teacher and student predictions via a reverse-KL barycenter that adapts per token. This mitigates privileged information leakage and preserves exploration, backed by theory and SciKnowEval experiments showing superior generalization to OOD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address privileged information leakage and reduced exploration inherent in dense token-level supervision from the teacher in on-policy self-distillation, which can overfit to in-domain patterns and hurt cross-domain generalization.

Method: Propose DemoPSD, which uses a reverse-KL barycenter target—an adaptive, weighted geometric blend of teacher and student distributions. The blend at each token is guided by the discrepancy between the two distributions, enabling selective adoption of teacher guidance without fully copying the teacher. The approach emphasizes leakage attenuation and exploration preservation.

Result: The authors provide theoretical proofs of leakage attenuation and exploration preservation. Empirically, DemoPSD outperforms GRPO and SDPO on SciKnowEval across four scientific fields, yields higher training entropy, and shows robust generalization to OOD GPQA benchmarks.

Conclusion: DemoPSD offers a principled, adaptive mechanism for on-policy self-distillation that mitigates privileged information leakage while maintaining exploration, achieving superior cross-domain generalization and empirical performance.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a practical method for training large language models (LLMs) to reason, where a single model acts as both the teacher and the student with different levels of information access. However, recent studies have found that the teacher's dense token-level supervision, conditioned on privileged information, can lead to overfitting to in-domain patterns, suppress exploration, and hurt cross-domain generalization, while also introducing a more fundamental issue: *privileged information leakage*, where the student encodes answer-dependent shortcuts that are unavailable at test time. We introduce **DemoPSD**, a novel framework that resolves such problems through the idea of *selective adoption of teacher guidance*. Instead of fitting the full teacher distribution, DemoPSD steers the student toward a *reverse-KL barycenter target*, a weighted geometric combination of the teacher and student distributions, that naturally balances learning from the teacher with preserving the student's own reasoning capacity. We measure the difference between their distributions and use such a discrepancy to adaptively control the blending at each token position. We provably show that DemoPSD achieves **(1)** *leakage attenuation*, i.e., effective mitigation of privileged information leakage; and **(2)** *exploration preservation*, i.e., preservation of exploration capacity under dense token-level distillation. Extensive experiments on SciKnowEval across four scientific fields show that DemoPSD outperforms both GRPO and SDPO while maintaining higher training entropy and robustly generalizing to out-of-distribution GPQA benchmarks.

</details>


### [266] [Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02512)
*Wentao Zhang,Liliana Hotsko,Woojeong Kim,Pengyu Nie,Stuart Shieber,Yuntian Deng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Fuzzy-function programming converts natural-language specs into compact, locally-executable neural artifacts via PAW, enabling reusable, memory-efficient function definitions with near-prompt performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based solutions and rely on costly, non-local LLM APIs; a local, reproducible tool-builder approach could improve locality, reproducibility, and cost.

Method: Train a 4B compiler on FuzzyBench (10M examples) to emit parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. Use a 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter to execute PAW-generated adapters, enabling local execution.

Result: PAW-enabled 0.6B Qwen3 matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B while using ~1/50 of inference memory and achieving 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3.

Conclusion: PAW reframes foundation models from per-input solvers to reusable tool builders: define a function once, then repeatedly call a small, offline artifact with cheap, scalable cost.

Abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally-executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [267] [PACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Plausible and Actionable Counterfactual Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01306)
*Pavel Iakovets,Liyanapathiranage Sudeepika Wajirakumari Samarathunga,Martin Thomas Horsch,Fadi Al Machot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PACE combines neural prediction with symbolic ASP-based reasoning to produce feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations; demonstrates improved plausibility on Adult Income dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactuals often yield unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to ignoring domain constraints. A neuro-symbolic approach can encode domain knowledge and intervention feasibility to improve interpretability and actionability.

Method: Two-component architecture: a neural predictor for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer (Answer Set Programming) that imposes domain-specific constraints on counterfactual generation, ensuring feasible interventions and preserving immutable attributes. Model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support.

Result: Case study on the Adult Income dataset using a multilayer perceptron coupled with ASP rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours. Demonstrates a trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility; symbolic constraints yield explanations better aligned with domain feasibility and interpretability.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that integrating symbolic domain constraints into counterfactual generation yields feasible, interpretable explanations and highlights the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for feasibility-aware explainable AI. Future work may address scalability, rule quality, and evaluation across domains.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations explain machine learning predictions by identifying minimal input changes that would alter a model's decision. Although many existing methods successfully generate prediction-changing alternatives, they often produce unrealistic or infeasible recommendations due to a lack of explicit mechanisms for incorporating domain knowledge and intervention constraints. Neuro-symbolic AI offers a promising direction by combining data-driven predictive models with symbolic reasoning capable of representing human-understandable rules and feasible actions. This paper presents PACE, a modular neuro-symbolic framework for generating feasibility-aware counterfactual explanations. The framework separates prediction and reasoning into two components: a neural predictive model for classification and a symbolic reasoning layer that enforces domain-specific constraints during counterfactual generation. By explicitly modeling feasible interventions, the framework produces explanations consistent with domain knowledge while remaining interpretable and actionable. The approach is model-agnostic and adaptable to domains requiring realistic decision support. A case study is conducted on the Adult Income dataset, combining a multilayer perceptron classifier with Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules encoding feasible modifications to education, occupation, and working hours while preserving immutable attributes. Results highlight the trade-off between counterfactual validity and plausibility and show that symbolic constraints yield explanations that better satisfy domain-specific feasibility requirements, illustrating the potential of neuro-symbolic methods for transparent, feasibility-aware counterfactual explanation in explainable AI.

</details>


### [268] [Auto-FL-Research: Agentic Search for Federated Learning Algorithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01366)
*Holger R. Roth,Ziyue Xu,Chester Chen,Daguang Xu,Peter Cnudde,Andrew Feng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Auto-FL-Research (AFR) uses autonomous coding agents to search FL algorithmic recipes under fixed mutation surfaces, evaluating on FLamby and LEAF; finds mixed improvements, with some gains due to recipe changes and others due to fixed-surface tuning or single-run artifacts; highlights the value of decomposing improvements into repeatable mechanisms and artifacts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FL experimentation involves many interacting design choices; manual exploration is costly and fair comparison is difficult; AFR aims to automate exploration while controlling mutation surface and budget to enable fair, repeatable analysis.

Method: Constrained coding-agent workflow; agents propose candidate training algorithms (server aggregation, client schedules, local objectives, model variants); task profiles fix mutation surface, budget, communication contract, and evaluation; campaigns log scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, failure status; evaluation on five healthcare FLamby tasks and LEAF datasets with multiple seeds; same-budget controls.

Result: Gains observed on several tasks; 5-seed repeats show improvements on 4 FLamby tasks and 5 of 6 LEAF profiles; some gains attributable to fixed-surface tuning or artifacts; seed sensitivity and selective failures expose limitations; overall, results support separating improvements into repeated mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning, and single-run artifacts.

Conclusion: AFR demonstrates a disciplined, repeatable approach to FL recipe search and emphasizes the importance of replication and surface-fixing to interpret improvements; the mixed outcomes illustrate how agent-generated candidates can be categorized into core FL mechanisms, surface-tuning, and artifacts, informing robust FL research.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) research often depends on many small but consequential algorithmic choices: optimizer variants, server aggregation rules, local training schedules, normalization, regularization, and model architecture. These choices are expensive to explore manually and difficult to compare fairly when candidate changes can also alter the FL training or evaluation path. In this work, we present Auto-FL-Research (AFR), a constrained coding-agent workflow for FL algorithmic recipe search. Agents may propose and implement candidate training algorithms, including server aggregation rules, client update schedules, local objectives, and registered model variants, while task profiles fix the mutation surface, compute budget, communication contract, and final model evaluation. Each campaign records candidate scores, runtime, edited files, artifacts, and failure status. We evaluate AFR on five healthcare cross-silo FLamby tasks and on grouped-client profiles for the five fixed LEAF datasets plus the LEAF synthetic task. Five-seed repeat evaluations support gains on four FLamby tasks and five of six LEAF profiles, while also exposing seed-sensitive and search-selected failure cases. Same-budget controls show that several gains correspond to FL-recipe changes, whereas other improvements are recovered by fixed-surface scalar controls or fail under repeat or held-out evaluation. These mixed outcomes are part of the contribution: they show how agent-generated candidates can be separated into repeated FL mechanisms, fixed-surface tuning effects, and selected single-run artifacts.

</details>


### [269] [The Wiola Architecture for Efficient Small Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01394)
*Aryuemaan Kumar Chowdhury,Afreen Shaik,Yaparla Bhargavi,Brahma Kumar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Wiola introduces five novel components for a fully original small LLM architecture and provides analyses, tests, and four model sizes; claims HuggingFace compatibility and comparisons to GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Mistral.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Create a genuinely original SLM architecture from first principles, avoiding lineage to existing model families while delivering practical performance and compatibility.

Method: Propose five components (SRPE, GCLA, ATM, DSFF, WiolaRMSNorm) with mathematical derivations, architectural diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic baselines against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, Mistral; release in 120M–1.5B sizes and ensure HuggingFace compatibility; report 22 architectural unit tests passing.

Result: Claims complete mathematical derivations, diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons; 4 model sizes; 22 unit tests pass; compatible with Transformers ecosystem.

Conclusion: Wiola presents a potentially impactful set of architectural novelties with purported benefits in efficiency and coherence, but requires detailed empirical benchmarks, reproducibility information, and ablation studies to validate claims and generalization across tasks.

Abstract: We present Wiola, a fully original Small Language Model (SLM) architecture built from first principles, sharing no structural lineage with any existing model family including GPT, LLaMA, Mistral, or Falcon. Wiola introduces five independently novel components: (i) Spiral Rotary Positional Encoding (SRPE), which embeds token positions on a three-dimensional helical manifold combining absolute, relative, and hierarchical positional signals; (ii) Gated Cross-Layer Attention (GCLA), providing each decoder layer with soft cross-attention access to compressed summaries of two preceding layers for inter-layer coherence; (iii) Adaptive Token Merging (ATM), which dynamically merges se mantically redundant adjacent tokens in middle network layers to reduce attention complexity without information loss; (iv) Dual Stream Feed-Forward (DSFF), replacing the conventional MLP with two parallel streams fused by a learned per-dimension gate; and (v) WiolaRMSNorm, a modified normalisation introducing a per-dimension learned offset vector that prevents representation collapse. We provide complete mathematical derivations, architectural block diagrams, complexity analyses, and systematic comparisons against GPT-2, LLaMA-2, and Mistral. Wiola is released in four sizes (120M, 360M, 700M, and 1.5B parameters) and is fully compatible with the HuggingFace Transformers ecosystem, with all 22 architectural unit tests passing.

</details>


### [270] [Agent4cs: A Multi-agent System for Code Summarization in Large Hierarchical Codebases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01425)
*Yongjian Tang,Ezgi Sarikayak,Doruk Tuncel,Jie M. Zhang,Thomas Runkler*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Agent4cs is a multi-agent framework for bottom-up summarization of large codebases, achieving higher semantic consistency and keyword coverage than baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Codebases are large and often obfuscated; treating code as flat text with a single language model ignores hierarchical, interdependent structure within repositories. A multi-agent, bottom-up approach can leverage folder-level dependencies for robust summaries.

Method: Three agents operate in a bottom-up workflow: (1) a summarization agent produces robust summaries of subfolders; (2) a keyword-extraction agent identifies critical information from subfolders; (3) a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated across 7 frontier models; measures semantic consistency across folder levels and keyword coverage.

Result: Semantic consistency across folder levels improved by an average of 8% over two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Real-world datasets show up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the baselines.

Conclusion: A multi-agent, hierarchical approach effectively improves readability, coherence, and completeness of codebase summaries, highlighting the value of agent collaboration for large-scale code understanding and suggesting broader applicability to complex software repositories.

Abstract: Understanding large, complex codebases, especially those with obfuscated structures and incomplete documentation, remains a significant challenge. Existing code summarization solutions often rely on a single language model or coding assistant like Claude Code, and treat source code as flat text, underutilizing the rich interdependencies and hierarchical information within a repository. To address these shortcomings, we propose Agent4cs - a multi-agent framework that summarizes large codebases in a bottom-up fashion, where a summarization agent focuses on producing robust summaries; a keyword-extraction agent proactively identifies critical information from subfolders; and a quality-assurance agent iteratively refines the outputs for readability, coherence, and completeness. Evaluated on 7 frontier models, Agent4cs improves semantic consistency across all folder levels by average 8% compared to two structured prompting baselines with code segments. Furthermore, extensive evaluation on real-world datasets demonstrates up to 38% gains in normalized keyword coverage rate over the same baselines.

</details>


### [271] [When Should Service Agents Reconsider? Difficulty-Routed Control in Customer-Service Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01426)
*Qian Chen,Chengyuan Liu,Xin Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A difficulty-routed service-control architecture that uses a lightweight router to separate routine conversations (fast baseline path) from operationally coupled sessions (escalated workflow), improving reliability for backend writes while preserving fallbacks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the service-control problem in autonomous customer-service agents where routine requests must stay fast but operationally sensitive writes risk errors due to policy constraints, firm records, and backend actions; the goal is selective, evidence-informed deliberation.

Method: Introduce a lightweight router that directs routine sessions to a low-cost baseline path and routed escalations to a more deliberative workflow with conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration; evaluate on τ²-bench retail and airline tasks; analyze routing evidence, dialogue/tool-use profiles, and case-level behavior to understand where control is applied and how it affects writes.

Result: Reliability improves on feasibly conflicted service requests; routing concentrates control on conflicted cases rather than applying broad control; added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering and pre-write reconsideration; escalated workflows preserve fallback plans, bind records to actions, and sequence writes; results extend from retail to airline reservation tasks.

Conclusion: Targeted, difficulty-aware routing can enhance service safety without sacrificing speed by focusing deliberation where it is most needed, and the gains stem from structured reconsideration and write separation rather than indiscriminate extension of tools or interactions.

Abstract: Autonomous customer-service agents are shifting from conversational interfaces toward operational execution roles: they retrieve firm records, apply service policies, and execute backend writes such as refunds, cancellations, exchanges, order modifications, and reservation changes. This shift creates a service-control problem: firms must keep routine service fast and low-friction while preventing operational errors on requests where customer instructions, policy constraints, firm records, and backend writes interact. We propose a difficulty-routed service-control architecture that asks when service agents should reconsider before acting. A lightweight router keeps routine sessions on a low-cost baseline path and routes operationally coupled sessions to an escalated workflow. The escalated path uses conflict-aware communication and write-triggered reconsideration to concentrate deliberation and safeguards before consequential backend writes, rather than applying additional control uniformly across all service sessions. We evaluate the architecture on human-verified retail and airline tasks from $τ^{2}$-bench. In retail, the method improves reliability consistently on service requests with operational conflict. Routing evidence shows that stronger control is directed toward conflicted requests rather than broadly applied to routine ones. Dialogue and tool-use profiles suggest that gains do not come from indiscriminate interaction expansion or broader tool chains; instead, added turns and tool calls support evidence gathering, write separation, and pre-write reconsideration. Case-level evidence shows that the escalated workflow preserves fallback plans, binds retrieved records to the correct action, sequences writes, and decomposes multi-entity requests. Airline results extend the same service-control logic to reservation operations.

</details>


### [272] [CreativityNeuro: Steering Language Model Weights to Improve Divergent Thinking and Reduce Mode Collapse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01433)
*Samuel Schapiro,Core Francisco Park,Felix Sosa,Lav R. Varshney*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Data-free weight-space contrastive steering (CreativityNeuro) enhances divergent thinking in LLMs, reduces mode collapse, and improves originality/surprise across multiple tasks without data or training; weight-space steering outperforms activation steering on transfer tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs tend to converge on similar outputs (mode collapse) and struggle with divergent thinking. A data-free, weight-space approach aims to steer models toward novelty without requiring training data or fine-tuning.

Method: Contrastive weight steering: data-free manipulation of model weights to encourage divergent thinking, contrasted with activation-based steering. Evaluation across Divergent Association Task (DAT), Alternative Uses Test (AUT), and Task Task with large-scale human evaluation (N=720) and additional metrics.

Result: CreativityNeuro yields up to 14 percentile-point gains on DAT; significant gains in originality, surprise, and creativity on AUT and Task Task; reduced mode collapse across all tasks; weight-space steering generalizes better than activation steering (DAT transfer absent for activation steering).

Conclusion: A scalable, data-free method to boost divergent thinking in LLMs, functioning without data collection, retraining, or gradient-based fine-tuning, and with transfer to unseen tasks.

Abstract: Divergent thinking is a crucial aspect of creativity, yet large language models (LLMs) tend to consistently generate similar responses to open-ended questions, in what has been termed the artificial hivemind effect. Here, we introduce CreativityNeuro, a data-free method for enhancing divergent thinking in LLMs via contrastive weight steering. We evaluate our method across multiple creativity assessments and report several main findings. On the Divergent Association Task (DAT), a vocabulary-space creativity test, CreativityNeuro improves performance by up to 14 human percentile points. Next, in a large-scale human evaluation (N=720) on the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) and the Task Task, CreativityNeuro achieves significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity, transferring to longer-form and more open-ended tasks. Importantly, we find that across all three tasks, CreativityNeuro demonstrably reduces measures of mode collapse. Moreover, activation steering achieves comparable performance to CreativityNeuro on the DAT, but it does not transfer to the AUT and Task Task, demonstrating the effectiveness of weight-space steering in generalizing to unseen tasks. In conclusion, CreativityNeuro improves divergent thinking and reduces mode collapse without requiring behavioral data, re-training, or gradient-based fine-tuning, providing a straightforward way to enhance LLM performance in creative domains.

</details>


### [273] [Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01436)
*Max Van Puyvelde,Halil Ibrahim Gulluk,Wim Van Criekinge,Olivier Gevaert*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DiffusionGemma-26B, a mixture-of-experts diffusion LM, matches/exceeds a same-size autoregressive baseline on medical VQA; offers faster decoding and any-order infill, enabling better drafting in radiology reports.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether diffusion-based language models can rival autoregressive models in a high-stakes medical domain and to enable flexible text infill/editing workflows.

Method: Adapt diffusion Gemma-26B; benchmark against autoregressive Gemma-4-26B with an identical LoRA adaptation on medical visual-question-answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge; analyze decoding speed; finetuning yields a 3.8B active model.

Result: Diffusion matches or exceeds autoregressive models on all datasets; finetuned diffusion is competitive with frontier vision-language models; decoding is 3.5–4.4x faster; provides any-order infill by bidirectional denoising, enabling drafting between fixed fragments.

Conclusion: Diffusion LMs can achieve parity with AR models in medical text tasks, with added efficiency and a drafting capability that aligns well with clinical report workflows.

Abstract: Diffusion language models, which generate text by denoising a token canvas bidirectionally instead of emitting tokens left to right, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) generation. Medical foundation models, however, remain almost entirely autoregressive. We adapt a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, and benchmark it against its same-size AR sibling Gemma-4-26B under an identical LoRA recipe on medical visual question answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge. Diffusion matches or exceeds AR on all of them, and the finetuned model (3.8B active) is competitive with frontier vision-language models; its decoding is also 3.5-4.4x faster. Beyond this parity, the diffusion model offers a drafting capability AR lacks: any-order infill. Because the canvas is denoised bidirectionally, a radiologist can fix report fragments and have the model fill the text between them, an operation inherent to diffusion but not to autoregression, which is subpar at it. This suits real reports, which are often terse or inconsistent across clinicians and institutions.

</details>


### [274] [Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01465)
*Karthikeya Aditya Vissa,Sankalp Mane,Ananya Mantravadi,Harshit Rajgarhia,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RLVR improves policy performance for LLMs in niche enterprise APIs by training in synthetic, verifiable environments; achieves near-optimal rewards on several tasks, but requires handcrafted rewards and shows saturation in one scenario.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address objective misalignment where LLMs predict next tokens but fail to act correctly in API-driven workflows; evaluate whether RL with verifiable rewards in the target environment can bridge this gap, using no live APIs or human labels.

Method: Five synthetic environments emulating Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs, with rewards computed from the tool-call trace alone; no live API, no learned judge, no human labeling; evaluate Qwen 3.1B/3.5B models; compare RL-trained policy against a 4B baseline using checkers from GRPO training.

Result: RLVR-trained policies raise average reward from a 4B baseline range of 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00 across four non-degenerate tasks; largest improvement is Confluence page creation (0.35 → 1.00).

Conclusion: Preliminary step toward outcome-optimized small models for niche enterprise APIs; key limitations include the scalability challenge of hand-crafting verifiable rewards and a saturating reward shape in one scenario where a 4B prompt already maxes out.

Abstract: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

</details>


### [275] [World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01470)
*Ananya Mantravadi,Harshit Rajgarhia,Prasanna Desikan,Abhishek Mukherji*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL for clinical protocol-execution tasks is limited by structural feedback and knowledge gaps; MedAgentBench-v3 narrows the ceiling but reveals two primary barriers (capability ceiling and format-knowledge barrier); pure RL underperforms relative to rule-based SFT; a taxonomy-based fix combining SFT-injected codes with RL-conditioned learning is proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate the learnability of RL for clinical protocol-execution tasks, identify bottlenecks, and propose a taxonomy to guide future design and remediation.

Method: Audit MedAgentBench versions (v1/v2); construct MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3) with 508 tasks; evaluate Qwen3-8B; diagnose capability and format-knowledge barriers; quantify RL vs rule-based SFT performance.

Result: Identified a silent-finish ceiling of 41.7% in earlier benchmarks, which is reduced to an 8.9% ceiling in MAB-v3. Found a capability ceiling (10/20 task types with 0% base performance) and a format-knowledge barrier (3/20 task types require exact clinical codes not discoverable by exploration). Pure RL achieves 18.2% pass@1, versus 34.1% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9 percentage-point gap is attributed entirely to these barriers.

Conclusion: A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy can predict RL learnability and guide remediation: inject codes via SFT and let RL learn conditional decision logic.

Abstract: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling). Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

</details>


### [276] [Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01480)
*Ye Liu,Srijan Bansal,Bo Pang,Yang Li,Zeyu Leo Liu,Yifei Ming,Zixuan Ke,Shafiq Joty,Semih Yavuz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PMD introduces online cross-episode procedural memory that is distilled into the policy, producing a memory-free model at inference and yielding gains over SDPO on SCIKNOWEVAL and LIVECODEBENCH; memory-policy co-evolution is key.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and self-distillation variants reuse episode-level signals but discard richer cross-episode procedural information. PMD aims to capture cross-episode patterns, failure modes, and recurring strategies to improve generalization.

Method: PMD builds memory at three abstraction levels (raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies/lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns) online from the agent's rollouts. A memory-conditioned self-teacher uses accumulated experience to supervise the student; the memory adapts as the policy updates, enabling co-evolution. The final policy is memory-free at inference.

Result: PMD improves SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B. Freezing either memory or policy reduces gains by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains, demonstrating the importance of co-evolution.

Conclusion: Cross-episode procedural knowledge can be effectively learned online and distilled into policy parameters, yielding substantial gains and enabling a memory-free deployed model. The three-level memory and the memory-conditioned teacher appear to be critical components.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

</details>


### [277] [The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01507)
*Jiacheng Miao,Jonathan K Pritchard,James Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI agents reveal multiverse analysis through personas; introduces m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to quantify credibility of analyses across plausible paths.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Analytical variation leads to divergent conclusions; need observable distribution of analyses to improve credibility.

Method: Use AI agents with different personas across four domains; compare with human teams analyzing immigration dataset; develop m-value and Agentic Bootstrap.

Result: Agents capture substantial portion of human ideological gaps; many analyses pass AI and human reviews; 13.5% of analyses in most extreme 5% (m<0.05).

Conclusion: Evaluation should consider the distribution of plausible analyses; Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and a credibility criterion.

Abstract: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

</details>


### [278] [Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01510)
*Natalie Grace Brigham,Eugene Bagdasarian,Tadayoshi Kohno,Franziska Roesner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Janus introduces a modular system and evaluation framework for user-involved agentic permission management, implementing six permission assistants, and demonstrates that user input and AI augmentation improve privacy/security and reduce cognitive load, but there is no single optimal design; system is publicly available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the underexplored role of users in controlling permission management for autonomous AI agents, and to evaluate how different interactive designs can balance privacy, security, and cognitive load in varied contexts.

Method: Janus comprises Janus-Core, a modular agentic platform supporting diverse permission-management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model of design axes for user involvement, the authors implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios with three synthetic responders.

Result: Key findings show that user input is critical and can strengthen privacy and security; AI augmentation of user decisions can reduce cognitive load; realistic user behavior, including permission fatigue, must be accounted for in design; no single permutation of permission assistants is optimal across all contexts.

Conclusion: A principled, context-sensitive approach is needed for deploying permission assistants in agentic systems, and Janus provides a publicly available platform to support further investigation into user-involved permission management.

Abstract: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

</details>


### [279] [Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01511)
*Hongyang He,Jiuming Liu,Victor Sanchez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Semi-CoT uses unlabeled questions to generate multiple pseudo-CoTs, selects low-entropy (high-confidence) chains as demonstrations, and trains with semi-supervised signals; results are mixed across datasets, with high pseudo-CoT precision but limited or negative gains on some tasks, indicating the need for stronger demonstration selection or student training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CoT reasoning improves LLMs but its traces are rarely reused for learning. Semi-CoT aims to exploit unlabeled data to produce pseudo reasoning supervision, extending CoT from inference-time prompts to semi-supervised learning signals.

Method: For each unlabeled question, Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This reframes CoT as semi-supervised pseudo-supervision, enabling self-training with pseudo-CoTs.

Result: Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate yields high-precision pseudo-CoTs (pseudo-answer precision 91.36%–100%). Semi-CoT yields small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, and a ceiling effect on MultiArith, indicating results are dataset-dependent.

Conclusion: Unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo-reasoning signals, but effective use requires stronger demonstration selection criteria or improved student training to avoid negative transfer and to surpass ceiling effects.

Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

</details>


### [280] [OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01531)
*David Courtis,Wenhao Li,Scott Sanner*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPINE-World learns an object-centric, programmatic world model online via a two-agent loop (model synthesis with CEGIS and action in the environment) using replay verification and model-based planning, guided by ontology error, achieving strong skill-learning efficiency on ARC-AGI-3 (20/25 games solved, 78.4 action-efficiency).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural world models are data-hungry and tend to transfer poorly beyond training; there is a need for reusable, data-efficient world models that can flexibly infer object vocabularies and action semantics in unknown environments.

Method: Two cooperating agents: one acts in the environment; the other synthesizes an object-centric world-model in code using counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) with replay verification. The model supports model-based planning; exploration is guided by a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy (ontology error).

Result: In ARC-AGI-3, OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency score of 78.4 relative to human baseline.

Conclusion: Demonstrates data-efficient, reusable, object-centric world models built from LLM-generated code, with ontology-guided exploration improving sample efficiency; offers a scalable path toward generalizable agents, though benchmark-specific and synthesis-cost considerations remain.

Abstract: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

</details>


### [281] [Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01567)
*Oskar J. Hollinsworth,Ann-Kathrin Dombrowski,Sam Adam-Day,Adam Gleave,Chris Cundy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Scaling SOLiD to very large LLMs reduces undetected deception and can remove human labeling from fine-tuning, but performance hinges on distribution alignment between detector and preference data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor; scalable oversight via lie detectors (SOLiD) aims to minimize human labeling while maintaining safety.

Method: Scale SOLiD to 405B-parameter models and evaluate across diverse preference-learning settings; measure loss of undetected deception at a fixed detector TPR (99%), and assess the need for human labelers during fine-tuning; analyze robustness to distribution shift between detector training data and preference-training data.

Result: Undetected deception drops from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at detector TPR 99%; expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception; detector false positives rise with distribution shift between training distributions, leading to impractical FP rates.
