Conclusion: SOLiD scales favorably with model size and reduces reliance on human labeling, but distribution-shift robustness is a critical limitation needing mitigation.

Abstract: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

</details>


### [282] [EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01584)
*Mahyar Ghazanfari,Amin Tabrizian,Armin Mehrabian,Peng Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A KG-grounded, multi-agent LLM pipeline generates and evaluates novel, plausible Earth-observation dataset pairings; validated on 1,475 NASA datasets, yielding 160 hypotheses across domains, with rankings robust across LLMs but scores sensitive to judge identity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the reliance on unstructured literature in scientific hypothesis generation by grounding exploration in a structured knowledge graph (NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph) to improve rigor, reproducibility, and discovery of novel dataset pairings in Earth science.

Method: 1) Ground hypotheses in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. 2) Train a heterogeneous graph neural network on historical co-usage relations to rank candidate dataset pairings. 3) Use a three-agent LLM pipeline to filter, generate, and evaluate structured hypotheses. 4) Apply to 1,475 NASA datasets to produce 160 hypotheses across domains. 5) Conduct a 2×2×2 factorial evaluation across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 to assess stability of rankings vs dependence on judge identity.

Result: Produced 160 hypotheses spanning ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol–cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel pairings rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages, indicating coherence and potential novelty. Rankings remained stable across the two LLMs; absolute scores varied with judge identity, highlighting evaluation variability.

Conclusion: A KG-grounded, multi-agent LLM pipeline can surface scientifically coherent yet unexplored Earth-observation dataset pairings. The approach demonstrates robustness of relative rankings across LLMs but underscores the need for multi-judge evaluation to mitigate bias in absolute scores.

Abstract: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [283] [Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01590)
*Junyi Wen,Ruiyan Zhuang,Yongjia Xu,Pengtu Li,Rui Zou,Hongyi Chen,Chingman Wan,Puxu Yang,Wuhui Chen,Yanlin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hawk is a training-free framework that uses hardware-aware priors to generate NPU kernels via three modules—Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis, Bottleneck-Aware Retrieval, and Effect-Driven Distillation—achieving substantial accuracy and speedups on real-world NPU workloads.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Developing high-performance NPU kernels is bottlenecked by implicit hardware constraints and memory hierarchies. LLMs lack hardware-specific priors and naive code transplantation often violates hardware constraints, causing runtime crashes and degraded performance.

Method: Hawk consists of three modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module using a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to couple error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module implementing a 2D-Retrieval to map queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module leveraging LLM-driven semantic arbitration to distill knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on empirical execution feedback.

Result: Evaluations on real-world NPU workloads show Hawk increases generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and achieves up to 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: Hawk demonstrates that a training-free, hardware-aware knowledge framework can effectively address NPUs’ hardware constraints, delivering significant accuracy and performance gains; the approach suggests promising automation for NPU kernel development, with potential limitations and avenues for broader generalization across architectures.

Abstract: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [284] [Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01595)
*Junyan Tan,Haoran Lin,Siyuan Guo,Yichen Fang,Xinyue Luo,Tianyu Shen,Zeyu Qiao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PASE redefines fault self-healing as neuro-symbolic program synthesis using LLM planning, a neural-symbolic world model for feasibility checks, and a DRL-tuned meta-prompt optimizer, achieving faster recovery and better fault detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address reliability of cloud AI systems by tightly integrating planning, semantic understanding, verification, and meta-learning to generate adaptive recovery strategies beyond fixed action sets.

Method: LLM-based plan synthesis from semantic primitives; neural-symbolic world model for feasibility simulation; DRL-trained Meta-Prompt Optimizer to generate effective prompts guiding LLM; loop: reason-plan-verify-adapt.

Result: Significant performance gains on real-world cloud fault data: >40% reduction in average recovery time; improved fault detection accuracy in unknown faults; outperforms state-of-the-art.

Conclusion: Unifies LLM reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-guided planning to enable dynamic, context-aware self-healing and broaden applicability beyond predefined action spaces.

Abstract: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

</details>


### [285] [SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01601)
*Xinyi Fang,Kejian Tong,Jiabei Liu,Tao Ning,Yuhang He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemHash LLM presents a multi-granularity framework for large-scale document deduplication, combining semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to efficiently detect semantic duplicates with minimal neural verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scale and diversity of large corpora demand robust, scalable deduplication that preserves semantic equivalence while remaining computationally efficient and robust to template pollution, perturbations, containment, and viral fragments.

Method: Unified framework that fuses character-, token-, and document-level signals via gated fusion, followed by a cascaded filtering pipeline. Key components: semantic projection hashing in distilled LLM embedding space to learn compact binary codes; attention-weighted MinHash to suppress boilerplate and emphasize informative content; contrastive boundary learning for robust representations; adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation for robustness.

Result: Empirical results claim strong duplicate detection quality with less than 1% neural verification cost.

Conclusion: SemHash LLM achieves efficient, robust large-scale deduplication by integrating multi-granularity signals, selective adjudication, and uncertainty-aware decision boundaries, reducing neural verification without sacrificing semantic accuracy.

Abstract: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

</details>


### [286] [Profit-Based Counterfactual Explanations for Product Improvement: A Case Study of Manga Sales in Japan](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01610)
*Keita Kinjo,Takeshi Ebina*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE), a target-free, profit-maximizing framework that reinterprets distance as cost, aligning counterfactuals with business decision objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Counterfactual explanations (CE) typically require exogenous targets and a distance metric. In regression and real-world decision contexts, target specification can be vague or misleading, and explanations focused on prediction changes may not support explicit objective optimization. A framework that ties explanations to economic outcomes is needed.

Method: Formulate counterfactual explanations as a profit maximization problem. Propose PBCE, which directly maximizes profit as the objective, interprets the distance term as the cost of modifying product attributes, and eliminates the need for an externally specified target.

Result: PBCE provides a coherent, economically grounded framework for counterfactual explanations. It removes the requirement for an exogenous target and reinterprets distance as modification cost, aligning explanations with business decision objectives in management/marketing contexts.

Conclusion: PBCE addresses major limitations of existing CE methods by enabling decision-objective oriented, economically meaningful explanations without external target specification.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanation (CE) is widely used to enhance the interpretability of machine learning models and support data-driven decision-making based on model predictions. However, existing CE methods typically require two exogenously specified inputs: a desired output value (target) and a distance function that quantifies changes in explanatory variables. In regression settings, neither the validity of target specification nor the practical interpretation of the distance metric has been sufficiently addressed. Furthermore, most existing CE methods focus on altering predictions rather than optimizing a decision objective, even though real-world decision-making often requires explicit objective maximization. To address these limitations, we formulate CE as a profit maximization problem in management and marketing contexts and propose a framework termed profit-based counterfactual explanation (PBCE). PBCE eliminates the need for exogenous target specification by directly maximizing profit as the primary optimization objective. Concurrently, the distance term is reinterpreted as the cost of modifying product attributes, providing a clear and economically grounded interpretation.

</details>


### [287] [Scaling with Confidence: Calibrating Confidence of LLMs for Adaptive Test Time Scaling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01612)
*Xuqing Yang,Yi Yuan,Shanzhe Lei,Xuhong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces C3RL to optimize RLHF for correctness and confidence calibration, and CAS for adaptive test-time scaling; shows improved calibration and efficiency across multiple datasets; code and models to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RL reward designs emphasize correctness but ignore confidence calibration, causing overconfident, poorly calibrated outputs and hallucinations; need calibrated confidence and resource-aware inference.

Method: Propose C3RL, integrating correctness, calibration, and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards for RL; evaluate on 8 text and multimodal datasets. Develop CAS, an inference-time strategy using calibrated verbalized confidence to allocate computation adaptively. Release code, data, and models.

Result: C3RL improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy and outperforms SOTA on both performance and calibration metrics. CAS reduces inference budget (up to 12.33x) and surpasses majority voting on in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

Conclusion: The combination of C3RL and CAS enables more reliable and resource-efficient LLM deployment; authors plan to release code, data, and models.

Abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning (RL) has significantly advanced their performance on reasoning and question-answering tasks. However, prevailing RL reward designs typically prioritize response correctness, neglecting to incentivize models to express their confidence accurately. This leads to a critical problem: performance gains are often accompanied by poor calibration between confidence and accuracy, misleading models to overconfidently hallucinate when uncertain. To address this limitation, we propose $\textbf{C}$orrectness and $\textbf{C}$onfidence $\textbf{C}$alibration $\textbf{R}$einforcement $\textbf{L}$earning ($\textbf{C3RL}$), a novel RL algorithm integrating correctness, calibration and dataset-informed reference accuracy rewards together. Comprehensive evaluation across 8 text and multimodal datasets demonstrates that C3RL enhances calibration without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming the current state-of-the-art method in both performance and calibration metrics. Utilizing the well-calibrated verbalized confidence from C3RL, we further introduce $\textbf{C}$onfidence-based $\textbf{A}$daptive Test Time $\textbf{S}$caling ($\textbf{CAS}$), an adjustable inference-time strategy that allocates computational resources based on response confidence. Experiments show that CAS surpasses majority voting on both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets while reducing the inference budget by up to 12.33 times. We believe the synergy of C3RL and CAS paves the way for deploying more reliable and resource-efficient LLMs. The code, data and models will be released.

</details>


### [288] [Spatial Support Matters: Geometry-Aware Graph Fusion for Rainfall Field Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01621)
*Low Jun Yu,Niramay Kachhadiya,Herath Mudiyanselage Viraj Vidura Herath,Sanka Rasnayaka,Lucy Amanda Marshall*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network for fine-scale rainfall reconstruction that models 0D, 1D, and 2D observation supports and fuses them via cross-support message passing, achieving substantial RMSE gains and revealing when fusion helps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Different sensors measure rainfall at incompatible spatial supports (points, lines, grids), and existing reconstructions ignore geometry, limiting performance.

Method: Build a multi-layer heterogeneous graph with separate node layers per support type, perform cross-support message passing, and use a point-support prediction layer to reconstruct the field; employ inductive masked-node formulation to decouple prediction resolution from sensing resolution; evaluate on Singapore and Sydney; release code.

Result: On Singapore data, RMSE reduced by 23.2% over baselines; outperforms convolutional fusion and support-agnostic baselines; generalization shows fusion gains depend on gauge spacing relative to the field's spatial correlation length; largest gains when under-sampled.

Conclusion: Geometry-aware fusion across heterogeneous supports is effective for rainfall field reconstruction, with gains contingent on sampling density; method generalizes across cities; code will be open-sourced.

Abstract: Fine-scale rainfall reconstruction is critical for urban flood modeling, but real rainfall sensing systems observe the field through incompatible spatial supports: gauges measure points, microwave links measure paths, and radar/satellite products measure gridded areas. These differences in measurement support impose geometrically distinct constraints on the rainfall field, yet existing heterogeneous graph approaches reconcile such sources in feature space, giving each its own embedding while discarding the geometry of its support. We propose a geometry-aware multi-support heterogeneous graph neural network that represents each observation according to its support type (0D point, 1D line, or 2D grid) as a distinct node layer, and fuses them through cross-support message passing into a point-support prediction layer from which the field is reconstructed. An inductive masked-node formulation decouples prediction resolution from sensing resolution, allowing the same trained model to reconstruct the field at user-defined target locations or display grids. On Singapore data, the proposed method reduces RMSE by 23.2\% over the classical interpolation baseline, inverse-distance weighting, and consistently outperforms other neural architectures such as convolutional fusion and support-agnostic heterogeneous graph baselines. A generalization study using data from Sydney, Australia lets us characterize when multi-support fusion helps: the available skill appears to depend on gauge spacing relative to the spatial correlation length of the field, so fusion delivers the largest gains where the field is under-sampled relative to its correlation length and little when it is already resolved. Code and models will be open-sourced upon paper acceptance.

</details>


### [289] [Autonomous discovery of traffic laws with AI traffic scientists](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01639)
*Xingyuan Dai,Yue Liu,Xiaoyan Gong,Qinghai Miao,Junyou Shang,Yutong Wang,Chao Guo,Yonglin Tian,Yizhang Chai,Chao Xiang,Yisheng Lv,Fei-Yue Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TrafficSci presents an agentic AI pipeline for discovering universal traffic laws in urban systems, autonomously rediscovering known laws and revealing a new temporal memory scale, validated across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limit of expert-driven discovery in traffic science and the difficulty of extending AI workloads to complex transportation domains; provide an auditable, iterative workflow for evidence scoping, hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation.

Method: TrafficSci is an agentic AI system that integrates evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation in an iterative workflow. It was evaluated across four case-study scales—population, network, control, and trajectory—demonstrating autonomous discovery of traffic laws.

Result: The system autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and uncovers an intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets.

Conclusion: TrafficSci offers a viable path for expanding AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled environments to complex urban systems, enabling auditable, scalable law discovery in transportation domains.

Abstract: Universal traffic laws describe recurrent patterns in congestion, mobility and driving behavior across cities, providing a scientific basis for transportation planning, management and control. Their discovery, however, remains expert-driven, requiring candidate regularities to be identified from heterogeneous observational evidence or validated through intervention experiments. Although autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems have advanced scientific discovery in controlled laboratory settings, extending them to complex transportation domains remains a challenge. Here we present TrafficSci, an agentic AI system that formulates traffic-law discovery as an iterative, auditable workflow integrating evidence scoping, critic-judge hypothesis induction, and observational-interventional validation. Across four case studies spanning population, network, control and trajectory scales, TrafficSci autonomously rediscovers three established traffic laws and identifies an unreported intrinsic temporal memory scale in urban driving behavior, statistically consistent across eight cities and two trajectory datasets. TrafficSci provides a route for extending AI-driven scientific discovery from controlled domains to complex urban systems.

</details>


### [290] [Diverse Evidence, Better Forecasts: Multi-Agent Deliberation Under Information Asymmetry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01661)
*Yuante Li,Yicheng Tao,Kate Zhang,Taozhi Wang,Gefei Gu,Yaxin Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduce information asymmetry among LLM agents to improve multi-agent forecasting. Proposes InfoDelphi with relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. Demonstrates 12–18% improvement in Brier score and 4–8 percentage points in accuracy on PolyGym; ablations show asymmetry is key to gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address herd behavior and limited belief revision when agents share identical evidence. By partitioning evidence into shared and private subsets, agents retain exclusive knowledge that only reaches others through deliberation, reducing correlated errors.

Method: Partition evidence into public/shared and private/disjoint subsets. Use relevance-aware routing to assign evidence, iterative deliberation with rationale, and confidence-weighted aggregation of agent opinions. Provide theoretical analysis showing reduced inter-agent error correlation. Empirically evaluate on PolyGym (375 binary forecasting questions) comparing to strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines. Conduct ablation to test role of information asymmetry.

Result: InfoDelphi achieves 12–18% better Brier score and 4–8 percentage points higher accuracy than baselines. Removing information asymmetry eliminates most gains; input diversity is crucial for effective multi-agent reasoning.

Conclusion: Designed information asymmetry is a viable path to improve multi-agent reasoning; diverse input among agents reduces correlated errors and yields stronger ensemble performance. The approach and findings argue for routing and partitioning information in AI ensembles and may generalize beyond forecasting to other decision tasks.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used for forecasting future events, as deliberation among multiple LLMs is believed to improve reasoning and calibration. Yet existing approaches overlook a critical design choice: what information each agent receives. When all agents are given identical evidence, deliberation collapses into herding rather than genuine belief revision, leaving multi-agent systems little better than a single agent. We identify this as a fundamental gap and propose designed information asymmetry to close it: by partitioning evidence into shared public and disjoint private subsets, each agent holds exclusive knowledge that can only reach others through deliberation. We theoretically show that this decomposition reduces inter-agent error correlation, and instantiate it in InfoDelphi, a framework combining relevance-aware evidence routing, rationale-based iterative deliberation, and confidence-weighted aggregation. On PolyGym, a benchmark of 375 binary forecasting questions derived from real-world prediction markets, InfoDelphi outperforms the strongest single-agent and multi-agent baselines by 12--18% in Brier score and 4--8 percentage points in accuracy. More detailed experiments confirm that removing information asymmetry eliminates most deliberation gains, establishing diversity of input as the key enabler of effective multi-agent reasoning.

</details>


### [291] [Separating Expert Retention from Autonomous Source Inference in Raw-ECG-Replay-Free Continual ECG Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01674)
*Yufan Lu,Xinhui Liu,Chenyang Xu,Yuxi Zhou,Hao Wang,Shenda Hong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An incremental, source-aware expert-bank approach for multi-source ECG with a frozen backbone; strong performance when source IDs are available; performance degrades without IDs; top-2 fusion provides marginal gains; main bottleneck is autonomous source inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need to preserve prior sources and integrate new ones without replaying raw data; handle absence of explicit source metadata in deployment; seek robust, scalable domain adaptation via per-source experts and lightweight routing.

Method: Freeze a 1024-dimensional ECGFounder backbone. For each incoming domain, add a balanced-softmax linear expert. Train a lightweight router on retained training features and domain labels from observed sources. Use a validation-calibrated margin rule to fuse the two most likely experts rather than committing to a single routed expert. Evaluate with source IDs (source-aware routing) and without IDs (MLP router with margin fusion) across four datasets (CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, Chapman-Shaoxing). Compare to a matched offline independent-head reference.

Result: Source-aware expert selection achieves Macro-F1 = 0.7915 ± 0.0036, closely matching the offline reference of 0.7885 ± 0.0009. Without source IDs, an MLP router attains 0.7756 ± 0.0027, and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782 ± 0.0022. The gain of top-2 fusion over hard MLP routing is small (+0.0026) with a 95% bootstrap CI that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2 to oracle gap remains 0.0111–0.0133, indicating autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed; however, training features are retained for router updates, so the method is not memory-free.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong retention of source-specific expertise with a frozen backbone, achieving near-parity with an offline reference when source IDs are available. In the absence of source IDs, performance remains limited by unsupervised source inference; marginal gains from top-2 fusion are small. The method is not memory-free due to retained features, raising considerations for practical deployment in streaming settings.

Abstract: In multi-source ECG deployment, models may need to incorporate new data sources when earlier raw ECGs cannot be retained or replayed. Freezing a pretrained backbone and assigning each source an isolated classifier prevents parameter interference, but deployment still requires selecting an expert when source metadata are unavailable. We study this distinction through \ours{}, an incremental expert bank built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features. Each arriving domain adds a balanced-softmax linear expert, while a lightweight router is fitted only on retained training features and domain labels from sources observed so far. A validation-calibrated margin rule fuses the two most likely experts instead of committing to a single routed expert.
  On CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches $0.7915\pm0.0036$ Macro-F1 and a matched offline independent-head reference reaches $0.7885\pm0.0009$, supporting strong source-aware expert retention. Without source IDs, an MLP router reaches $0.7756\pm0.0027$ and top-2 margin fusion reaches $0.7782\pm0.0022$. The top-2 gain over hard MLP routing is small ($+0.0026$), with a 95\% confidence interval from paired bootstrap that includes zero. Across three domain orders, the top-2-to-oracle gap remains $0.0111$--$0.0133$, identifying autonomous source inference as the main remaining bottleneck. No raw ECGs are replayed, but frozen training features are retained for router updates; the method is therefore not memory-free.

</details>


### [292] [Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01690)
*Joshua Penman*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Goggles is a gradient-editing module added to LoRA finetuning that imposes a chosen epistemic frame on how the model interprets trained documents. It converts negation neglect into correct fiction identification, achieving ~91% fiction detection after training, while preserving or improving GPQA/TruthfulQA performance. The method generalizes to other frames (e.g., AI-safety evaluations) and suggests a path to training on misaligned data without adopting its undesired behaviors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address Negation Neglect: models trained on fiction-annotated documents continue to internalize the core claims. The goal is to steer finetuning signals without changing data, enabling controlled epistemic framing.

Method: Introduce Goggles: a gradient-editing module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient received by a LoRA-equipped LLM. Trained once per base model, frame, and LoRA config, then frozen at inference. Applied to documents it was not trained on. In experiments, a Goggles-trained model on fiction-annotated data flags content as fictional ~91% of the time on that data, while maintaining GPQA and TruthfulQA performance; the same architecture supports other frames (e.g., treating docs as AI-safety evaluations).

Result: The Goggles intervention yields a marked increase in fictional content flagging (≈91%) on previously annotated documents without sacrificing core task performance; original baseline capabilities are preserved or exceeded.

Conclusion: Gradient-level interventions can reframe model interpretation of misaligned data without internalizing the misalignment themselves. Goggles offers a reusable mechanism to train models on misaligned data while mitigating undesirable behaviors and can be extended to alternative epistemic frames.

Abstract: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

</details>


### [293] [COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01709)
*Zongxia Li,Dawei Liu,Fuxiao Liu,Yuhang Zhou,Xiyang Wu,Jingxi Chen,Jing Xie,Xiaomin Wu,Lichao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: COMFYCLAW introduces skill-evolving agents for recurring, workflow-based image generation. It uses typed graph editing, staged tools, automatic reversal of invalid edits, and a region-level VLM verifier. A progressively disclosed Agent Skill library distills past runs into reusable skills, improving reliability and performance; it outperforms verifier-only baselines and is preferred by humans.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agents need to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences across repeated runs in domain-specific tasks, to improve reliability and efficiency in recurring visual workflows.

Method: Construct workflows via typed graph editing; expose tools by construction stage; automatically revert invalid edits; employ a region-level vision-language model verifier to translate visual failures into repair actions; evolve a skill library by distilling trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills; evaluate across multiple benchmarks, agent models, and image backbones against a verifier-only baseline.

Result: COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across six configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline; human annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.

Conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism to improve agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

Abstract: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

</details>


### [294] [Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01710)
*Yongqin Zeng,Sicheng Pan,Jiale Wang,Hai-tao Zheng,Hong-Gee Kim,Chunxia Ma,XiuTeng Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new MoE pruning method, Generic TB-Coverage, uses per-corpus utility profiles and a fixed-budget coverage rule to prune experts without downstream calibration data, improving zero-shot accuracy and reducing perplexity degradation across two MoE models and multiple pruning budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sparsely activated MoE models exhibit structured redundancy; single aggregated importance scores bias pruning toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. A generic-data prior that preserves cross-corpus high-utility experts could enable effective pruning without downstream calibration data.

Method: Profile per-expert utility separately on each corpus (WikiText2 and C4). Enforce a fixed-budget coverage rule to retain high-utility experts from each corpus, then construct the final pruning mask. Evaluate at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, comparing against random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity.

Result: Under 25%, 50%, and 75% retention, the method improves average zero-shot accuracy across six benchmarks versus baselines and reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain). The approach works with fixed budgets and requires no downstream calibration data.

Conclusion: Cross-corpus coverage acts as a robust generic-data prior for MoE pruning, enabling effective pruning without downstream calibration data and improving performance especially under aggressive pruning.

Abstract: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

</details>


### [295] [Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01715)
*Xudong Wu,Jian Qian,Pangpang Liu,Vaneet Aggarwal,Jiayu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A robust listwise Plackett-Luce objective under ranking-label uncertainty, with a decomposition into a nominal loss plus a worst-case correction. It enables tractable optimization (O(K log K) for the inner maximization) and provides strong theoretical guarantees in offline (convex) and online (weakly convex) settings, with empirical gains in robustness for offline and online LLM alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address robustness for ranking-based supervision in language-model alignment under listwise uncertainty. Prior work focused on pairwise robustness and affected dataset/prompt/pair-level robustness. This work targets label uncertainty in listwise rankings (annotations, near-ties, lossy feedback, reward-model noise).

Method: Introduce a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective that robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The objective decomposes exactly into a nominal Plackett-Luce loss plus a worst-case PL correction. The worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores ascending, reducing the inner maximization from factorial to O(K log K). This leads to tractable offline and online optimization with theoretical guarantees.

Result: Offline fixed-list: the robust objective is convex; projected stochastic subgradient achieves global ε-suboptimality with O(ε^{-2}) sample complexity. Online policy-induced setting: weak convexity and ~O(ε^{-2}) Moreau-envelope stationary points. Empirically, robust correction preserves performance with clean labels and improves robustness under noise; online alignment shows more reliable reward-model-ranked candidate expansion and improved reward-model and GPT-4 judge metrics.

Conclusion: The proposed robust listwise approach provides a theoretically sound and computationally efficient method to handle ranking-label uncertainty in LLM alignment, yielding strong offline and online guarantees and practical robustness benefits.

Abstract: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

</details>


### [296] [DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01729)
*Yueming Huang,Wenhan Yao,Fen Xiao,Xiarun Chen,Weiping Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes DRL-CLBA, a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification using DDPG RL to align target samples with trigger-bearing anchors embedded via deep audio steganography, enabling label-migration-free poisoning and evading several defenses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap where traditional backdoors rely on poisoned labels or sample-specific triggers, by enabling stealthy clean-label backdoors in speech systems and testing robustness of defenses.

Method: Embed triggers into source audio via deep audio steganography to create sample-specific anchors. Use Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning to optimize latent-space representations so that target samples move toward trigger-bearing anchors, achieving poisoning without label changes.

Result: High attack success rate across three datasets and four DNNs; effectively bypasses some backdoor defenses and shows strong resistance to fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a potent clean-label backdoor in speech classification, challenging current defenses and underscoring need for stronger detection; suggests future work on reducing detectability, improving generalization, and evaluating real-world risk.

Abstract: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

</details>


### [297] [Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01734)
*Simon Guilloud,Sankalp Gambhir,Samuel Chassot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem across Mizar→Lean, HOL Light→Lean, and HOL Light→Agda illustrate how pipeline design choices shape reformalization outcomes and provide practical guidance for cross-system formalization tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enhance interoperability among formal proof systems and advance autoformalization by using existing formal developments as inputs. The Jordan Curve Theorem serves as a nontrivial benchmark across heterogeneous foundations (Mizar, HOL Light, Lean, Agda).

Method: Empirical case study of three reformalization pipelines. Analyze interface-level design choices, including representation of topology and real analysis, library compatibility and abstractions, translation of types/predicates, proof term generation, and automation support. Compare outcomes, identify bottlenecks, and distill design guidelines for practical reformalization tasks.

Result: Pipeline design choices materially affect reformalization feasibility and quality. Key factors include alignment of foundational notions, compatible library structures and abstractions, encoding granularity, and support for proof automation. Some source–target pairs transfer more smoothly than others, highlighting the importance of careful encoding strategies and tooling to manage concept drift and proof term translation.

Conclusion: Provide concrete best-practice guidelines for reformalization workflows (e.g., harmonize foundational assumptions, reuse and adapt libraries thoughtfully, and plan translation steps to minimize drift). Suggest tooling directions and standardization efforts to reduce friction in cross-proof-system reformalization.

Abstract: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

</details>


### [298] [Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01740)
*Blair Hudson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-benchmarking framework aggregates 452 public benchmarks into 41 O*NET tasks and 38 BIAN banking domains, using a multiplicative discrimination×coverage×recency weighting over a rolling window to scale an Elo-based K-factor, enabling cross-benchmark comparability without raw score normalization; demonstrated on 288 models from 25 organizations as of June 2026; aims for reproducible governance-friendly model selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize global averages and miss domain-specific cognitive demands of financial-services work. A framework aligning benchmarks with real job tasks is needed to improve domain relevance and governance, avoid saturation of legacy tests, and provide cross-benchmark comparability.

Method: Map 452 public benchmarks to 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and 38 BIAN banking domains. Apply a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) on a rolling model window. Use these weights to scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, yielding cross-benchmark work-activity Elos. Compute domain scores as weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos. Validate on a point-in-time snapshot of 288 models across 25 organizations (as of June 2026).

Result: Demonstrates a reproducible meta-benchmarking framework that produces cross-benchmark, domain-relevant scores without raw normalization, and provides a complete methodology, taxonomy, design choices, and limitations for governance-oriented model selection.

Conclusion: The approach offers a governance-friendly, domain-aligned benchmarking pathway that mitigates legacy test saturation and enables cross-benchmark comparability, supporting institutions in selection and governance challenges.

Abstract: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

</details>


### [299] [Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01754)
*Sung June Kim,Sangpil Kim,Honglak Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Phi-Nav introduces an on-policy, dual-supervision framework that uses hindsight reasoning to align an agent's exploratory trajectories with language instructions, enabling dense semantic supervision with limited expert demonstrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On-policy exploration in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) creates semantic mismatch between executed visual streams and original instructions. Semantic supervision is needed to leverage exploratory data efficiently and reduce annotation cost.

Method: A three-stage cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert-action feedback, (2) a hindsight speaker generates a path-level instruction from collected visuals, (3) a second imitation pass treats the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as additional expert data.

Result: Phi-Nav achieves competitive results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring substantially fewer expert demonstrations than baselines, highlighting the value of semantic exploration for VLN.

Conclusion: Phi-Nav bridges the semantic supervision gap in on-policy VLN by converting semantically unlabeled movements into dense training signals, enabling effective learning with limited annotated data.

Abstract: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

</details>


### [300] [Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01764)
*Mingzhe Du,Luu Anh Tuan,Tianyi Wu,Renyang Liu,Zhijiang Guo,Dong Huang,See-Kiong Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Mastermind introduces a dual-loop learning framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience to improve repository-level vulnerability reproduction; a trainable planner learns reusable strategies via supervised fine-tuning and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local records; achieves high pass rates and cross-executor improvements on CyberGym.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Strategy-level learning is a compact, concrete, and reusable unit that better guides execution and generalizes across tasks and executors, addressing failures due to poor strategy choices in repository-scale SE agents.

Method: A dual-loop architecture: a trainable planner (SFT + milestone-based GRPO) learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies; an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records to guide attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, enabling strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without changing their action-generation capability. Evaluation on CyberGym with 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks, using GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor.

Result: With GPT-5.5 as executor, Mastermind achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM-5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%, respectively.

Conclusion: Learning high-level, transferable strategies is effective for improving repository-scale SE agents, achieving strong cross-executor gains and robust performance improvements.

Abstract: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

</details>


### [301] [SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01766)
*Chunjiang Liu,Xiaoyuan Wang,Haoyu Chen,Yizhou Zhao,Ming-Hsuan Yang,László A. Jeni*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text using Blender, featuring a planner-coder-reviewer workflow, a layered scene protocol with a deterministic verifier, and runtime inspection tools, plus a 4DBuildBench benchmark; experiments show it surpasses prior dynamic Blender baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dynamic 4D scene generation from text is underexplored and challenging due to coordinating layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera/lighting, and verifying motion across rendered video.

Method: Introduce SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework with Blender-specific procedural knowledge; a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages via a planner-coder-reviewer workflow; a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier; and runtime-state inspection tool suite to catch mechanism failures.

Result: Development of SimWorlds and 4DBuildBench; experiments demonstrate superior visual fidelity and physical consistency compared to prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

Conclusion: SimWorlds enables editable, physics-grounded 4D scene generation from text and provides a benchmark for assessing visual and physical quality, along with tools to diagnose failures beyond what rendered frames convey.

Abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

</details>


### [302] [Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01767)
*Xinyuan Song,Zekun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair) outperforms engineering in-graph repair for large planning graphs by targeting a causal amplification subgraph; it stabilizes near-whole graph with compact region under token budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As planning graphs grow to thousands of steps, failures occur inside the graph; full-graph replay is costly, consumes large context, and degrades long-context retrieval. A in-place world-model corrector is needed.

Method: Compare two corrector families: engineering local-region repair using LLM on suspicious nodes/edges; WM-SAR identifies the subgraph responsible for repeating errors by backward amplification, extracts that causal subgraph, and sends only it to the LLM for repair.

Result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact subgraph, and provides a cleaner repair target for LLMs; validated across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments.

Conclusion: A targeted, amplification-based subgraph repair approach yields more efficient and effective repairs for large planning graphs, reducing context burden and improving stabilization when leveraging LLMs.

Abstract: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

</details>


### [303] [Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01773)
*Yujin Yang,Heejung Lee*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Retrieval-augmented SLM with FCA verification yields inspectable implications for knowledge expansion; results show modest F1 gains dependent on seed size; challenges in identifying positive object-attribute pairs persist.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate unreliability and inconsistency in LM-derived knowledge structures by coupling a retrieval-grounded SLM with a symbolic FCA verification loop that inspects implications, counterexamples, and corrections.

Method: Start from seed attributes; FCA derives implications over a growing formal context; a retrieval-grounded SLM oracle validates each implication or provides counterexamples; oracle supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals; results include ablations to assess the impact of different components.

Result: In a rare ataxia setting derived from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs yield relation F1 of 0.29–0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22–0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. Lower scores reflect stricter evaluation; ablations show incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores, but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even with fixed candidate objects/attributes.

Conclusion: The framework provides inspectable implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections, enabling verification and refinement of knowledge structures; however, strict evaluation reduces scores and pinpointing positive object-attribute pairs remains challenging, indicating a need for better seed selection and OA identification.

Abstract: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

</details>


### [304] [Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01774)
*Maximo Rulli,Thomas Fontanari,Simone Petruzzi,Federico Alvetreti,Giorgio Strano,Donato Crisostomi,Giorgos Nikolaou,Tommaso Mencattini,Andrea Santilli,Emanuele Rodolà,Simone Scardapane,Alessio Devoto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Diffusion Language Models implicitly encode denoising progress in their residual activations; this latent signal is decodable and can be steered in a low-dimensional subspace to modulate model confidence and entropy, with a structured, interpretable activation geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how diffusion language models operate without explicit timestep conditioning and whether they internally represent the denoising progress that guides generation.

Method: Probe hidden activations across layers to decode a latent timestep signal; train or apply probes to extract denoising-progress information; rotate or steer the model along a low-dimensional subspace aligned with the inferred timestep to modulate progress; analyze effects on confidence/entropy and study the geometry of the activation representations.

Result: A decodable latent signal corresponding to denoising progress exists across layers; steering along the inferred timestep subspace produces systematic, predictable changes in model confidence and entropy; the activation space exhibits structured and interpretable geometry.

Conclusion: DLMs maintain an internal latent representation of denoising progress that can be extracted and manipulated, providing mechanistic insight into how these models operate and offering a lever for controllability.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

</details>


### [305] [Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01793)
*Yunhao Feng,Ruixiao Lin,Ming Wen,Qinqin He,Yanming Guo,Yifan Ding,Yutao Wu,Jialuo Chen,Yunhao Chen,Xiaohu Du,Jianan Ma,Zixing Chen,Zhuoer Xu,Xingjun Ma,Xinhao Deng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety-testing framework for non-deterministic LLM agents, using a three-stage pipeline to discover, instantiate, and evaluate safety risks across tool-use scenarios, exposing weaknesses with executable safety cases and adaptive sandboxes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address evolving safety risks of autonomous LLM agents that interact with external tools by moving beyond static, expert-designed violations and hard-coded rules toward scalable, data-driven safety testing.

Method: Three-stage pipeline: (1) literature-driven taxonomy construction of safety risks, attack methods, and tool environments; (2) combinatorial generation of executable safety cases with concrete goals, initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution in sandboxed agents with a control agent steering multi-turn interactions and evidence-grounded verifiers judging outcomes from environment state and tool-call traces.

Result: Evaluation across four production frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code) reveals substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates of 93.9% under multi-channel attacks; Vera-Bench release includes 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings; code released publicly.

Conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure like Vera is essential for rigorous, scalable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems; the framework enables systematic discovery and verification of safety risks and can guide defenses and design improvements.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

</details>


### [306] [MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01814)
*Lihui Luo,Joongwon Chae,Ziyan Chen,Yang Liu,Siyi Cheng,Weihan Gao,Zelin Zeng,Xiaoming Yin,Samaneh Beheshti Kashi,Dongmei Yu,Lian Zhang,Jing Sui,Zeming Liang,Jiansong Ji,Peter E. Lobie,Peiwu Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MMIR-TCM is a three-stage multimodal AI framework that bridges tongue visuals with textual reasoning via memory-augmented segmentation and RAG, validated on a new MedTCM dataset with a domain metric (TDEU), outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis is highly subjective and suffers from poor reproducibility due to a semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual clinical reasoning, plus a lack of large standardized multimodal datasets.

Method: Three-stage architecture: (1) Memory-SAM for training-free tongue extraction; (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured tongue-diagnosis generation; (3) Qwen3-based RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Introduces MedTCM, a large-scale multimodal dataset, and TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric.

Result: Experiments show MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, demonstrating improved clinical accuracy and robust tongue extraction and evidence-grounded diagnosis generation.

Conclusion: MMIR-TCM advances multimodal AI for TCM diagnosis by integrating memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation with a domain-focused evaluation metric and a new dataset; it enhances reproducibility and clinical decision support in TCM and may generalize to similar multimodal diagnostic tasks.

Abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
