Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

</details>


### [307] [Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01829)
*Alex Brooker,Tim Hughes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A domain-specific aviation benchmark (Pre-Flight) reveals persistent gap between current LLMs and expert-level performance on safety-critical aviation knowledge, with strongest model at 82.7% accuracy vs ~95% expert reference; dataset and evaluation harness released to enable responsible deployment in aviation operations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the misalignment of general benchmarks with aviation safety and regulatory reasoning; high-stakes domain demands reliable, rule-consistent AI beyond generic QA.

Method: Construct 300 MCQs from ICAO/FAA standards and ground ops material; questions authored/reviewed by practitioners; evaluate models using Inspect framework with standard MCQ scoring; maintain rolling leaderbord; open-source dataset/harness.

Result: Strongest 2026 model: 82.7% accuracy; earlier 2025 ≈75%; informal expert baseline ≈95%; significant performance gap; progress gradual; dataset/harness released; benchmark integrated into inspect_evals.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is essential for safe deployment of generative AI in aviation; open-source benchmark enables community evaluation and tracked progress; more work needed to reach expert reliability and to test non-MCQ reasoning.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

</details>


### [308] [Actual causality in fault trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01840)
*Georgiana Caltais,Milan Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg,Mariëlle Stoelinga*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fault trees analyzed through Halpern & Pearl's actual causality to diagnose 'why' failures, with a complete classification linking graph/logical structure to minimal cut sets as actual causes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable failure diagnostics by answering 'why did the system go wrong?' by grounding fault-tree analysis in formal actual causality theory.

Method: Map fault tree graphs and logical connectors to Halpern & Pearl's notions of actual causality; provide a complete classification of these notions in terms of the FT structure; demonstrate how minimal cut sets instantiate actual causes.

Result: A complete classification of the different notions of actual causality within fault trees; an explicit mapping from minimal cut sets to actual causes, clarifying when a cut set constitutes an actual cause under various definitions.

Conclusion: Integrating fault trees with actual causality theory enhances failure diagnostics by enabling precise 'why' explanations and a principled interpretation of minimal cut sets as actual causes.

Abstract: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

</details>


### [309] [CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01846)
*Fangfei Li,Chenyang Zhao,Long Wang,Feng Tian,Zhiyue Zheng,Lv Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CLAP is a closed-loop post-training framework that converts domain business data into structured samples for SFT, decision preferences, holdouts, and risk/gate records to guide adapter selection for a target application chain. It integrates data validation, normalization, reward/KL diagnostics, offline gates, and application-chain replay. Experiments on anonymized manufacturing batches show modest average gains but mixed batch-level improvements; RAG helps factual extraction but increases latency, supporting an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop over a single offline score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Domain agents contend with noisy data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and release risk. A closed-loop, integrated post-training workflow aims to reliably select and deploy adapters within target application chains.

Method: CLAP converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. It combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to assess adapter suitability for a given application chain.

Result: QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280; hallucination and wrong facts decline. However, only 3 of 5 batches improve; some regress. GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application-chain replay with RAG improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG for a 3B backbone with 100 replay cases, but increases latency.

Conclusion: An integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop is more effective for managing domain-agent post-training than relying on training completion or a single offline metric.

Abstract: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

</details>


### [310] [Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01988)
*Xue Qin,Simin Luan,Cong Yang,Zhijun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deterministic, auditable memory consolidation for long-running agents that preserves the certified identity by updating a separate semantic knowledge layer without mutating the manifest.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Resolve the tension between learning from experience and maintaining cryptographically certified identity in regulated autonomous deployments.

Method: Define a deterministic f: M^ep -> M^sem that updates semantic knowledge; formalize agent representation; prove identity invariance via a hash-input-set lemma; implement auditable aggregation producing provenance-enabled database rows; validate with synthetic experiments showing per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across passes, and reduced unproductive planner attempts.

Result: Demonstrates byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, per-field correctness, and an average 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%]); corroborated by an embodied service agent case study.

Conclusion: Proposes a knowledge-update discipline that accumulates stored facts while keeping the agent’s certified identity stable, enabling auditable, compliant autonomic agents.

Abstract: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

</details>


### [311] [Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01859)
*Joshua Adrian Cahyono*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multilingual safety gap in LLMs; STEER exploits code-switching to suppress refusals; strong transferability across models; implies need for multilingual safety alignment and OOD abstention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety training is English-centric; unclear generalization to low-resource languages and code-switching; leads to epistemic risk where harmful prompts receive no refusal in non-English inputs.

Method: STEER: gradient-guided attack selecting words contributing to refusal; iteratively translates them to low-resource languages to suppress refusals while preserving harmful intent; evaluation across six open-source 8B-parameter models; baselines include random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG); transfer tests on GPT-4o-mini.

Result: Attack success: up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench, 96.7% on AdvBench; STEER outperforms baselines; prompts transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% attack success without access to target model.

Conclusion: Multilingual safety cannot be assumed to generalize from English; to improve, require broader multilingual alignment coverage and explicit detection/abstention on out-of-distribution inputs.

Abstract: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

</details>


### [312] [CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01870)
*Dawei Ren,Yan Zhang,Hongying Tang,Qiaoling Zhou,Jianpo Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A NAS-based COD framework (CamoNAS) that searches both operation cells and downsampling paths, plus a frequency-aware dual-stream (learnable wavelet + RGB) architecture; achieves SOTA on four COD benchmarks; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) is hard due to weak boundaries and edge cues. Hand-designed architectures and intuition-driven fusion are limited; neural architecture search (NAS) can discover architectures tailored to COD and multi-scale, frequency-aware representations can reveal camouflaged cues.

Method: CamoNAS performs hierarchical NAS to simultaneously search cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a search space specialized for COD. It uses a frequency-aware RGB dual-stream: a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream, enabling fusion of spatial and frequency information for improved camouflage detection.

Result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON). The authors provide the code at the referenced GitHub repository.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates that NAS can yield COD-specific architectures and that incorporating a learnable frequency-domain stream with RGB information enhances camouflaged object detection performance.

Abstract: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

</details>


### [313] [SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01874)
*Jiayin Zhu,Kelong Mao,Yudong Guo,Dengbo He,Sulong Xu,Simiu Gu,Yutao Yue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillCoach introduces a self-evolving rubric framework to evaluate and improve agentic skill-use by deriving process rubrics from real rollouts across four dimensions, separating verifier outcomes from process quality; experiments show rubrics improve evaluation, reveal hidden failures, and provide stronger supervision than outcome-only filtering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overlapping skills in real repositories cause unreliable skill-use and coarse final success signals. There's a need for fine-grained evaluation and supervision that distinguishes process quality from end-task success.

Method: Derive skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts. Evaluate trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. Maintain an external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be evaluated independently. Evolve rubrics to serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories.

Result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

Conclusion: Skill-grounded, evolving rubrics enable more reliable assessment and supervision of agentic skills, enabling better training and deployment by separating process quality from final task success.

Abstract: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

</details>


### [314] [Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01893)
*Tianjian Yang,Meng Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AUF is a minimal modification to the cross-entropy loss for mask-only block drafters in speculative decoding. By concentrating supervision on the accepted prefix (via a simple, detached CE-support change), it yields consistent improvements in average emitted length across backbones and benchmarks, without altering inference or the contract.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In block-drafter speculative decoding, training signals supervise every position in the draft block, but inference only uses the accepted prefix. This misalignment can hamper efficiency. The idea is to align supervision with the decoding behavior by concentrating loss on the accepted prefix.

Method: Introduce AUF as a single, detached change to the CE loss support: keep cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure for a mask-only block drafter. No auxiliary objectives, verifiers, rollouts, or changes to the inference pipeline.

Result: In Qwen3-8B backbones, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length τ from 2.40 to 2.61 across six benchmarks (and to 2.68 for Domino in its two-branch head). The decay-only baseline achieves higher token accuracy on the shared block mask but decodes worse; on DFlash, AUF truncation renders standard exponential position-decay weighting empirically inert.

Conclusion: AUF demonstrates that a minimal, prefix-focused adjustment to training loss can yield consistent decoding-length and benchmark gains without modifying inference or model contracts, highlighting a mismatch between block-training signals and prefix-based decoding behavior.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

</details>


### [315] [Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01903)
*Zihao Xu,Yuekang Li,Gelei Deng,Yi Liu,Zhenchang Xing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HECATE analyzes complexity in LLM-integrated apps across both prompt and code layers, introducing Prompt-as-Specification and a set of structural-breadth metrics that outperform traditional code-only metrics in predicting maintenance effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing complexity measures focus only on code and miss the behavioral logic encoded in prompts. There's a need to quantify prompt-layer complexity to understand and predict maintenance costs in LLM-enabled software.

Method: Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies, HECATE derives 52 candidate metrics. It evaluates 118 components from 18 open-source repos using maintenance activity as a proxy for complexity, discarding metrics whose significance vanishes after controlling for code size. The surviving set includes 10 metrics (7 new, emphasizing structural breadth of LLM calls, memory attributes, and prompt templates) and 3 conventional metrics (RFC, Halstead N, Halstead V). The prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when a strong code-size metric is included. Final validation on 20 components from 6 held-out repos shows the top metrics predict maintenance effort.

Result: Out of the 52 metrics, 10 remain significant after accounting for code size; 7 are novel and capture structural breadth in prompt usage, while 3 conventional metrics show limited breadth-only utility. The best two metrics generalize to held-out data and continue to predict maintenance effort.

Conclusion: Prompt complexity constitutes a distinct dimension in software complexity for LLM-integrated applications. HECATE demonstrates how prompt-level behavior—captured via Prompt-as-Specification and structural-breadth metrics—adds explanatory power for maintenance, beyond traditional code-centric metrics.

Abstract: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

</details>


### [316] [ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01916)
*Chiwang Luk,Matin Mohammad Najafi,Zhifeng Jia,Wei Yang,Xiuchang Li,Jinwei Zhu,Yang Ren,Lei Chen,Gao Cong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContextSniper is a token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair, reducing token usage and cost while maintaining evidence quality; evaluated on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code; results show significant token/cost reductions with a slight drop in submitted-resolution rates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents incur large token costs reading whole files, performing broad searches, and emitting long outputs; a compact, evidence-focused retrieval mechanism is needed to enable efficient repository-level repair.

Method: Sniper feature retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks via hybrid retrieval signals, filters outputs with an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable context outside the prompt. Evaluated on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code (50 task runs per host-agent). Open-source pilot scripts at the provided GitHub link.

Result: Token usage reductions of 51.5% (OpenClaw) and 38.9% (Claude Code); estimated cost reductions of 36.4% and 27.3% respectively; submitted-resolution rates declined slightly from 26.0% to 24.0% (OpenClaw) and 32.0% to 30.0% (Claude Code).

Conclusion: ContextSniper demonstrates meaningful token efficiency gains for repository-level repair with a modest, likely acceptable impact on success rate; open-source scripts enable reproducibility and broader adoption.

Abstract: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

</details>


### [317] [ElephantAgent: Contextual State Continuity in Agentic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01919)
*Jiankai Jin,Xiangzheng Zhang,Zhao Liu,Wenzhuo Xu,Dongdong Yang,Deyue Zhang,Quanchen Zou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ElephantAgent enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend agentic systems against contextual state poisoning by digest-based verification, replicated trusted hardware ledgers, and historical traceability for post-hoc recovery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: External tool and memory dependencies introduce new attack surfaces; malicious tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. There is a lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning/execution. The approach extends prior state-continuity work (e.g., Nimble).

Method: Define contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's context (e.g., tool state, memory). Before processing each query, recompute the digest of the local contextual state and verify it against the latest authorized digest. Use replicated trusted hardware to maintain a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detect out-of-band state tampering. For in-band semantic abuse, provide Historical Traceability enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

Result: Proposal and architectural protocol; the abstract outlines the mechanisms (digest verification, replicated ledger, and historical traceability) but does not present empirical results. The work promises tamper detection and recoverability for contextual state.

Conclusion: ElephantAgent extends prior state-continuity concepts to evolving contextual state in agentic systems, offering a defense against contextual state poisoning through digest-based verification, a trusted-hardware ledger, and post-hoc audit/recovery capabilities.

Abstract: Agentic systems enhance their capabilities by invoking external tools and maintaining persistent memory. However, these external dependencies introduce novel attack surfaces. Recent tool and memory poisoning attacks show that maliciously crafted tool descriptors and poisoned memory can covertly bias agent behavior. These threats reflect a deeper issue: the lack of verifiable continuity in the agent's contextual state for planning and execution. We present ElephantAgent, a protocol that enforces Contextual State Continuity to defend against contextual state poisoning. Inspired by prior state-continuity mechanisms (e.g., Nimble), ElephantAgent extends this protection to the evolving contextual state of agentic systems. We define the contextual state as the bounded, security-critical subset of the agent's entire context (e.g., tool state and memory). Before processing each query, ElephantAgent recomputes the digest of the local contextual state and verifies it against the latest authorized digest. Using replicated trusted hardware, ElephantAgent maintains a linearizable ledger of authorized contextual state transitions and detects out-of-band state tampering. To handle in-band semantic abuse, ElephantAgent additionally provides Historical Traceability, enabling conditional post-hoc audit and recovery to a known-good prior state.

</details>


### [318] [A-TMA: Decoupling State-Aware Memory Failures in Long-Term Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01935)
*Zitong Shi,Yixuan Tang,Anthony Kum Hoe Tung*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Ghost memory in LLMs: a memory-coordination failure; ATMA overlay preserves state and helps retrieval; introduces LTP benchmark; shows improvements over Graphiti baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term memory for LLMs risks mixing current, past, and transition facts; need state-aware memory and separate evaluation.

Method: ATMA overlay that keeps superseded/transition records, builds evidence packets for the query's state view, and exposes current/historical/transition labels at QA; three-level framework: bank maintenance, retrieval, answer-time resolution; introduces LTP benchmark; evaluation on LoCoMo Temporal Plus; compare Graphiti vs Graphiti+ATMA.

Result: On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, temporal F1 improves from 0.0295 to 0.1705.

Conclusion: Explicit state roles reduce ghost memory errors; advocate decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer levels; gains are host-dependent but positive; suggests future refinements.

Abstract: Long term memory lets LLM agents act as persistent assistants, but user facts change. A useful memory system must know what is true now, what used to be true, and what changed. We study \emph{ghost memory}, a state coordination failure in which old, current, and transition facts coexist in the memory bank, remain mixed during retrieval, and mislead the answer model. We argue that memory systems should be understood and optimized from three levels: bank maintenance, retrieval, and answer time resolution. We propose ATMA, a state aware overlay for existing memory systems. ATMA keeps superseded and transition records in the bank, builds evidence packets for the query's requested state view, and exposes current, historical, and transition labels to QA. We further call for decoupled evaluation of bank, retrieval, and answer level failures, since final QA accuracy can hide where ghost memory occurs. To make this failure measurable, we build LTP (LoCoMo Temporal Plus), a conflict heavy benchmark for ghost memory, and evaluate on LoCoMo for long conversation generalization. On LTP, Graphiti+ATMA improves conflict accuracy by 0.240 absolute over Graphiti. On LoCoMo, Graphiti+ATMA raises temporal F1 from 0.0295 to 0.1705. The gains are host dependent, but they indicate that explicit state roles can reduce memory failures hidden by final QA accuracy.

</details>


### [319] [Atomic Task Graph: A Unified Framework for Agentic Planning and Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01942)
*Yue Zhang,Sihan Chen,Ziwen Huang,Hanyun Cui,Kangye Ji,Zhi Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATG introduces an explicit Atomic Task Graph to structure planning and execution for LLM-based agents, enabling parallel execution, localized repair, and improved performance on multi-step tasks with small backbones (7B-8B).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current prompt-based control methods rely on implicit task trajectories, making verification, reuse of intermediate results, and efficient parallel execution difficult; scaling or fine-tuning are costly or not generalizable.

Method: ATG maintains an explicit directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks. Planning recursively decomposes high-level tasks into DAGs; execution uses graph dependencies to run branches in parallel; upon failures, the evolution history localizes the error and repairs only the affected region, preserving validated portions.

Result: Empirical evaluation on three interactive benchmarks shows ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency using 7B-8B backbones.

Conclusion: ATG provides a unified, reusable planning-execution framework that exposes dependencies, enables parallelism, and supports targeted repair, yielding better performance with small LLM backbones.

Abstract: LLM-based agents have shown strong potential for solving complex multi-step tasks, yet existing performance improvements often rely on either scaling to larger backbone models or task-specific fine-tuning. The former incurs substantial computational costs, while the latter typically generalizes poorly across different tasks. Although prompt-based control is training-free and broadly applicable, existing methods still leave input-output dependencies between subtasks implicit in textual trajectories, making verified intermediate results difficult to reuse. To address these limitations, we propose Atomic Task Graph (ATG), a unified control framework for planning and execution. Specifically, ATG maintains an explicit graph to expose dependencies and support reuse. During planning, it recursively decomposes a high-level task into subtasks, forming a sequence of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) whose evolution can be traced. During execution, the dependencies exposed by ATG allow independent branches to be executed in parallel, thereby improving execution efficiency. When failures are detected, ATG leverages the graph evolution history to localize the error source and repair only the affected region, preserving validated regions unchanged. Experiments show that ATG consistently outperforms strong baselines in success rate and execution efficiency across three interactive benchmarks using only 7B-8B backbones.

</details>


### [320] [OntoLearner: A Modular Python Library for Ontology Learning with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01977)
*Hamed Babaei Giglou,Jennifer D'Souza,Andrei Aioanei,Nandana Mihindukulasooriya,Sören Auer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes OntoLearner, a modular cross-domain framework that unifies ontology access, LLM-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking for ontology learning (OL), supported by large-scale datasets and benchmarks across 22 domains; finds that ontological complexity, not model size, governs failure modes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OL progress is fragmented with no shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation or ontology access, hindering progress toward scalable, cross-domain solutions.

Method: Introduce OntoLearner with 180 machine-readable ontologies across 22 domains; provide train/dev/test splits for three OL tasks (term typing, taxonomy discovery, non-taxonomic relation extraction); benchmark 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks; perform a large-scale empirical study.

Result: Empirical findings converge on a central bottleneck: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architecture; the primary bottleneck is a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it.

Conclusion: Cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking via OntoLearner enables effective OL; the framework is open-source (MIT) and ready for broad adoption to unify evaluation and access in OL.

Abstract: Ontology learning (OL) aims to automatically construct structured knowledge models from text, yet progress remains fragmented across methods, domains, and evaluation practices. Despite decades of research, OL lacks a shared infrastructure for systematic evaluation and ontology access. This absence has hindered progress and fragmented research, leaving the central challenges of OL largely unaddressed. We introduce OntoLearner, a modular, cross-domain, and first-of-its-kind framework that unifies ontology access, large language model (LLM)-driven learning pipelines, and standardized benchmarking. OntoLearner releases 180 machine-readable ontologies spanning 22 domains and provides pipeline-ready datasets with train/dev/test splits for three core OL tasks: term typing, taxonomy discovery, and non-taxonomic relation extraction. Using this infrastructure, we conduct a large-scale empirical study of OL, evaluating 22 retrieval models and 12 LLMs across domains and tasks. The results converge on a finding that reframes the central challenge of OL: failure modes scale with ontological complexity rather than model size or architectural sophistication. The primary bottleneck is not model capability, but a structural mismatch between how models encode knowledge and how ontologies organize it. These findings establish that effective OL is reachable through the cross-domain, multi-task benchmarking enabled by OntoLearner. OntoLearner is open-source (MIT license) at https://github.com/sciknoworg/OntoLearner/.

</details>


### [321] [Multimodal Knowledge Edit-Scoped Generalization for Online Recursive MLLM Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01978)
*Siyuan Li,Youyuan Zhang,Ruitong Liu,Junxi Wang,Jing Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ScopeEdit is a scope-aware online editor for multimodal LLMs that splits edits into a local, modality-specific absorption branch and a shared, evidence-gated generalization branch, using orthogonal low-rank updates and Sherman–Morrison recursions to ensure constant per-edit overhead while controlling cross-modal propagation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing online MLLM editors emphasize reliability and long-horizon stability but poorly control the semantic boundary of edits, leading to possible cross-modal leakage or ineffective generalization despite instance-level success.

Method: Decompose updates into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch; apply scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces; maintain branch-specific preconditioners via Sherman–Morrison recursions; enable cross-modal propagation only when visual-textual evidence align; achieve constant per-edit overhead.

Result: Empirical evaluation across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, backbones, and VL architectures shows improved trade-off: stronger in-scope cross-modal transfer with reduced leakage to unrelated inputs, while preserving edit reliability, stability, and online efficiency; code released at provided URL.

Conclusion: ScopeEdit effectively closes the scope gap in online multimodal editing by enforcing scope-aware propagation boundaries without sacrificing reliability or efficiency, demonstrating robust performance across models and real-world scenarios.

Abstract: Online multimodal knowledge editing requires injecting a continual stream of visual-textual corrections into multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with bounded overhead and minimal disruption to unrelated behaviors. Existing editors mainly emphasize edit reliability and long-horizon stability, but rarely control the semantic boundary of each edit. Our pilot analyses of post-edit behaviors and internal neuronal activities reveal a scope gap behind reliable edits: instance-level success neither guarantees transfer to valid cross-modal variants nor prevents leakage to unrelated inputs, while edit-related cross-modal responses concentrate in deeper semantic layers. Therefore, we formulate Edit-Scoped Generalization, reframing online MLLM editing from merely correcting an instance to controlling the propagation boundary of each edit. To this end, we propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor that decomposes each update into a modality-local absorption branch and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch. The local branch supports stable edit absorption, whereas the shared branch enables cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence are sufficiently aligned. Both branches perform scope-separated write geometries in orthogonal low-rank spaces and maintain branch-wise preconditioners via Sherman--Morrison recursions, yielding constant per-edit overhead. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks, long-horizon edit streams, MLLM backbones, real-world VLKEB scenarios, and complex vision-language architectures show that ScopeEdit consistently improves the trade-off between in-scope cross-modal transfer and out-of-scope locality, while preserving edit reliability, stability and online efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/lab-klc/ScopeEdit.

</details>


### [322] [Traceable Fault Diagnosis for Battery Energy Storage Systems via Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Agent O&M Assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01992)
*Jiangdi Ru,Bing Li,Yage Huang,Ding Wang,Keru Hua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Traceable fault-diagnosis assistant for large-scale BESS using retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to fuse operational data, domain knowledge, visuals, and reports; preliminary evaluation indicates promise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: O&M for BESS is complex and currently relies on alarms/thresholds without explainability. There is a need to connect sensor data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and generated reports to enable actionable, traceable diagnostics.

Method: Retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning framework with (i) BESS-specific task routing, (ii) schema-constrained natural-language database access, (iii) hybrid text-image retrieval, and (iv) evidence-based answer synthesis for report generation.

Result: Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

Conclusion: The approach demonstrates feasibility and potential to improve reliability and explainability in BESS fault diagnosis, but requires broader validation and integration into O&M workflows.

Abstract: Large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESSs) require O&M decisions that combine alarms, cell-level measurements, device topology, diagnostic tables, historical cases, and maintenance documents. Monitoring platforms can flag threshold violations, but they often cannot explain whether voltage inconsistency, resistance drift, short-circuit risk, capacity divergence, or thermal abnormality needs intervention. This digest presents a traceable BESS fault-diagnosis assistant that uses retrieval-augmented multi-agent reasoning to connect operational data, domain knowledge, visual evidence, and report generation. Reliability is improved through BESS-specific task routing, schema-constrained natural-language database access, hybrid text-image retrieval, and evidence-based answer synthesis. Preliminary internal evaluation is reported for routing, database access, and diagnostic reasoning.

</details>


### [323] [InduceKV: Fixed-Footprint Continual Adaptation of Multimodal LLMs via Inducing KV Memories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02010)
*Qianyu Chen,Ziteng Feng,Canran Xiao,Runxuan Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InduceKV is a retrieval-based fixed-footprint continual adaptation method for multimodal LLMs that externalizes task-specific updates as compact, attention-ready memory entries under a fixed memory budget, bypassing backbone updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual learning in multimodal LLMs typically requires parameter updates or large replay stores, causing unbounded growth of adaptation state. A fixed-footprint approach is needed to adapt to evolving tasks/domains without changing the backbone or accumulating memory.

Method: Store each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry with a frozen retrieval key and compact per-layer key–value payloads that can be appended to the model’s self-attention cache. Use bilevel selection to build a compact inducing set: a lightweight calibration is learned for retrieval, and memory is chosen to balance current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space, all under a strict memory budget.

Result: Empirically, across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. Diagnostics show gains are not due to stronger backbones, additional replay, or unbounded candidate pools.

Conclusion: InduceKV enables effective fixed-footprint continual adaptation by externalizing compact, attention-ready memory, achieving consistent performance gains across diverse multimodal continual-learning scenarios without updating the backbone.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models must adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet continual improvement under bounded deployment footprint remains difficult because repeated parameter updates or growing replay stores can accumulate adaptation state over time. We study fixed-footprint continual adaptation: the deployed adaptation state is kept under a fixed memory budget, while the backbone model is left unchanged and task-specific updates are externalized. We propose InduceKV, a retrieval-based method that stores each selected training prefix as an attention-ready memory entry, consisting of a frozen retrieval key and compact layerwise key--value (KV) payloads that can be appended to the model's self-attention cache. Under a strict memory budget, InduceKV constructs a compact inducing set through bilevel selection: a lightweight calibration is fit for retrieval, while the selected memory balances current-task likelihood, anchor-based retention, and coverage in the frozen retrieval space. Across task-incremental instruction tuning, continual VQA, domain-incremental adaptation, and lifelong multimodal instruction tuning, InduceKV consistently improves over PEFT, MoE, replay, and prompt-retrieval baselines under matched memory budgets. We further report backbone-matched, stage-1 CoIN, compute-matched, and scalability diagnostics, showing that the gains are not due to a stronger backbone, replay alone, or an unbounded candidate pool.

</details>


### [324] [Hidden Forgetting in Continual Multimodal Learning: When Accuracy Survives but Grounding Fails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02020)
*Qianyu Chen,Canran Xiao,Runxuan Tang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RCL tackles hidden evidence-use forgetting in continual multimodal learning by preserving evidence paths rather than just answers, using replay-free, reliance-constrained learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current continual learning metrics neglect how evidence channels (visual/text/OCR/chart/document) influence answers; multimodal grounding can drift without changing accuracy.

Method: Freeze the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference; estimate teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles via counterfactual channel interventions; jointly optimize task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation; no added inference-time cost.

Result: RCL consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting versus replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines; also lowers modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates.

Conclusion: Robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models must continually adapt to evolving tasks and domains, yet standard continual learning metrics mainly measure whether old answers remain correct, leaving the stability of multimodal grounding largely unexamined. We study this overlooked failure mode and ask whether a continually adapted MLLM can preserve not only what it answers, but also how it uses visual, textual, OCR, chart, and document evidence. We identify \emph{hidden evidence-use forgetting}, where answer accuracy is retained while the model silently shifts toward different or less grounded evidence channels, and propose \textsc{RCL}, a replay-free reliance-constrained continual learning framework. \textsc{RCL} freezes the previous checkpoint as a behavioral reference, estimates teacher and student evidence-reliance profiles through counterfactual channel interventions, and jointly optimizes task learning, prediction preservation, and reliance preservation without adding inference-time cost. Across CoIN, COAST, MCITlib, and an evidence-sensitive multimodal stream, \textsc{RCL} consistently improves final performance and reduces forgetting over replay-free, PEFT, routing, and memory-assisted baselines, while substantially lowering modality reliance drift, dominant evidence flips, and hidden forgetting rates. These results suggest that robust continual multimodal learning requires preserving the evidence path behind correct answers, not merely the answers themselves.

</details>


### [325] [PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02032)
*Yueqi Song,Lintang Sutawika,Jiarui Liu,Lindia Tjuatja,Jiayi Geng,Yunze Xiao,Daniel Lee,Aditya Bharat Soni,Vincent Lo,Xiang Yue,Graham Neubig*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PACE constructs proxy benchmarks (PACE-Bench) by selecting a small, informative subset of non-agentic task instances to predict agentic benchmark performance, enabling cheap, accurate evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic benchmarks for LLMs are costly and time-intensive. A lightweight surrogate is needed to estimate agentic performance from cheaper, non-agentic tasks.

Method: Two instance-selection strategies are used: target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection, to curate a compact subset of non-agentic tasks. A regression maps model scores on these source tasks to scores on the target agentic benchmarks; LOOCV evaluates prediction accuracy.

Result: PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV MAE < 4%, Spearman correlation > 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy ~85% across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, at <1% of full evaluation cost.

Conclusion: PACE enables reliable estimation of agentic performance during model development and deployment with substantially reduced cost, and reveals which non-agentic skills are most predictive of each agentic benchmark.

Abstract: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

</details>


### [326] [Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02069)
*Hiroki Arimura*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC) provides a unified semiring-based framework to exhaustively analyze optimal/near-optimal decision trees via sum-of-products; uses dynamic programming to achieve O^*(n^{O(Δ)}) time; introduces model behavior tensors to handle multi-criteria constraints; implemented in emtrees and validated on real data for evidence-based model selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global reliability assessment of explainable AI requires exploring the entire hypothesis space, which is doubly exponential in depth; there is a need for a formal, scalable framework to optimize, count, and sample decision trees and to trade off criteria.

Method: Reformulates tasks into a unified sum-of-products over a semiring R using Algebraic Model Counting; leverages dynamic programming across features; extends with model behavior tensors using tensor semirings to aggregate semiring values via convolution; builds a global model profile.

Result: Algorithmic framework achieves subexponential dependence in features for fixed depth; demonstrates utility via emtrees and real-world datasets; enables evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

Conclusion: ADTC unifies optimization, counting, and sampling for decision trees, enabling global landscape analysis of trade-offs among accuracy, size, fairness; practical via emtrees; future work includes scalability, semiring choices, and broader applicability.

Abstract: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

</details>


### [327] [Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02073)
*Ya Gao,Pekka Marttinen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Maven is an RL framework for long-context reasoning with an editable evidence memory and action-level rewards, improving evidence navigation and reducing distractors compared to baseline RL methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context reasoning requires persistent evidence management; existing RL approaches focus on end results or static evidence and miss intermediate state feedback.

Method: Introduce an answer-conditioned evidence-state value; reward add actions based on marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence; assign rewards to action spans in GRPO; evaluate on Llama/Qwen with LongBench v2, LongReason, RULER.

Result: Outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines across datasets/models; yields more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention; demonstrates value of stateful evidence navigation.

Conclusion: Optimizing stateful evidence navigation and action-level rewards improves long-context RL beyond one-shot evidence extraction.

Abstract: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

</details>


### [328] [SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02087)
*Tomoshi Iiyama,Masahiro Suzuki,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SUNTA introduces surprise-based chunking for hierarchical state-space models, using decoupled training and internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise signal to determine chunk boundaries in imagined rollouts, yielding superior long-horizon video prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve long-horizon predictions by aligning chunk boundaries with when longer-range context is needed, addressing hierarchical collapse and lack of surprise signals in end-to-end training.

Method: Decoupled training to preserve prediction-surprise signals; internal inconsistency is used as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts in SUNTA's hierarchical framework.

Result: SUNTA outperforms baselines on 2D and 3D video prediction tasks, maintaining accurate predictions up to 250 timesteps, whereas baselines degrade within 10 timesteps.

Conclusion: Prediction-error-driven, surprise-aware chunking in HSSMs mitigates training collapse and enables robust long-horizon prediction in complex visual domains.

Abstract: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

</details>


### [329] [ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02116)
*Misha Sulpovar,Benn R. Konsynski,Qaish Kanchwala,Gabe Goodhart*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ContextNext defines an open 'context governance' layer for AI knowledge vaults, adding provenance, versioning, integrity, and determinism to retrieval; it complements RAG and shows governance-led retrieval can outperform BM25 in quality and improve reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern AI agents rely on external knowledge stores but lack durable guarantees for provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. This undermines accountability and reproducibility of model outputs.

Method: Proposes an open specification and reference implementation (ContextNext) that uses typed Markdown with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URIs, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) plus audit traces to govern what artifacts are approved and current before retrieval. Includes a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

Result: Empirical findings: (1) In a stale-version attack, governed selection Pareto-dominates BM25 with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% vs 93–90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. (2) In a retrieval-determinism test on 1,060 docs, deterministic selectors+BM25 yielded stable results (Jaccard 1.0) across repeats; dense+HNSW was non-deterministic for 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst 0.210).

Conclusion: Context governance addresses failure modes not solvable by retrieval quality alone, enabling reproducible, verifiable, and AI-eligible knowledge use. The authors release an open core engine, CLI, and MCP server.

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

</details>


### [330] [Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02118)
*Xingtao Zhao,Tian Yang,Han Jiang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FitOne is a domain-specific fitness LLM series (8B and 32B) built on Qwen3, using a three-stage post-training pipeline to enhance SFC reliability and domain knowledge, achieving notable exam performance gains over base models and supported by ablation of each training stage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the domain knowledge gaps and reliability issues of general-purpose LLMs in scientific fitness coaching, enabling accessible, high-quality guidance.

Method: Three-stage post-training pipeline: continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality, knowledge-engineered datasets; evaluation on professional certifications (ACSM-EP, NSCA-CSCS) and general capabilities.

Result: FitOne-8B/32B show average improvements over Qwen3 base models of up to 10.09%/9.29% on ACSM-EP and 12.73%/7.01% on NSCA-CSCS (per exam, with 8B vs 32B). Ablation studies confirm each training stage is necessary; model maintains strong general abilities.

Conclusion: Domain-specific LLMs like FitOne can achieve reliable fitness intelligence, balancing domain expertise with general capabilities, and offer a blueprint for future domain-focused LLM development in SFC.

Abstract: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

</details>


### [331] [Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02134)
*Atharva Hans,Ilias Bilionis*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Paper-replication is a coding-agent workflow that converts each paper claim into verifiable targets with provenance, reimplements methods, runs experiments, and validates evidence before completion; evaluation shows complete execution across 12 runs with all 158 targets matched, but internal variability remains in target decomposition, numerical fidelity, and evidence rules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve reliability and traceability of computational claims in scientific ML by enforcing evidence-based replication and provenance tracking, reducing reliance on the agent's final autogenerated message.

Method: Identify all explicit claims in a target paper and record them as targets with provenance; reconstruct the paper's method; execute computational experiments; generate outputs linked to provenance; compare outputs to targets; record where evidence supports claims; apply completion gates/validation checks; evaluate across multiple independent runs on several papers.

Result: All twelve workspace runs passed the completion gate; 158 targets were tracked and matched with report coverage; outputs are linked to provenance and cross-validated against claims; replication results highlight variability in target partitioning, numerical fidelity, replication duration, intermediate steps, and acceptance rules.

Conclusion: The workflow shifts completion criteria from agent-generated messages to workspace evidence and validation checks, enhancing reproducibility and accountability, while acknowledging inherent variability in decomposition and evidence acceptance across runs.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

</details>


### [332] [A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02141)
*Shuo Ren,Yaohui Han,Yifan Shi,Libo Shen,Haodong Lu,Dongfang Wu,Rongliang Fu,Bei Yu,Tsung-Yi Ho*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A^2utoLPBench is a generator-based, text-based linear programming benchmark that guarantees ground-truth answers by construction, enabling calibrated, leakage-resistant evaluation of LLM-driven agents with unlimited, difficulty-tunable problems and a built-in baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome limitations of static, hand-authored LP benchmarks—fixed size/difficulty, potential data leakage into training sets, and lack of calibration/reproducibility for evaluating LLM-driven agents on LP problems.

Method: Construct LP instances by selecting a feasible primal point and a dual solution, then form a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known; this yields ground-truth without solver calls or human annotation. The evaluation environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image with operator instructions for LLM-driven agents, enabling a one-command run.

Result: Generates an unlimited stream of fresh LP problems with tunable difficulty via (n,m); ground-truth answers are correct by construction; low per-problem LLM cost; scores are repeatable across batches; the benchmark is resistant to training-data leakage thanks to post-cutoff fresh seeds.

Conclusion: The benchmark presents a robust, scalable framework for evaluating LLM-driven agents on LP problems with controlled ground-truths and leakage resistance; future work could extend to other problem classes and enhance calibration and baselines.

Abstract: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

</details>


### [333] [A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02175)
*Samiha A. Ismail,Fan X. Chen,Ali Merali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five clinician-authored clinical tasks with a MECE, weighted rubric show current frontier LLMs struggle with high-stakes criteria; supports building a scalable benchmark pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
