Motivation: Address saturation of MCQ benchmarks and the gap in open-ended clinical reasoning by designing a difficult, rubric-based evaluation that emphasizes critical criteria.

Method: Five tasks across anaesthesia, internal medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics; clinician-drafted golden answer; atomic MECE rubric with 184 criteria total; 3 frontier LLMs (GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro); 3 autoraters; 552 graded criteria; pass/fail per criterion; analysis of weight-5 vs weight-1 criteria.

Result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. High-weight criteria pass 32.4–41.7%. 56 of 108 weight-5 criteria (52%) satisfied by no model. Autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8–94.7% of 552 graded criteria.

Conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable, defensible pipeline for large-scale clinical benchmarks; initial findings reveal misalignment between model performance and clinical priorities; positions the work as a foundation for expansion.

Abstract: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

</details>


### [334] [UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02186)
*Temitayo Olamilekan Ogunsusi,Lijun Qian,Xishuang Dong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UA-ChatDev proposes an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that quantifies uncertainty at token level and triggers retrieval-based verification to prevent hallucination propagation, achieving superior performance on SRDD across completeness, executability, consistency, and quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To mitigate hallucination propagation due to unequal reliability of intermediate agent outputs in autonomous multi-agent software development, which degrades final software quality.

Method: Introduce token-level log-probability based uncertainty estimation; phase-aware threshold calibration to decide when to invoke retrieval-based verification; integrate with an overarching multi-agent architecture (UA-ChatDev); evaluate on SRDD benchmark; perform ablations and communication analyses.

Result: Consistent improvement over single-agent and other multi-agent baselines on completeness, executability, consistency, and quality; uncertainty-aware interactions improve code execution reliability; ablations validate the role of uncertainty estimation and verification steps.

Conclusion: Uncertainty-aware coordination can effectively mitigate error propagation in multi-agent software development, improving overall software quality; the approach is effective and validated on SRDD, with potential for further refinement and broader benchmarking.

Abstract: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels. Extensive experiments on the SRDD benchmark demonstrate that UA-ChatDev consistently outperforms existing single-agent and multi-agent software development frameworks across completeness, executability, consistency, and overall quality metrics. Further ablation studies and communication analyses verify that uncertainty-aware interactions enhance code execution reliability.

</details>


### [335] [Criticality-Based Guard Rail Validation for AI Agent Decisions in Autonomous Telecom Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02210)
*Ravi Kant Sharma*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Guard Rail Validation (GRV): a standardizable runtime framework for intercepting and validating AI-driven network decisions in autonomous telecom networks (O-RAN), using multi-criteria criticality scoring and graduated validation to prevent erroneous actions and enable regulatory conformance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the absence of runtime interception/validation mechanisms for AI-driven decisions in autonomous networks, reducing risk of unsafe actions and enabling traceability/regulatory compliance in 4-5G/6G telecommunication systems.

Method: Proposes a layered GRV architecture that scores decisions across weighted dimensions (action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, temporal patterns) to assign a criticality level. Applies graduated validation (execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent validation, multi-agent consensus) accordingly; includes cross-agent conflict detection with priority resolved by criticality weights and runtime conformance logging. Discusses architecture, algorithms, O-RAN deployment model, and threat coverage evaluation against known AI/ML attacks in telecoms.

Result: Introduces GRV architecture and procedures, plus O-RAN deployment model and threat coverage assessment, positioned to standardize runtime interception/validation and improve safety/regulatory conformance in autonomous networks.

Conclusion: GRV provides a standardizable, multi-layered runtime validation framework that can intercept and validate AI-driven decisions before execution, handle cross-agent conflicts, and support regulatory compliance, thereby reducing risk in Autonomous Network Levels 4-5.

Abstract: The evolution toward fully autonomous telecommunications networks (Autonomous Network Levels 4-5) requires AI/ML agents to make real-time network decisions without human intervention. However, no standardized runtime mechanism exists to intercept and validate individual inference outputs before they trigger live network state changes, creating risks of erroneous autonomous decisions. This paper proposes the Guard Rail Validation (GRV) framework, a standardizable runtime architecture for intercepting and validating AI-driven decisions before execution. The framework evaluates decisions across multiple weighted dimensions -- including action scope, action type, service criticality, agent autonomy level, reversibility, and temporal behavioural patterns -- to determine a criticality level. Based on this level, graduated validation mechanisms are applied: execute-with-logging, bounds checking, independent agent validation, or multi-agent consensus. The framework additionally provides cross-agent conflict detection with criticality-weighted priority resolution and runtime conformance logging for regulatory compliance (e.g., EU AI Act Article 14). We present the architecture, algorithmic procedures, O-RAN deployment model, and evaluate threat coverage against known AI/ML attacks in telecommunications.

</details>


### [336] [Purified OPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation Without Losing How to Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02234)
*Zhanming Shen,Jintao Tong,Shaotian Yan,Chen Shen,Hao Chen,Wentao Ye,Xiaomeng Hu,Rui Miao,Haobo Wang,Junbo Zhao,Gang Chen,Jieping Ye*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two-step OPSD fix isolates transferable signal via a reference-only teacher and PMI residual distillation, yielding consistent gains on long-CoT without destabilizing epistemic behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD underperforms on long-CoT due to reference-induced memorization dominating supervision; need to separate non-transferable shortcuts from transferable inference.

Method: (1) Train a reference-only teacher conditioned on the reference (no question) to capture non-transferable supervision. Subtract this from full supervision to obtain the transferable residual. (2) Use pointwise mutual information (PMI) to transform the residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution for direct distillation.

Result: In four long-CoT models across two datasets, the proposed method improves over the base model and standard OPSD while preserving epistemic behavior during training.

Conclusion: Decomposing the supervision signal and PMI-based refinement mitigates reference shortcuts and yields improved long-CoT reasoning without destabilizing reflective capabilities.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving LLM reasoning, where a privileged teacher with access to reference solutions provides token-level supervision on the student's own generated trajectories. However, we find that OPSD consistently fails on long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning models, yielding at best marginal gains while destabilizing the reflective reasoning capability these models depend on. Through a novel decomposition of the teacher's supervision signal, we identify the root cause: the teacher's supervision is dominated by a reference-induced component that drives rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts, while the question-conditioned, inference-transferable component is ignored or actively opposed. Based on this diagnosis, we propose a two-step solution. First, we construct a reference-only teacher (the same model conditioned on the reference without the question) to isolate the non-transferable component of the supervision signal; the residual after subtracting this component captures the question-conditioned, inference-transferable correction. Second, we use pointwise mutual information (PMI) as the mechanism to transform this residual into a well-formed PMI target distribution that the student can directly distill from, filtering out the reference-induced shortcut. Experiments on four long-CoT models across two datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over both the base model and standard OPSD, while preserving the models' natural epistemic behavior throughout training.

</details>


### [337] [Copewell: A Multi-Agent Swarm Architecture for Equitable Mental Wellness Support](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02245)
*Seren Yenikent,Jack Vinijtrongjit,Katherine Ng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multi-agent swarm framework (Copewell) for mental wellness delivering multi-source assessment, circumplex emotion routing, and dual-mode interventions, with privacy/ethics focus and practitioner-informed design; early-stage with planned empirical evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To close the global treatment gap in mental health by enabling accessible, safe, equitable AI-supported care in LMIC contexts.

Method: Architectural design introducing: (1) multi-source data fusion to reduce bias; (2) valence-arousal mapping via Russell's Circumplex to route to specialized agents; (3) combined conversational support and sensory wellness protocols; plus privacy-first architecture, Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design with practitioners; early engagement and beta deployment.

Result: Conceptual framework and design decisions; demonstration of how technical architecture can embed equity and safety principles; no reported empirical results yet; identifies future evaluation directions.

Conclusion: Copewell contributes to responsible AI in mental health by integrating technical and sociotechnical considerations from inception, with emphasis on equity, safety, and practitioner-informed design, and outlines empirical evaluation needs.

Abstract: Mental health disorders affect nearly one billion people globally, yet 75% of individuals in low- and middle-income countries receive no treatment due to workforce shortages, cost barriers, and stigma. Current AI-powered wellness solutions predominantly rely on single-mode conversational interfaces that suffer high abandonment rates and fail to provide measurable, immediate relief calibrated to users' dynamic emotional states. This paper presents Copewell, a novel multi-agent swarm system designed to expand access to mental wellness support through human-centered AI principles. Our architecture introduces three technical innovations: (1) a multi-source assessment framework integrating self-reported, physiological, and contextual data to mitigate algorithmic bias; (2) valence-arousal emotion mapping using Russell's Circumplex Model of Affect to route users to specialized AI agents; and (3) dual-mode intervention delivery combining conversational support with evidence-based sensory wellness protocols. We examine the sociotechnical design considerations underlying Copewell's development, including a privacy-first architecture, embedded ethical oversight through a dedicated Ethics Supervisor agent, and participatory design informed by mental health practitioners. Early practitioner engagement and beta deployment inform design decisions and identify directions for future empirical evaluation. This work contributes to responsible AI discourse by demonstrating how technical architecture can operationalize equity and safety principles from inception.

</details>


### [338] [AgenticSTS: A Bounded-Memory Testbed for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02255)
*Xiangchen Cheng,Yunwei Jiang,Jianwen Sun,Zizhen Li,Chuanhao Li,Xiangcheng Cao,Yihao Liu,Fanrui Zhang,Li Jin,Kaipeng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Bounded memory contract for long-horizon LLM agents; uses per-decision fresh user messages via typed retrieval; avoids cross-decision transcripts; tested in Slay the Spire 2; provides reproducible dataset; memory layer effects observed though not statistically decisive due to small sample.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Isolate and understand the influence of explicit memory components on long-horizon decision-making in LLM agents; address noisy, entangled past-context in standard concatenated histories.

Method: Introduce a bounded memory contract; per-decision prompt assembled via typed retrieval; no raw cross-decision transcript; instantiate in Slay the Spire 2; ablation study: no-store baseline vs skill layer; compare against public benchmarks; release dataset and scripts.

Result: Largest observed difference with strategic skills enabled: no-store 3/10 vs with skill layer 6/10; Fisher p ~ 0.37; cross-backbone probe and public baselines used as references; reproducible testbed: 298 trajectories and analysis scripts.

Conclusion: Explicit memory layering under a bounded contract modulates long-horizon decisions; the methodology enables isolation and study of memory components; results suggest memory design matters, but statistical significance requires larger samples.

Abstract: Memory for a long-horizon LLM agent is a contract about what each future decision is allowed to see. The simplest contract appends past observations, tool calls, and reflections to every prompt, which makes prior context easy to access but also turns it into a jumbled mixture in which the effect of any single memory component is hard to isolate. We introduce and instrument an alternative bounded contract: every decision is made from a fresh user message assembled by typed retrieval, with no raw cross-decision transcript appended. The prompt thus stays bounded across runs of any length, and any single layer can be ablated in isolation. We instantiate the contract in Slay the Spire 2, a closed-rule stochastic deck-building game whose runs require hundreds of tactical and strategic decisions. A public online benchmark of frontier LLMs on the same game reports zero wins at the lowest difficulty across five configurations, and the developer-reported human win rate at the same difficulty is 16%; the task is hard but not saturated. Within our harness, a fixed-A0 ablation shows the largest observed difference when triggered strategic skills are enabled: the no-store baseline wins 3/10 games and adding the skill layer 6/10. At this sample size the comparison is directional rather than statistically decisive (Fisher exact p\approx0.37); a cross-backbone probe and public accumulating-context baselines are reported as operational comparisons rather than controlled tests of the contract variable itself. We release a reproducible testbed: 298 completed trajectories with condition tags, frozen memory/skill snapshots, prompt records, and analysis scripts -- an agent design and a validated, reusable methodology for studying how explicit memory layers shape long-horizon LLM-agent decisions.

</details>


### [339] [A Hippocampus for Linear Attention: An Exact Memory for What the Recurrent State Forgets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02303)
*Wanyun Cui*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid memory for linear attention (HOLA) combines a compressive delta-rule state with a bounded exact KV cache to form a semiparametric memory, improving perplexity and retrieval with O(1) memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate the lossy memory of fixed-size recurrent states in linear-attention models by preserving important vault of exact KV pairs, inspired by hippocampal complementary learning systems.

Method: Maintain conventional delta-rule state as a compressive memory; add a bounded, exact Key-Value (KV) cache with decoupled RMSNorm-gamma reads. Cache writes favor tokens with large prediction residual, with no learned eviction module. Evaluate on 340M-param model trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens; compare against full-attention Transformer++, and baselines on Wikitext, LAMBADA, and RULER needle-in-haystack recall.

Result: Wikitext perplexity improves from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), beating full-attention Transformer++ at 26.88; LAMBADA perplexity improves from 30.95 to 30.26. Achieves best linear in-context retrieval and superior robustness to GDN/recency caches on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall up to 32k tokens (16x training length).

Conclusion: HOLA provides a semiparametric memory that preserves exact KV information for important associations while maintaining a compressive state for general structure, yielding strong language modeling and long-context retrieval with significantly larger effective context without sacrificing O(1) memory.

Abstract: Linear-attention and state-space language models compress the prefix into a fixed-size recurrent state, yielding O(1) memory at the cost of a lossy exact memory: when many key--value associations compete, earlier facts are overwritten and needle recall degrades. Inspired by Complementary Learning Systems, we give linear attention a hippocampal complement. HOLA (Hippocampal Linear Attention) keeps the usual delta-rule state as a compressive memory and adds a bounded exact KV cache, forming a semiparametric test-time memory: the state models linearly compressible structure, while the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state. The cache writes without a learned eviction module, keeping tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state; a decoupled RMSNorm-gamma cache read then turns these exact KV pairs into sharp retrieval rather than soft averaging. At 340M parameters trained on 15B SlimPajama tokens, HOLA lowers Wikitext perplexity from 27.32 to 22.92 (-16.1%), below a full-attention Transformer++ (26.88), and improves LAMBADA perplexity from 30.95 to 30.26. It also achieves the best linear in-context retrieval and remains much more robust than GDN or a matched HOLA+recency cache on RULER needle-in-a-haystack recall out to 32k tokens (16x its training length).

</details>


### [340] [Grounded autonomous research: a fault-tolerant LLM pipeline from corpus to manuscript in frontier computational physics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02329)
*Haonan Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fully autonomous, literature-grounded end-to-end research pipeline delivering a publication-grade manuscript from 11,083 condensed-matter arXiv papers, demonstrating three findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism; employs fault-tolerant design with six phases, 47 sessions, and 2,162 literature-consultation events; bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address grounding gaps in autonomous scientific agents for high-stakes physical sciences where external literature anchors are required and internal priors risk hallucinations; enable robust, verifiable autonomous research.

Method: End-to-end pipeline: map corpus to conceive research direction; calibrate methodology by reproducing published references; conduct novel first-principles computations; write manuscript—grounded in literature throughout; implemented across six phases with shared on-disk state, 47 fresh-context sessions, and 2,162 literature-consultation events; fault-tolerant design via fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review; evaluated with pre-architecture baseline and no-pilot ablation to isolate calibration-driven grounding at checkpoints.

Result: Publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings on altermagnetic piezomagnetism; demonstrates autonomous research with literature-grounded methodology; provides quantified intervention patterns, primitives, and failure modes; shows fault-tolerant, end-to-end autonomy.

Conclusion: Establishes a foundational framework for autonomous research in high-stakes domains beyond computational physics, highlighting the importance of literature-grounded calibration, fault tolerance, and operational knowledge curation; suggests directions for reducing human intervention and extending to other disciplines.

Abstract: Autonomous-research agents have demonstrated end-to-end LLM automation in machine-learning sandboxes where execution provides calibration. Frontier physical science differs categorically: physical reasoning underlies every methodology choice, toolchains are often underdocumented, and calibration must come from external literature anchors - which unscaffolded agents cite but do not confront, hallucinating plausible, unverifiable results from internal priors. We present a pipeline that runs end-to-end from a corpus of 11,083 recent condensed-matter physics arXiv papers to a publication-grade manuscript with three substantive physics findings (here on altermagnetic piezomagnetism): the agent autonomously conceives a research direction by mapping the corpus, calibrates methodology by reproducing published references, conducts novel first-principles computations, and writes the manuscript - grounded in literature throughout, across 47 fresh-context sessions in six phases sharing only on-disk state, with 2,162 literature-consultation events. Fault tolerance emerges from redundancy: fresh-context isolation, distributed grounding, and adversarial review catch what any single session misses; pre- and post-pilot stages are fully autonomous, and pilot requires bounded human intervention only at reproduction failures - operational knowledge curation, not scientific direction. Two paired failure modes - a pre-architecture baseline and a no-pilot ablation - isolate structurally enforced numerical confrontation at calibration checkpoints as the operative grounding mechanism. The primitives, characterized failure modes, and quantified intervention pattern lay a foundation for autonomous research in high-stakes scientific domains beyond computational physics.

</details>


### [341] [DRIFTLENS: Measuring Memory-Induced Reasoning Drift in Personalized Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02374)
*Xi Fang,Weijie Xu,Yingqiang Ge,Yuhui Xu,Stephanie Eckman,Chandan K. Reddy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Personalization via user-attribute memory can shift an LLM's reasoning steps; introduces DRIFTLENS to quantify drift; drift is significant across models/attributes and only partly mitigated by GRPO/DPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand whether memory-based personalization reshapes reasoning in open-ended tasks lacking a ground-truth answer, and to quantify it with a ground-truth-free metric.

Method: Develop DRIFTLENS mapping each expressed reasoning step to a value category and compute divergence between no-memory and memory-injected trajectories; validate that it separates pragmatic noise from substantive changes; test across 4 LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories; evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods to reduce drift; assess downstream performance.

Result: Memory-induced reasoning drift is medium-to-large above pragmatic-noise floor; final answers remain fluent and on-topic; DRIFTLENS detects drift; GRPO/DPO methods reduce drift but do not uniformly dominate; effects depend on model and reward; drift is measurable and only partly mitigated.

Conclusion: Memory-induced reasoning drift is a real, measurable failure mode of personalized LMs; mitigations exist but are not universally effective; further work needed to manage personalization-induced reasoning changes.

Abstract: Personalization changes what a model says to a user; we show that it can also change the reasoning trajectory used to justify the response. Modern LLMs personalize interactions by storing user attributes, preferences, and prior context, then injecting this information into future prompts. We study whether such memory reshapes reasoning on open-ended questions where no single ground-truth answer exists. To quantify this effect, we introduce DRIFTLENS, a ground-truth-free framework that maps each expressed reasoning step to a value category and measures divergence between a question's no-memory trajectory and its trajectory under injected user-attribute memory. We first validate that DRIFTLENS distinguishes content-free pragmatic noise from substantive reasoning changes. Across four LLMs and 10 user-attribute categories, including age, occupation, and disability, user-attribute memory induces medium-to-large reasoning drift above each model's pragmatic-noise floor, even when final answers remain fluent, on-topic, and plausible. We then evaluate GRPO- and DPO-based post-training methods for reducing drift. Both reduce drift, but neither uniformly dominates; effects on downstream capability, helpfulness, and instruction following are model-and reward-dependent. These results suggest that memory-induced reasoning drift is a measurable and only partly mitigated failure mode of personalized language models.

</details>


### [342] [Hardware-Enforced Semantic Coordination for Safety-Critical Real-Time Autonomous Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02376)
*Uwe M. Borghoff,Paolo Bottoni,Remo Pareschi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes hardware-enforced semantic coordination using TB-CSPN mapped to FPGAs to achieve deterministic, bounded coordination for agentic AI, separating semantic reasoning from interaction management and prioritizing hardware-level guarantees over acceleration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Software-mediated coordination faces challenges with bounded latency, determinism, and enforceable safety in real-time, heterogeneous AI systems; a hardware layer can provide deterministic coordination guarantees.

Method: Map TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms onto FPGA primitives to create a hardware-native semantic coordination layer that enforces temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination, while keeping semantic reasoning software-driven.

Result: Conceptual architecture and mapping are proposed; discusses the design and implications but reports no empirical evaluation or results.

Conclusion: Hardware-enforced coordination can provide deterministic guarantees and safety in complex AI systems, by decoupling semantic reasoning from interaction management and embedding coordination semantics in hardware.

Abstract: Recent advances in agentic AI are producing increasingly complex autonomous systems that integrate large language models, world models, optimization engines, specialized neural architectures, autonomous platforms, and human operators. While much current research focuses on improving reasoning capabilities, safety-critical real-time deployment also requires bounded and verifiable coordination among heterogeneous components operating concurrently under uncertainty. Software-mediated coordination presents fundamental limitations in domains where bounded latency, deterministic coordination, and enforceable safety guarantees are essential.
  Hence, we propose a hardware-enforced semantic coordination architecture in which selected coordination semantics are implemented directly at the hardware level via field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). The approach builds on the Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Net (TB-CSPN) framework, which separates semantic reasoning from interaction management.
  In this approach, selected TB-CSPN coordination mechanisms are mapped onto FPGA primitives, creating a hardware-native semantic coordination layer. Focus is not on acceleration, but on enforcing temporal synchronization, semantic gating, authorization constraints, and bounded coordination behavior directly in hardware. Semantic reasoning remains adaptive and software-driven, while embedded coordination semantics become deterministic.

</details>


### [343] [Steerability via constraints: a substrate for scalable oversight of coding agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02389)
*Thomas Winninger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Constrained substrate plus tooling improves recall in detecting backdoors in agent-generated code; traditional access-control-like governance outperforms unconstrained agent scaffolding and is cheaper in tokens; the controlled experiment shows recall rising from 54.5% to 90.9%, with additive contributions from substrate and tools; results suggest generalization to languages like Rust.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate security and scalability risks of unconstrained coding agents by borrowing decades of human-engineering governance (access control, policies, tooling) and applying them to agents, to enable scalable oversight without excessive reviewer cost.

Method: Propose a start-to-end governance system using access controls, network policies, and tooling-enforced conventions for coding agents. Validate via a controlled experiment in Python: a human reviewer inspects a codebase containing 11 injected backdoors. Compare unconstrained conditions to constrained substrate plus a ~200-line-of-code docs CLI, assessing recall. Analyze contribution of substrate vs tools.

Result: Recall improves from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus docs CLI). Substrate and tooling contribute independently to the gain. Python chosen because its weaker default guarantees; findings noted as likely extendable to languages like Rust.

Conclusion: Governance-inspired controls for coding agents can yield substantial, additive improvements in oversight effectiveness and may scale more cost-efficiently than rich agent scaffolding; results motivate broader validation and cross-language generalization (e.g., Rust).

Abstract: Coding agents are capable; human oversight is the bottleneck. Unconstrained agents introduce security risks, erode codebase scalability, and make human review increasingly costly. We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

</details>


### [344] [Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02396)
*Thomas Winninger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A fast, probe-informed RFM identifies multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs (including reasoning models) in seconds, enabling scalable steering and monitoring with strong ablation performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current subspace extraction methods are computationally expensive, especially for models with long reasoning traces; understanding multi-dimensional refusals is important for safety and interpretability.

Method: Adapt Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm with probe-informed initialization; apply to Qwen 3 (reasoning) and Qwen 2.5 (non-reasoning); compare speed and ablation performance to alternative methods.

Result: RFM identifies the multi-dimensional refusal subspace quickly (seconds) and shows superior ablation performance vs. alternatives.

Conclusion: RFM is a cheap, scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods for LLMs; warrants further study on relations between subspaces found by different methods.

Abstract: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

</details>


### [345] [Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02407)
*Xianhui Meng,Zirui Song,Yuchen Zhang,Li Zhang,Yongxuan Lv,Xiuying Chen,Kun Wang,Yan Luo,Kai Chen,Hangjun Ye,Long Chen,Jun Liu,Xiaoshuai Hao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework for synthesizing physically plausible 3D indoor scenes in non-Manhattan environments by using object-distribution priors and a hierarchical layout that places large objects first; it outperforms baselines on a 500-environment benchmark and will release code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis struggles with non-orthogonal layouts in non-Manhattan settings, causing geometric violations and low physical fidelity.

Method: Incorporates statistical priors of object distributions to guide training; uses a hierarchical layout strategy prioritizing large objects to reduce violations; text-driven framework for complex environments.

Result: SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods in both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments on a 500-environment benchmark.

Conclusion: The approach achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility; code will be released.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

</details>


### [346] [Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02432)
*Manuel Alonso-Carracedo,Ruben Fernandez-Boullon,Pedro Celard,Francisco J. Rodriguez-Martinez,Lorena Otero-Cerdeira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) were evaluated for grading short Linux/bash command responses. With rubric-guided prompting, Gemini 3.0 Pro achieved the best human–AI agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888, MAE=0.10, bias=-0.014). Agreement drops at higher cognitive levels; rubric quality and structured prompts improve performance; study provides a taxonomy-based framework for AI-assisted grading and a transferable evaluation protocol.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations is hindered by rising enrolments and the limitations of rule-based autograders, which struggle with partial credit, equivalent solutions, and syntactic variation.

Method: The study evaluates four frontier LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) on 1200 real student responses graded by three experts. A four-level taxonomy (L1–L4) combines cognitive complexity with operational impact. Two prompt variants are used: a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version. Evaluation metrics include ICC(3,1), MAE, and Bland-Altman bias. Rubric-guided prompting and higher rubric quality improve agreement.

Result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric prompting achieved the highest agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888; MAE=0.10; Bland-Altman bias=-0.014). Agreement generally declines with higher taxonomy levels; the largest discrepancies occur at L3–L4. Across models, rubric quality exerts a larger effect than model selection; structured prompts consistently improve agreement. The study establishes a taxonomy-based framework to decide which questions are suitable for AI grading and provides a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

Conclusion: LLMs can approximate expert grading for short command-line responses, particularly with rubric-guided prompting at lower cognitive levels. The degree of automation is constrained at higher levels; the framework helps identify questions suitable for AI-assisted grading and informs the design of robust evaluation prompts for scalable assessment.

Abstract: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

</details>


### [347] [EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02440)
*Zhilin Wang,Han Song,Runzhe Zhan,Jusen Du,Jiacheng Chen,Tianle Li,Qingyu Yin,Yulun Wu,Zhennan Shen,Tong Zhu,Yanshu Li,Guanjie Chen,Derek F. Wong,Yafu Li,Yu Cheng,Yang Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Autonomous Policy Evolution and EvoPolicyGym to study iterative, autonomous improvement of executable policies under a fixed interaction budget; GPT-5.5 dominates across environments; provides trajectory-level diagnostics to analyze budget use and parametric tuning; success relies on discovering task-specific mechanisms under bounded feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing evaluations collapse policy evolution into a single final score and conflate feedback processing with broad software-engineering progress. A controlled benchmark is needed to study how agents iteratively improve policies under budget constraints and feedback.

Method: A harness-model agent repeatedly edits a policy system within a fixed interaction budget. EvoPolicyGym is a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments to evaluate iterative policy improvement. The framework provides trajectory-level diagnostics to understand how feedback is converted into parametric tuning.

Result: GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank and top-two performance on all 16 environments in EvoPolicyGym. The benchmark offers trajectory-level diagnostics showing how agents allocate budget and convert feedback into tuning. Findings indicate that strong autonomous policy evolution relies on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

Conclusion: Autonomous policy evolution requires more than isolated task wins; progress rests on discovering suitable mechanisms and effective refinement under bounded feedback. EvoPolicyGym serves as a principled benchmark to study and diagnose such evolutions.

Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

</details>


### [348] [G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02491)
*Timo Bertram,Sidhant Bhavnani,Richard Freinschlag,Erich Kobler,Andreas Mayr,Günter Klambauer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SE-RRMs (symbol-equivariant RRMs) guided by neural hints (G-RRM) can accelerate symbolic constraint solvers when the search space is expansive and the solver can overwrite branching decisions; demonstrates substantial speedups on 9x9 Sudoku and smaller gains on larger perfect-hint grids, while some solvers (CaDiCaL) do not benefit due to overhead and non-overwriting behavior.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limited extrapolation of neural solvers to larger problem sizes and improve CSP solving by combining neural guidance with symbolic solvers; identify when neuro-symbolic guidance yields practical speedups.

Method: Introduce G-RRM, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0). Evaluate on Sudoku instances (9x9 and 25x25), analyze conditions for speedups, and report median conflicts and wall-clock speedups under varying hint quality and solver behavior.

Result: Two conditions for neural guidance to help: (1) the problem has an expansive combinatorial search space; (2) the solver can dynamically overwrite branching decisions when neural hints are imperfect. Under these, guidance reduces median conflicts to zero and yields large speedups: 33.3x on 9x9 with backtracking, 1.70x (median) for Glucose 4.1 (p<0.001); 1.17x on 25x25 with perfect hints. CaDiCaL 3.0.0 shows no significant speedup (1.02x, ns) and slight slowdown (0.90x). SE-RRM solves 91.1% of 9x9 instances.

Conclusion: Neural guidance via G-RRM can offer practical speedups in constraint solving, but benefits depend on the solver’s ability to overwrite hints and the problem’s search space; delineates regimes where neuro-symbolic guidance is effective and informs solver design for future neuro-symbolic CSP methods.

Abstract: In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

</details>


### [349] [What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02507)
*Arman Ghaffarizadeh,Danyal Mohaddes,Aliakbar Izadkhah,Shahriar Noroozizadeh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dual-channel (public vs off-the-record) evaluation reveals that social-structure pressures induce large divergences in LLM agent expressions between channels, rising public-OTR alignment divergence from ~3% to ~40% across models and scenarios; four aggregate analyses corroborate the effect; OTR responses sometimes attribute public accommodations to relational pressures (career risk, sponsorship obligations).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address how socially structured settings shape what agents express publicly, even without explicit prompts; investigate whether unobserved (OTR) signals reveal emergent alignment objectives beyond stated goals; support development of more robust evaluation frameworks that capture hidden alignment pressures.

Method: Introduce a dual-channel debate framework where each agent produces a public utterance and a separate OTR response that is recorded but not shown to the partner. Evaluate across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations per scenario, applying alignment-inducing settings. Analyze divergences using four methods: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses.

Result: Public-OTR divergence increases from a ~3% baseline to ~40% in the targeted agent under alignment-inducing settings. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses (stance, semantic similarity, NLI, survey responses). In some cases, OTR attributes public accommodation to relational pressures (career risk, sponsorship obligations).

Conclusion: Agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals to detect emergent objectives; propose a dual-channel evaluation framework and behavioral measures to operationalize assessment of hidden alignment pressures in socially structured settings.

Abstract: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

</details>


### [350] [ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02509)
*Yanjun Zhao,Ruizhong Qiu,Tianxin Wei,Yuanchen Bei,Zhining Liu,Lingjie Chen,Ismini Lourentzou,Hanghang Tong,Jingrui He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RECONTEXT is a training-free inference method that replays model-internal evidence to improve long-context reasoning, achieving better evidence utilization across multiple backbones without training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a gap between access to long input context and effective use by LLMs; long contexts are underutilized, motivating a training-free approach to better leverage evidence.

Method: Constructs a query-conditioned evidence pool from model-internal relevance signals and replays it before final generation while preserving the full context; uses recursive evidence selection to separate evidence organization from answer generation; requires no training, external memory, or context pruning; supported by a theoretical associative-memory view.

Result: Evaluated on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length; shows consistent improvement in evidence utilization across Qwen-3/4B, Qwen-3/8B, and Llama3-8B; achieves the best average rank on all three backbones.

Conclusion: RECONTEXT provides a robust, training-free methodology to enhance long-context reasoning with no extra memory or training, and is readily applicable across models; code is available.

Abstract: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications. Although recent LLMs support increasingly long context windows, they often fail to use relevant evidence that is already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning (RECONTEXT), a training-free inference method for improving long-context reasoning. RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals to construct a query-conditioned evidence pool and replays it before final generation while preserving the full original context. This recursive selection process separates evidence organization from answer generation without training, external memory, or context pruning. We also provide a theoretical analysis based on associative memory, which characterizes the context as a memory store, the question as a retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation. Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length show that RECONTEXT consistently improves evidence utilization across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3-8B, achieving the best average rank on all three backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/Yanjun-Zhao/ReContext.

</details>


### [351] [Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02510)
*Mona Schirmer,Metod Jazbec,Alexander Timans,Christian Naesseth,Maja Waldron,Eric Nalisnick*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A simple threshold-based real-time safety monitor for LLM outputs using an external verifier signal, calibrated via risk control, achieving competitive performance with sequential hypothesis testing monitors on math reasoning and red-teaming datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable low-latency, reliable detection of unsafe outputs in deployed LLMs by a lightweight monitor; address limitations of complex sequential testing approaches.

Method: Convert external verifier scores into an alarm by applying a threshold; calibrate the threshold using risk-control criteria; compare to more advanced monitors on benchmark datasets.

Result: The simple monitor is competitive with state-of-the-art sequential hypothesis testing monitors on mathematical reasoning and red-teaming tasks.

Conclusion: A threshold-based, verifier-driven, risk-controlled online monitor provides an effective, low-complexity solution for real-time safety monitoring of LLM outputs.

Abstract: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

</details>


### [352] [Distributed Attacks in Persistent-State AI Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02514)
*Josh Hills,Ida Caspary,Asa Cooper Stickland*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Iterative VibeCoding uncovers a persistent-state attack surface in AI coding agents; attackers can distribute payloads across PRs and time attacks to blend with normal activity. Gradual vs non-gradual strategies evade monitors differently; a stateful link-tracker monitor plus trajectory monitors in an ensemble substantially reduces evasion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As coding agents operate over persisting codebases across PRs and sessions, misalignment or prompt injection can spread attacks across multiple PRs and over time, creating a new attack surface not captured by single-shot monitors.

Method: Benchmark framework (Iterative VibeCoding) with two task families (CLI tools, Flask web services) across 20 task variations. Attack agent: Claude Sonnet 4.5; monitor: GPT-4o. Compare gradual attacks (distributed across PRs) versus non-gradual attacks (concentrated in one PR). Develop a stateful link-tracker monitor to detect buildup across PRs and evaluate a four-monitor ensemble including trajectory monitors. Test across multiple model backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5).

Result: High evasion (≥65%) for both attack styles; no single monitor blocks both strategies; evasion depends on monitor type. Stateful link-tracker detects gradual buildup much better than diff-history monitors. A four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% (diff monitor baseline) to 47%.

Conclusion: Persistent-state attack surfaces are a fundamental risk for iterative AI coding agents. Defenses require multi-monitor ensembles that include stateful trajectory monitoring; protecting against gradual attacks is feasible but relies on robust, history-aware monitoring.

Abstract: As AI coding agents become more autonomous, they increasingly ship code iteratively, with the codebase persisting across sessions. This persistence creates a new attack surface: a misaligned or prompt-injected agent can distribute attacks across pull requests (PRs) and time its payload for the PR with the best natural cover. To study the resulting dynamics, we introduce Iterative VibeCoding, a setting for AI control, the study of safely deploying capable but potentially untrusted AI. In Iterative VibeCoding, a coding agent builds software over a sequence of PRs in a persistent codebase while pursuing a covert side task. Our benchmark includes two task families: CLI tools and Flask web services, across 20 total task variations. We use Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the attack agent and GPT-4o as the monitor. We compare gradual attacks, which distribute the side task across PRs, against non-gradual attacks concentrated in a single PR. No single monitor is robust to both: which strategy evades best (success while evading the monitor) depends on the monitor type, so a defender cannot close off both gradual and non-gradual attacks with any one monitor. High evasion (>= 65%) generalizes across model attack agent backends (Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Kimi K2.5), confirming this is a property of the persistent-state attack surface rather than a single model's capability. Evasion also remains high across state-of-the-art monitor models and the gap between gradual and non-gradual evasion widens for more capable models. We introduce a stateful link-tracker monitor that tracks suspicious buildup across PRs. On both task families, it detects gradual attacks substantially better than diff monitors that merely see more accumulated history. Combining this stronger monitor with trajectory monitors in a four-monitor ensemble reduces gradual-attack evasion from 93% under the weakest standard diff monitor to 47%.

</details>

# cs.CG [[Back]](#toc)

### [353] [On Reconstructing a Convex Polygon from Partial Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01423)
*Alexander Baumann,Therese Biedl,Mahmoud Elashmawi,Simon D. Fink,Maria Saumell,André Schulz*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Systematically analyzes polygon reconstruction from one or two feature sets (edge lengths and/or angles), mapping known results, algorithms, hardness, and open problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand inverse reconstruction of convex polygons from limited data; unify disparate results; guide future research.

Method: Survey across all one- or two-feature scenarios; characterize algorithmic feasibility and hardness; develop testing algorithms where applicable; highlight open problems.

Result: A comprehensive taxonomy of reconstruction problems; identification of which cases admit algorithms, which are NP-hard or otherwise intractable, and a collection of open questions.

Conclusion: The paper provides a roadmap for future work and consolidates scattered results into a unified framework.

Abstract: The reconstruction problem asks to construct a (convex) polygon that has a specified set of features, such as an ordered set of edge-lengths or an ordered set of polygon-angles. In this paper, we do a systematic exploration of the reconstruction problem in all scenarios where one or two sets of features have been specified. Some of these scenarios were well-studied already, for some we develop testing-algorithms and/or hardness results, and many give rise to interesting open problems for future study.

</details>


### [354] [From Ham-Sandwich to Centerpoints: Semialgebraic Algorithms for Cutting Polytopal Measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02400)
*Marie-Charlotte Brandenburg,Jesús A. De Loera,Chiara Meroni*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: Cap-volume for polytopal measures is piecewise rational, enabling semialgebraic, exact algorithms for ham-sandwich and centerpoint; fixed-dimension poly-time; extends to center transversal; centerpoints align with the floating body at level 1/(d+1).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To obtain exact, computable cuts for polytopal measures and to unify ham-sandwich/centerpoint theory via semialgebraic geometry; connect centerpoints with floating bodies and semialgebraic descriptions.

Method: Analyze cap-volume function on oriented hyperplanes, show it is piecewise rational on a natural decomposition; recast prescribed-proportion cuts as semialgebraic feasibility problems; extend to deep affine flats; derive semialgebraic descriptions of centers via floating body.

Result: Polynomial-time algorithms in fixed dimension for existence, full solution set description, sampling/enumeration; semialgebraic characterizations of solution spaces; centerpoints coincide with the floating body at level 1/(d+1).

Conclusion: Provides a unifying semialgebraic framework for cutting problems and centerpoint theory, enabling exact computation in fixed dimension and extending to center transversal; links centerpoints with floating-body descriptions.

Abstract: We design exact algorithms for the ham-sandwich and centerpoint theorems for polytopal measures. Our key observation is that the cap-volume function of such a measure, i.e., the volume cut off by a halfspace, is piecewise rational on a natural decomposition of the space of oriented hyperplanes. This lets us recast prescribed-proportion cutting problems as semialgebraic feasibility problems. For fixed ambient dimension, this yields polynomial-time algorithms to decide the existence of cuts, describe the full solution set, and sample or enumerate solutions. We extend this framework to the center transversal theorem, showing that spaces of deep affine flats are semialgebraic, which holds for centerpoints. We further show that the set of centerpoints of a convex polytope coincides with its floating body at level $1/(d+1)$, a useful semialgebraic description.

</details>
